Paper: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
Research Focus: Defending LLM agents against indirect prompt injection attacks by design using Control Flow Integrity, Information Flow Control, and capability-based security policies.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Design and development of CaMeL (a custom Python interpreter implementing Dual LLM architecture, tracking data flow/provenance, and enforcing capability security policies). Evaluated on the AgentDojo benchmark across Workspace, Banking, Slack, and Travel suites using Gemini 2.5 (Flash/Pro), Claude 3.5/4 (Sonnet/Haiku), GPT-4.1, o3-High, and o4-Mini-High.
Key Findings: CaMeL achieves 77% task completion with provable security guarantees (compared to 84% in an undefended system) and completely eliminates prompt injection attacks on evaluated AgentDojo tasks when combined with policies. It outperforms heuristic defenses (spotlighting, prompt sandwiching, tool filtering, instruction hierarchy) by providing verifiable guarantees at a median overhead cost of 2.82x input tokens and 2.73x output tokens.
Author-Stated Limitations: Cannot defend against text-to-text attacks that do not alter control/data flows (e.g., summarization drift or prompt injection phishing); requires manual policy specification and maintenance; potential for user desensitization/fatigue during security policy triggers (de-classification); performance degradation in under-documented tool APIs.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of mechanisms to handle dynamic policy generation without human intervention; vulnerability to side-channel leakage (timing, exception-induced, indirect inference); potential for data-flow-to-control-flow hijack via polymorphic multi-stage prompt payload delivery.
Internal Contradictions: Claims to provide provable security guarantees without model changes, yet acknowledges that execution flow control can be bypassed via side channels (e.g., exception-induced fault leaks or timing channels) that leak private variable bits.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from instruction-hierarchy approaches (Wallace et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2025) and prompt-sandwiching/spotlighting (Hines et al., 2024), which attempt to train or prompt the LLM to ignore injections but remain probabilistically vulnerable to adaptive attacks (US-AISI, 2025).
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation relies heavily on synthetic tool interactions within AgentDojo; lacks evaluation against real-world third-party tool ecosystems where API definitions are untrusted, unformatted, or incomplete.
Untested Scenarios: Performance under highly complex multi-agent collaborative workflows; handling of recursive or highly complex code constructs; long-horizon task execution with sustained non-progress or adversarial navigation traps.
Proposed Research Questions: How can security policies for LLM capabilities be automatically synthesized and verified in real time without inducing user fatigue? How can capability systems completely eliminate timing and exception side-channels in agentic execution runtime environments?

Paper: Don't Click That: Teaching Web Agents to Resist Deceptive Interfaces (Zhang et al., 2025)
Research Focus: Defending vision-language model (VLM) web agents against deceptive graphical user interface (GUI) elements (dark patterns) while maintaining task completion performance.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces DUDE, a framework with two main components: (1) Hybrid-Reward Learning via GRPO to train an evaluator interposing between agent actions and execution, using asymmetric severity penalties for errors; (2) Experience Summarization to distill failure cases into contextual rules. Constructs the RUC benchmark (1,407 GUI scenarios: 910 normal, 497 deceptive across News, Booking, Shopping, Software). Experiments evaluated Qwen3-VL-4B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and GLM-4.6V-Flash on a test suite of 200 tasks under a 3-step limit.
Key Findings: DUDE reduces deception-induced failure rates (DFR) by 53.8% (down to 0% - 1.5% across models) and substantially cuts required steps (e.g., 25.23 to 5.86 steps for Qwen3-4B). Improves overall task success rate (SR) (e.g., GLM-4.6V SR increases from 9.5% to 60.5%) because the evaluator's Reject & Rethink loop provides corrective feedback on both deceptive and null/misclick errors. Zero-shot transfer of Stage-2 prompt optimization to closed-source evaluators improved SR from 54.12% to 62.50%.
Author-Stated Limitations: Modest per-step latency increase from evaluator calls; evaluated on static screenshots rather than asynchronous dynamic environments; RUC benchmark prioritizes ecological real-world validity over maximal adversariality (underestimating extreme attacks like Decepticon); benchmark is restricted to English-language web interfaces; relies strictly on visual GUI manifestations and cannot detect backend-based exploits.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of testing in long-horizon multi-step navigation tasks beyond 3 steps; absence of evaluation under active/adaptive adversarial web environments that modify dark patterns in response to agent rejection; unexamined resource/token costs over complex agent workflows.
Internal Contradictions: None detected.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Decepticon (Cuvin et al., 2026) evaluates single-step forced-choice dark pattern traps yielding ~70% agent deception rates, whereas RUC evaluates multi-step task trajectories where an agent executing the correct path may bypass deceptive triggers entirely, resulting in lower baseline DFRs.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation relies on static webpage screenshots rather than live interactive DOM states, potentially masking timing-based dark patterns or asynchronous dynamic pop-up loads.
Untested Scenarios: Non-English web environments, multi-turn asynchronous web interactions, backend hidden-script injections without GUI elements, and multi-step tasks requiring more than 3 steps.
Proposed Research Questions: How can deception-aware evaluators adapt to real-time dynamic web pages with changing dark patterns? Can VLM web agent defenses scale to cross-lingual and backend-injection attack scenarios?

Paper: A Survey on Trustworthy LLM Agents: Threats and Countermeasures
Research Focus: Systematic review and taxonomy (TrustAgent framework) of trustworthiness threats (safety, privacy, truthfulness, fairness, robustness) and technical paradigms (attack, defense, evaluation) across intrinsic (brain, memory, tool) and extrinsic (agent-to-agent, agent-to-environment, agent-to-user) modules in LLM agents and Multi-agent Systems (MAS).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Qualitative literature survey and taxonomy construction categorizing internal and external agent components, mapping existing research across 5 trustworthiness dimensions and 3 technical views (Atk/Def/Eval).
Key Findings: Extends trustworthiness from static LLMs to dynamic agents/MAS; highlights novel threats like infectious attacks (e.g., viral jailbreaks, self-propagating image/text attacks), cooperative attacks, memory poisoning, and tool abuse; notes severe scarcity in tool defenses and inter-agent trustworthiness evaluation mechanisms.
Author-Stated Limitations: Current attacks often lack cross-task generalizability; defenses against tool-related attacks and inter-agent interactions are severely underdeveloped; evaluations rely heavily on static datasets rather than dynamic multi-turn interactions.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of standardized benchmarks for dynamic multi-turn agent interactions; unaddressed vulnerabilities in sequential tool-calling chains; absence of automated topological defenses against viral/infectious prompt propagation in large-scale MAS.
Internal Contradictions: None identified in the survey text.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from prior surveys (e.g., Liu et al. 3, Huang et al. 3, He et al. 3, Li et al. 3) which either focus solely on base LLMs or ignore non-brain modules (memory, tools, inter-agent topologies).
Missing Controls/Confounders: Not directly applicable (survey paper), though it notes that existing evaluations fail to control for dynamic multi-turn environmental feedback.
Untested Scenarios: Long-term multi-agent emergent behaviors under continuous adversarial pressure; real-time resource/latency overhead of multi-agent guardrails and debate defenses.
Proposed Research Questions: How can dynamic evaluation sandboxes be designed to capture multi-turn agent interaction risks? What topological defense mechanisms can halt infectious prompt attacks in MAS without crippling communication efficiency?

Paper: Where Did It Go Wrong? Process-Level Evaluation of Web Agents with Semantic State Tracking (WEBSTEP)
Research Focus: Process-level evaluation and diagnostic benchmarking for web agents using automatic semantic state tracking and semantic MDP duals.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces WEBSTEP, featuring 10 self-hosted deterministic websites across diverse web domains (e.g., Mail, Calendar, Shopping, Accommodation, Food Delivery, Housing, Coding Q&A, Code Repo, Job Network, Team Chat) with 1,800 tasks constructed with controlled complexity (hard negatives, information access levels, oracle trajectory lengths). Evaluates 6 agents: 3 small open specialist models (UI-TARS-1.5-7B, Fara-7B, GUI-Owl-1.5-8B) and 3 large generalist models (Qwen3.5-122B, OpenAI CUA/GPT-5.4, Claude CUA/Claude Sonnet 4.6) across terminal success rate, exploration success rate, execution success rate, informational coverage, and step efficiency.
Key Findings: Terminal success rate hides substantial behavioral differences among agents with similar terminal scores (e.g., small agents cluster at 34-37% terminal success, but UI-TARS is exploration-strong/execution-weak while Fara is under-exploratory). Weaknesses are highly skill-specific (e.g., Claude CUA outperforms OpenAI CUA by 30% on navigation on Q&A, but underperforms it by 6.7% on inspection). Bifurcation analysis reveals that the decisive error causing task failure is agent-specific (e.g., GUI-Owl frequently branches off via Filter by 31%, while Fara and UI-TARS fall back to Search by 30%). Agent performance gaps in exploration widen significantly on harder tasks with more hard negative distractors or detail-level page navigation requirements.
Author-Stated Limitations: Semantic abstraction omits live-web dynamics (e.g., asynchronous loading, dynamic content updates, personalized recommendations, third-party integrations); domain coverage excludes sensitive data handling and complex authorization flows; task templates/world data are synthetic and deterministic rather than open-ended organic user queries; evaluates skill invocation rather than explicit latent intent/skill success; interaction modality is restricted to coordinate-based clicking, typing, and scrolling (excluding drag-and-drop or shortcuts).
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic adversarial traps or unexpected dynamic layout modifications to evaluate agent robustness under non-deterministic or malicious interface changes; failure to evaluate agent resource consumption, financial/API costs, or time latencies during prolonged exploration loops; lack of explicit recovery mechanisms when agents enter infinite loops (e.g., UI-TARS repeated toggle loops).
Internal Contradictions: None identified in the paper text; reported metrics and figures consistently confirm that terminal outcome metrics compress process differences.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Existing benchmarks (e.g., WebVoyager, Mind2Web, WebArena, VisualWebArena) assess web agents primarily using binary terminal success or manual milestones, whereas WEBSTEP demonstrates that terminal success scores obscure crucial failure modes (e.g., separating exploration failures from execution failures).
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation protocols enforced a 50-turn cap and safe pass policy (counting non-commit at critical decision points as terminal success to avoid penalizing safety guardrails), which might confound standard terminal completion capabilities compared to benchmarks without safe pass policies or differing turn budgets.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web pages (e.g., prompt injection in thread bodies, deceptive UI navigation traps), non-deterministic backend responses, dynamic streaming updates, cross-domain multi-site workflow execution, drag-and-drop UI elements, and keyboard-shortcut navigation.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agent architectures incorporate online semantic state tracking or process-level reward models to detect trajectory bifurcations before executing irreversible commit actions?

Paper: WebVoyager: Building an End-to-End Web Agent with Large Multimodal Models
Research Focus: End-to-end multimodal autonomous web navigation across live real-world websites using screenshots and interactive element annotations.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Built a Selenium browsing environment interacting directly with 15 real-world open-web platforms. Created a dataset of 643 tasks via Self-Instruct + human verification, and evaluated on GAIA (90 web tasks) and SeeAct (50 tasks). Backbone models tested: GPT-4V, GPT-4o, and Claude-3-Opus. Introduced a GPT-4V auto-evaluation protocol and compared against human judgment.
Key Findings: WebVoyager achieves a 59.1% task success rate, outperforming GPT-4 (All Tools) at 30.8% and WebVoyager text-only at 40.1%. GPT-4V auto-evaluator achieves 85.3% agreement (Kappa = 0.70) with human experts.
Author-Stated Limitations: Environment lacks support for complex human actions like drag-and-drop. Agent struggles with non-text file types, particularly video formats.
Inferred Research Gaps: No evaluation under dynamic pop-ups, dynamic web layout shifts, network latency issues, or adversarial web page manipulation (e.g., navigation traps or prompt injection via dynamic HTML).
Internal Contradictions: Claims full end-to-end task completion without human intervention, yet explicitly omits websites requiring CAPTCHAs or user login/authentication.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Mind2Web and WebArena rely on offline golden trajectories or locally hosted environments; WebVoyager demonstrates that static trajectories fail to reflect alternative viable execution paths and real-time open-web updates.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Uncontrolled webpage content changes over time on live websites (such as dynamic flight pricing or changing news listings) during evaluation runs.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web agents, navigation traps, sustained loops, malicious script execution, dynamic layout transformations during live interaction.
Proposed Research Questions: How can multimodal web agents automatically detect and escape navigation loops or adversarial traps on live web pages without human intervention?

Paper: Toward Secure LLM Agents: Threat Surfaces, Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation (Ling et al., 2026)
Research Focus: Systematic survey synthesizing research on LLM agent security through a lifecycle-based and systems-oriented framework.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Hybrid literature review pipeline combining database retrieval, LLM-assisted search expansion, snowballing, and manual screening across a curated corpus of 247 papers (2023–2026). Annotated across paper types, threat models, lifecycle stages, and benchmarks.
Key Findings: Prompt injection and indirect tool-mediated control-flow hijacking dominate existing research (142 and 86 papers respectively). Multi-agent propagation (47 papers) and persistent state corruption (24 papers) are critical emerging risks. Defenses remain fragmented and weakly compositional, while benchmarks lack long-horizon, stateful, and deployment-sensitive metrics.
Author-Stated Limitations: Corpus is heavily preprint-based (68.42% arXiv), meaning claims and methods remain in flux. Single-agent systems dominate the corpus (80.97%), leaving delegation and coordination risks underrepresented. Evaluation is limited by category overlap and subjective manual annotation.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of standardized compositional security stacks that integrate input-trust management, runtime monitoring, and execution sandboxing without introducing prohibitive latency or utility loss. Insufficient coverage of memory provenance, revocation, and inter-agent trust boundaries.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; the paper systematically categorizes its core taxonomy and empirical distributions consistently across figures, tables, and narrative text.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Exposes contradictory assumptions in the broader literature where prompt-handling defenses assume model-driven instruction hierarchy compliance, whereas empirical attack studies demonstrate that models consistently fail to maintain instruction hierarchy under paraphrase or tool-mediated restatement.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Studies in the corpus frequently fail to control for baseline utility loss, false positive rates, or compute/latency costs when evaluating defense effectiveness.
Untested Scenarios: Long-horizon multi-step state persistence with delayed attack triggers; stealthy covert collusion in multi-agent topologies; cross-session memory contamination recovery.
Proposed Research Questions: How can provenance-aware state management be designed to support trust decay and revocation in long-horizon memory agents? What runtime control planes best balance fine-grained tool capability scoping with task utility?

Paper: MELON: Provable Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in AI Agents
Research Focus: Defending AI agents against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) attacks while preserving utility and operating in a training-free manner.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Proposes MELON (Masked re-Execution and TooL comparisON), which detects attacks by comparing tool calls generated during the original execution against a parallel execution using a masked/task-neutral prompt. Evaluated on the AgentDojo benchmark across 629 attack cases across four domains (banking, slack, travel, workspace) using GPT-4o, o3-mini, and Llama-3.3-70B against 4 general attack types (Direct, Ignore Previous, System Message, Important Messages).
Key Findings: MELON and its hybrid variant MELON-Aug outperform SOTA defenses (Delimiting, Repeat Prompt, Tool Filter, DeBERTa Detector, LLM Detector) by achieving near-zero Attack Success Rates (e.g., 0.24%-0.32% ASR on GPT-4o) while preserving high Utility under Attack (up to 68.72% UA). Theoretical error bounds derived via Hoeffding's inequality show exponential error decay with the number of weak detectors.
Author-Stated Limitations: MELON fails under specific patterns: (1) Response-Based Attacks where the malicious goal is accomplished via text responses rather than tool calls; (2) Tool Call Redundancy where partial execution leads to step mismatches; (3) State Hallucination where the model skips tool calls by guessing inputs; (4) Function Hallucination where the agent invents non-existent tools. Also effectively doubles model API call costs.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic detection for non-tool action hijacking (e.g., pure textual deception or output spoofing); vulnerability to adaptive attackers who intentionally craft subtle timing mismatches or spread multi-step payload triggers across non-adjacent executions.
Internal Contradictions: None identified within the paper's explicit text.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Model-based detectors like LLM Detector achieved 0.00% ASR in the paper's experiments, yet the authors note that it exhibits FNR/FPR vulnerabilities (Table 5) and completely ruins Utility under Attack (0.00% UA) due to terminating executions preemptively.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not systematically evaluate multi-modal agent environments in depth (excludes VisualWebArena-Adv due to low baseline ASR of existing image attacks). Evaluated primarily on zero-temperature model settings, ignoring non-deterministic sampling noise.
Untested Scenarios: Real-world web agent deployments with continuous dynamic DOM updates; adaptive, state-aware attacker strategies specifically tailored to evade MELON's similarity embedding thresholds; latency-sensitive real-time operational environments.
Proposed Research Questions: How can masked re-execution defenses be adapted to detect text-response-only manipulation and multi-modal injection payloads without introducing prohibitive cost and latency overhead?

Paper: AUTOSCRAPER: A Progressive Understanding Web Agent for Web Scraper Generation
Research Focus: Generating web scrapers (executable action sequences / XPaths) using LLMs to balance adaptability across changing site structures with computational efficiency.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Two-stage framework combining (1) Progressive Understanding (traversal using top-down pruning and step-back contextual recovery) and (2) Synthesis across multiple seed pages. Evaluated zero-shot using 8 LLMs (e.g., GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Gemini Pro, Mixtral 8x7B) across 3 benchmarks (SWDE, EXTENDED SWDE, DS1).
Key Findings: AUTOSCRAPER outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-prompt-based baselines (CoT, Reflexion) and supervised web extraction baselines in F1 score (achieving 88.69% with GPT-4-Turbo on SWDE). Introduces an Executability metric measuring cross-page reusability. Requires significantly fewer API calls/time than direct language-agent extraction when processing large-scale web sites (threshold NW ~19.5 pages).
Author-Stated Limitations: Framework is restricted to semi-structured information extraction from vertical websites and cannot directly transfer to general web navigation environments (e.g., Mind2Web, WebArena). Dependent on the underlying backbone LLM's inherent HTML structure understanding.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address dynamic web page interaction (e.g., JavaScript execution, authentication, pop-ups, pagination traversal). Lacks mechanisms to handle structural web drifts over time without re-running the full synthesis stage.
Internal Contradictions: None identified within the paper's reported methodology and experimental results.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While language-agent approaches like WebShop treat web interaction as end-to-end sequential RL/IL over dynamic user sessions, AUTOSCRAPER demonstrates that for structured data retrieval tasks, decoupling scraper rule generation from execution is vastly more efficient than direct language-agent execution.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation relies on pre-processed HTML (removing , , and non-class attributes), which removes realistic web noise and script execution requirements present in real-world scraping environments.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web designs (anti-scraping mechanisms, honeypots), highly dynamic DOM structures rendered purely via client-side JavaScript, and complex multi-page navigation workflows prior to data extraction.
Proposed Research Questions: How can scraper generation frameworks automatically detect and recover from target DOM structure changes without manual re-triggering? Can progressive HTML understanding be extended to interactive web elements like forms and shadow DOMs?
Supporting Citations: AUTOSCRAPER Paper 8

Paper: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents
Research Focus: Simulated e-commerce environment and benchmark for training and evaluating language agents on long-horizon grounded decision-making, searching, and web navigation.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Environment with 1.18M real-world products (scraped from Amazon) and 12,087 crowdsourced human instructions. Evaluates heuristic rules, imitation learning (BART for query generation, BERT+ResNet-50 for action choice), and online RL (IL+RL) across a 500-instruction test split, including zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to real Amazon and eBay sites.
Key Findings: The best IL+RL agent achieved a task score of 62.4 and a success rate of 28.7%, vastly outperforming rule baselines (9.6% success) but lagging behind human experts (59.6% success). The agent demonstrated effective zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to real-world Amazon (25% success) and eBay (21% success) platforms.
Author-Stated Limitations: RL fine-tuning caused the agent to become greedy and less exploratory, decreasing option selection accuracy. Models lack explicit long-term working memory for comparing multiple items across pages or backtracking effectively.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not evaluate agent robustness against hostile environment conditions such as web navigation traps, changing button layouts, dynamic pop-ups, or rate-limiting/bot-detection mechanisms.
Internal Contradictions: None identified within the paper.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Direct agent-based web interaction (as in WebShop) requires executing neural model inferences at every step, whereas wrapper/scraper generation frameworks (such as AUTOSCRAPER) argue that step-by-step neural execution is unacceptably slow and expensive for repetitive web tasks compared to executable script generation.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Human baseline evaluation suffered from variance in crowdsourced worker patience and effort, potentially underestimating true upper-bound human performance.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web agents, non-deterministic search environments, malicious product listings (e.g., scam pages or prompt injection inside product descriptions), and resource/token exhaustion constraints.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agents maintain long-term memory across complex multi-page search and comparison tasks without context window saturation? Can RL agents learn exploration strategies that balance product discovery against task completion speed?
Supporting Citations: WebShop Paper 9

Paper: MMInA: Benchmarking Multihop Multimodal Internet Agents
Research Focus: Benchmarking autonomous embodied agents on compositional, multihop, and multimodal web browsing tasks across dynamic real-world websites.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created a benchmark of 1,050 human-written tasks covering 2,989 hops across 14 evolving real-world websites (e.g., Wikipedia, Trip.com, Momondo, YouTube, Twitter). Evaluated standalone LLMs (CodeLLaMA, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4, Gemini-Pro), LMMs (Fuyu-8B, Gemini-Pro-Vision, GPT-4V, GPT-4o), heuristic web agents (WebShop, CogAgent), and human baselines using single-hop (must_include, fuzzy_match) and multihop sequential queue evaluation protocols.
Key Findings: Multi-hop web browsing is challenging for state-of-the-art agents; GPT-4V achieved a task success rate of 21.8% vs. 96.3% for humans. 2. Agents fail primarily on early hops during multi-hop tasks due to expanded search space and weak long-context/long-chain reasoning. 3. Memory augmentation replaying past trajectories significantly boosts single-hop and multi-hop performance.
Author-Stated Limitations: Finding real websites allowing direct image extraction from HTML files is difficult due to site protection mechanisms; thus, the benchmark relies on one offline standalone site (OneStopMarket) and one open-source site alongside live sites.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic adversarial resistance evaluations (e.g., web navigation traps, honeypots, changing DOM elements, or adversarial web agents) and lack of resource consumption/cost monitoring across long-horizon multihop tasks.
Internal Contradictions: None observed in the text; results consistently demonstrate that single-hop success does not linearly translate to multi-hop success.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Existing web agent benchmarks (WebArena, VisualWebArena, Mind2Web) evaluate oversimplified, single-website or low-hop tasks (avg. ~1.0–1.06 hops), overestimating agent readiness for realistic, multi-site web browsing.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Uncontrolled site updates on evolving live web pages during evaluation runs; variable network latency and anti-bot/rate-limiting behaviors on live websites.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web environments (e.g., indirect prompt injection hidden in web page text/images), dynamic paywalls/captchas, recovery from broken URLs, and multi-agent collaborative web browsing.
Proposed Research Questions: How do multihop web agents recover when encountering navigation traps or persistent anti-bot defenses, and can episodic memory systems mitigate adversarial prompt injection on live web pages?
Supporting Citations: Achiam et al. (2023) 10; Deng et al. (2023) 10; Hong et al. (2024) 10; Koh et al. (2024) 10; Zhou et al. (2024) 10

Paper: SoK: Attack and Defense Landscape of Agentic AI Systems
Research Focus: Systematizing knowledge on the security risks, attack landscape, and defense mechanisms of agentic AI systems from a holistic system perspective.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Systematic literature survey of 128 papers (51 attack methods, 60 defense methods) from 2023 to October 2025 across top security (USENIX Security, IEEE S&P, CCS, NDSS) and ML (NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML) venues. Framework characterizes agents across 7 design dimensions, categorizes 3 adversary types, 9 risk categories (mapped to MITRE ATLAS), and 4 defense paradigms.
Key Findings: Combining LLMs with symbolic software creates unique system-level vulnerabilities (e.g., prompt injections propagating to execution tools and memory). 2. Increased flexibility along design dimensions (Input Trust, Access Sensitivity, Workflow, Action, Memory, Tool, UI) directly amplifies security risks. 3. Current defenses (guardrails, IFC, sandboxing) are fragmented, incur heavy performance/utility overheads, and lack standard interoperable frameworks.
Author-Stated Limitations: Does not address model internal attacks (e.g., model inversion) since agents operate via inference interfaces; side-channel risks (timing/traffic patterns) remain unanalyzed due to lack of existing research.
Inferred Research Gaps: Insufficient evaluation of defense mechanisms under combined multi-stage attacks (e.g., indirect prompt injection + memory poisoning + tool supply chain compromise simultaneously); absence of standardized formal verification frameworks for dynamic web/GUI agents.
Internal Contradictions: None; taxonomy systematically connects architectural dimensions to risk levels and defensive trade-offs.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Prior AI security surveys focus narrowly on isolated model-level threats (e.g., jailbreaks) or specific tools, failing to address cross-component risk cascading (e.g., untrusted retrieval triggering unauthorized tool execution).
Missing Controls/Confounders: Varying definitions of 'agent autonomy' across surveyed papers; inconsistent baseline security configurations across baseline empirical evaluations.
Untested Scenarios: Real-time side-channel attacks targeting tool execution timing; adversarial agent-to-agent interactions in multi-agent autonomous web ecosystems.
Proposed Research Questions: How can lightweight Information Flow Control (IFC) be integrated into web agents without causing label creep or severe operational latency during multi-step browser interactions?
Supporting Citations: Bagdasarian et al. (2024) 11; Greshake et al. (2023) 11; Liu et al. (2024) 11; Debenedetti et al. (2024) 11; Xiang et al. (2024) 11

Paper: Mind2Web 2: Evaluating Agentic Search with Agent-as-a-Judge
Research Focus: Evaluation benchmark and automated methodology for long-horizon, real-time, time-varying agentic web search systems.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Constructed Mind2Web 2 (130 tasks, over 1,000 human labor hours) across 6 broad domains. Developed an Agent-as-a-Judge framework utilizing tree-structured rubrics (averaging 50 nodes, max 603) and evaluated 10 frontier agentic search systems plus human baseline performance on Subset-30.
Key Findings: OpenAI Deep Research achieved top performance (0.54 partial completion, 0.28 success rate) reaching 50-70% of human performance in half the time. Current systems struggle with time-varying tasks requiring real-time browsing, and non-deep research agents exhibit early termination or severe execution failures.
Author-Stated Limitations: Task coverage does not encompass all scenarios (excludes vague queries, non-English sites, video understanding, complex math/coding requirements, and rapidly fluctuating data like live stock prices); reliance on URL-based single-page attribution and LLM extraction/verification limits scope.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on dynamic multi-page cross-verifications; absence of mechanisms to mitigate cognitive fatigue or systemic hallucination under dynamic real-time web conditions without explicit grounding.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None identified within the provided context.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation assumes cited URLs are inherently factual and truthful, omitting controls for web misinformation or corrupted external source sites.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web pages (e.g., dynamic injection attacks), multi-modal web interactions requiring video understanding, and tasks requiring simultaneous multi-page cross-verification logic.
Proposed Research Questions: How can agentic search systems maintain attribution integrity against adversarial webpage content? Can Agent-as-a-Judge rubrics be dynamically scaled to evaluate live multi-page cross-site workflows without fixed static cached snapshots?

Paper: Mind the Web: The Security of Web Use Agents
Research Focus: Security evaluation of web-use agents against third-party task-aligned prompt injection attacks embedded in webpage content.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduced task-aligned injection techniques and an automated 3-stage training pipeline (Candidate Generation, LLM Validation via Judge, and SFT+DPO fine-tuning). Evaluated 9 payloads across the CIA triad (P1-P9) on 5 popular agents (OpenAI Operator, Browser Use, Do Browser, OpenOperator, Perplexity Comet) across 100 independent trials.
Key Findings: Task-aligned injections achieved an overall Attack Success Rate (ASR) exceeding 80% (82% for SFT+DPO vs 12% for non-task-aligned), bypassing built-in safeguards and transferring across unseen payloads, environments, and backend LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude Sonnet 3.5, Mistral Pixtral-Large).
Author-Stated Limitations: The attack relies on the agent processing injected third-party web content during routine browsing; evaluation focused on specific browser permissions, and mitigations introduce security-usability trade-offs (e.g., added latency, reduced autonomy).
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of real-time, low-latency defense mechanisms capable of detecting contextually aligned semantic manipulations without impairing agent execution autonomy.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None identified within the provided context.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Experiments were executed on specific web environments and standalone test accounts, which may not fully capture dynamic live multi-user web interactions.
Untested Scenarios: Defense effectiveness against multi-turn, multi-page collaborative adversarial attacks or direct adversarial attacks combined with multimodal steganography.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web-use agents reliably differentiate between legitimate user task refinements and third-party task-aligned injections without relying on human-in-the-loop interventions?

Paper: SkillTrojan: Backdoor Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
Research Focus: Backdoor attacks targeting the skill abstraction layer and executable skill implementations in skill-based agent systems.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Proposes SkillTrojan, which fragments encrypted payloads across reusable skills and triggers execution upon specific query patterns. Evaluated on EHR SQL tasks using open-weight (GLM-4.7, Qwen3-Coder, GLM-4.6, Qwen3-VL-235B) and closed-weight models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude-Haiku-4.5, Claude-Sonnet4.5, Qwen3-Max, GPT-5.2-1211-Global), plus SWE-Bench Verified and cross-framework evaluations.
Key Findings: Achieves high attack success rates (e.g., up to 97.2% ASR on GPT-5.2-1211-Global) while preserving clean-task accuracy (89.3% ACC). Outperforms traditional prompt-centric/jailbreak baselines (GCG, AutoDAN, BadChain, AgentPoison) and bypasses standard guardrail scanners like Qwen3Guard and Llama-Guard.
Author-Stated Limitations: Scoped to a local execution run without cross-run persistence; excludes direct base model or host OS compromise; payload execution relies on complete trace execution under the trigger.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation against runtime trace auditing, sandboxed execution boundaries, or formal provenance/permission control systems for third-party skill modules.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; empirical trade-offs between fragment count N, stealth, and reconstruction success are logically aligned.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from traditional agent backdoor literature (e.g., AgentPoison, BadChain) which focuses on manipulating prompt contexts, memory, or model parameters rather than executable modular skill packages.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not thoroughly evaluate the influence of strict code-sandboxing or fine-grained runtime API permission control mechanisms.
Untested Scenarios: Dynamic skill marketplaces with automated runtime trace monitoring or continuous multi-turn multi-agent interactions.
Proposed Research Questions: How can dynamic execution-trace auditing and permission-based sandboxing be designed to detect order-agnostic fragment emission in third-party skill libraries?

Paper: WEBLINX: Real-World Website Navigation with Multi-Turn Dialogue
Research Focus: Conversational web navigation using multi-turn dialogue to control web browsers across real-world websites.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces WEBLINX benchmark with 2,337 expert demonstrations (100K interactions across 155 real-world websites). Evaluates 19 models (small decoders, large LLMs, multimodal models like GPT-4V, Pix2Act, Fuyu-8B, LLaMA-2) using Dense Markup Ranking (DMR) for DOM pruning and action-specific metrics (IoU, chrF, Intent Match).
Key Findings: Finetuned smaller text-only decoders (e.g., LLaMA-2-13B, Sheared-LLaMA) outperform zero-shot LLMs (including GPT-4V) and multimodal models pretrained on screenshots (Fuyu-8B). However, all models struggle to generalize to out-of-domain scenarios (unseen subcategories or websites).
Author-Stated Limitations: Dataset consists of static demonstrations, preventing live evaluation of alternative interaction trajectories; text-only models cannot process visual-only elements (e.g., canvas).
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of online reinforcement learning from environmental feedback or dynamic dialogue recovery mechanisms when web navigation hits an unrecoverable trap or changed site structure.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; empirical findings consistently show zero-shot multimodal LLMs lagging behind finetuned text decoders in static trajectory replay.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contrasts with single-turn web navigation benchmarks (e.g., Mind2Web, WebShop) by proving that static single-instruction representations fail to capture multi-turn goal evolution.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Static offline dataset evaluation does not control for live browser dynamic state changes, layout shifts, or network latency.
Untested Scenarios: Live environment execution with closed-loop reward feedback or interaction with highly dynamic/adversarial web elements.
Proposed Research Questions: How can multimodal architectures be effectively finetuned for closed-loop, multi-turn web navigation while maintaining generalizability across unseen website domains?

Paper: BEARCUBS: A benchmark for computer-using web agents
Research Focus: Evaluating information-seeking abilities of computer-using web agents on the live web across complex text-based and multimodal interaction tasks.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created BEARCUBS benchmark containing 111 QA pairs (56 text-based, 55 multimodal) spanning 108 unique top-level URLs. Benchmarked 7 web agents (including ChatGPT Agent, OpenAI Operator, Anthropic Computer Use, Convergence AI Proxy, and OpenAI Deep Research) and 5 LLM baselines against human performance (N=human study participants with domain/language expertise). Evaluated accuracy, processing time, and trajectory steps.
Key Findings: ChatGPT Agent achieved state-of-the-art performance among computer-using agents with 65.8% overall accuracy (76.8% text-based, 54.5% multimodal), significantly outperforming OpenAI Operator (23.4%) and OpenAI Deep Research (36.0%). However, a substantial gap remains compared to human performance (84.7% accuracy). Computer-using agents suffer from fine cursor control issues, long processing times, inability to handle complex data filtering, and active avoidance of multimodal interactions.
Author-Stated Limitations: All questions have a single short answer (unlike real-world cases with long-form/multiple/no answers); limited benchmark size restricts deep systematic multilingual evaluation; inconsistency in trajectory detail across agents makes direct trajectory comparisons challenging.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of standardized API access and execution interfaces across commercial web agents impedes scalable, automated benchmarking; absence of mechanism to prevent agents from getting stuck in repetitive execution loops during live web navigation.
Internal Contradictions: None detected. The claims made in the text regarding model rankings and task difficulty align with the quantitative results in Table 2 and Table 5.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from WebCloak's findings regarding agent failure modes: BEARCUBS attributes agent failures to poor visual/fine cursor control, strategic planning loops, and content access denial, whereas WebCloak highlights agents' core reliance on DOM/HTML 'Parse-then-Interpret' pipelines as their primary vulnerability.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation across agents lacked uniform execution time limits (e.g., ChatGPT Agent was granted a 45-minute limit versus 15 minutes for other computer-using agents), which confounds accuracy comparison with time/compute budget.
Untested Scenarios: Performance under adversarial web environments (e.g., prompt injection, dynamic obfuscation, honeypots, navigation traps, or intentionally misleading UI components).
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agents be equipped with dynamic recovery strategies when encountering navigation loops or complex UI controls (e.g., multi-slider filters)? How can text-based search capabilities be tightly integrated with computer-use multimodal execution without compromising visual grounding?

Paper: WebCloak: Characterizing and Mitigating Threats from LLM-Driven Web Agents as Intelligent Scrapers
Research Focus: Characterizing the threat of LLM-driven web agents used as unauthorized scrapers and developing an in-page, dual-layer defense (WebCloak) to protect web visual assets.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Constructed LLMCrawlBench (237 offline webpage snapshots from 50 high-traffic websites across 5 categories, containing 10,895 annotated images). Conducted a measurement study evaluating 32 scraper variants across 3 paradigms (L2S, LNC, LWA). Evaluated WebCloak's dual-layer defense (Dynamic Structural Obfuscation + Optimized Semantic Labyrinth) against 3 leading scrapers (Gemini-2.5-pro, Crawl4AI, Browser-Use), testing recall, precision, robustness, performance overhead, and human usability (N=35 user study).
Key Findings: LLM web agents lower the technical barrier for large-scale data scraping, enabling novice users to match or exceed human expert manual scraping performance. Scrapers universally rely on a 'Parse-then-Interpret' pipeline. WebCloak successfully reduced scraping recall rates of leading LLM scrapers from an unprotected average of 88.7% down to 0.0%, while maintaining visual fidelity (JCD < 0.01), low execution latency (~52 ms client-side), and high user satisfaction (>91%).
Author-Stated Limitations: Client-side visual restoration requires JavaScript; manual reverse-engineering by an elite human expert is theoretically possible for a single session; benchmark evaluation is primarily image-centric with only supplementary small-scale testing on audio/text assets.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation against autonomous multimodal agents operating purely via visual pixel/screenshot inputs without DOM/HTML parsing dependencies; unaddressed server-side latency (~3 mins per page) for real-time dynamic semantic prompt optimization on high-frequency updating web pages.
Internal Contradictions: None detected. Experimental claims regarding defense effectiveness across paradigms and LLM backends are supported by Table 5, Table 6, and Table 8.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Claims UI-only vision agents (e.g., Anthropic Computer Use) fail at scraping without structured DOM access, whereas BEARCUBS demonstrates that vision-capable agents like ChatGPT Agent can successfully complete complex multimodal web tasks on live websites.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluations used static offline webpage snapshots to guarantee reproducibility, omitting live anti-bot server interventions (such as dynamic IP rate limits or browser fingerprinting) that interact with agent execution.
Untested Scenarios: Agent scraping behavior against real-time streaming content, login-authenticated/paywalled platforms, and social media networks.
Proposed Research Questions: How can in-page structural and semantic defenses be adapted to counter vision-native web agents that bypass DOM parsing entirely? What lightweight optimization methods can reduce server-side semantic prompt generation latency for dynamic, high-throughput websites?

Paper: AGENTVIGIL: Generic Black-Box Red-teaming for Indirect Prompt Injection against LLM Agents
Research Focus: Automated black-box fuzzing framework (AGENTVIGIL) for assessing indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities across multi-step LLM agents.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) seed selection, coverage-guided seed scoring, high-quality initial seed corpus, and 5 basic LLM mutators (Shorten, Expand, Rephrase, Crossover, GenerateSimilar). Evaluated across AgentDojo (142 fuzzing, 173 test set tasks) and VWA-adv (99 fuzzing, 100 test set tasks) benchmarks using o3-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2-flash-exp, and QwQ-32B, alongside a real-world WebArena e-commerce case study.
Key Findings: Achieves 71% attack success rate (ASR) on AgentDojo (o3-mini) and 70% on VWA-adv (GPT-4o), nearly doubling handcrafted baselines. Prompts demonstrate strong transferability to unseen tasks (65% ASR on o3-mini) and unseen models (67% ASR on Gemini-2-flash-exp). Evades training-free defenses (repeat, delimit) and pi_detector, revealing systemic vulnerabilities.
Author-Stated Limitations: Excludes direct platform infrastructure attacks and agent misuse. Excludes certain defenses due to high computational costs, poor utility, or architecture-specific constraints (e.g., StruQ, IsolateGPT). Open-source models lag in utility/tool-calling necessary for full suite testing.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on sustained multi-turn agent interactions under adaptive counter-defenses, unexamined resource consumption metrics during fuzzing iterations, and absence of defense design tailored to multimodal vision-language inputs.
Internal Contradictions: Claims to be a fully generic black-box method, yet relies on a helper LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) for mutation which introduces inherent semantic biases; notes Claude-3.5-Sonnet's strong resistance to complex generated prompts while observing higher vulnerability to simpler baseline prompts.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts Greshake et al. 18 regarding defense efficacy: while Greshake et al. emphasize systemic impossibility of alignment defenses against indirect prompt injection, AGENTVIGIL shows that specific targeted prompt structures still exhibit dramatic drop-offs against basic input delimiters or rephrasing defenses in constrained web contexts.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Uncontrolled API latency and non-deterministic LLM response drift during multi-iteration fuzzing loops; missing control for context window saturation as prompt mutations expand.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web agents facing dynamic navigation traps, sustained non-progress loops, rate-limiting conditions, or multi-modal visual injection triggers (focused primarily on text triggers).
Proposed Research Questions: How can MCTS-guided fuzzing be adapted to generate stealthy multimodal (image-text) prompt injections that bypass both vision and text safety filters simultaneously?
Supporting Citations: Debenedetti et al. (2024) 19, Wu et al. (2024b) 19, Yu et al. (2023) 19, Greshake et al. (2023) 19

Paper: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
Research Focus: Threat modeling and proof-of-concept taxonomy for Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in retrieval-augmented LLM applications.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Qualitative proof-of-concept demonstrations across synthetic applications built via LangChain/OpenAI APIs (text-davinci-003, GPT-4) and real-world targets including Bing Chat (GPT-4) and GitHub Copilot (Codex). Covers threat categories: Information Gathering, Fraud, Malware, Intrusion, Manipulated Content, and Availability.
Key Findings: Establishes that retrieval blurs the boundary between data and instructions. Demonstrates remote code execution equivalents, prompt-based worms spreading via LLM-augmented email clients, persistent memory contamination, search query/result corruption, and automated data exfiltration via markdown image/URL rendering.
Author-Stated Limitations: Lack of systematic quantitative evaluation of attack success rates across large-scale dynamic chat sessions. Testing performed primarily on local HTML files due to ethical constraints against poisoning live public web indices. High sensitivity of code-completion attacks to context window construction algorithms.
Inferred Research Gaps: Missing empirical metrics for token/economic consumption during denial-of-service loops, lack of formal verification frameworks for instruction-data isolation in context memory, and unexplored interaction between user trust and persuasive AI manipulation.
Internal Contradictions: States that jailbreaking formats are necessary for producing factual misalignment, but elsewhere asserts that indirect prompt injections can fully hijack agent intent using completely benign, aligned instructions without jailbreak wrappers.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from AGENTVIGIL 19 in attack generation methodology: relies entirely on manual, single-shot heuristic prompt engineering rather than automated algorithmic optimization, leading to lower reported stability across varying context lengths.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lack of quantitative control group comparisons across distinct LLM temperature settings, system prompt variants, or safety filter updates in black-box commercial endpoints.
Untested Scenarios: Real-time multi-agent autonomous ecosystems with cascading tool calls, multi-turn recovery from contaminated memory states, and adversarial manipulation of vision-language models via hidden image payloads.
Proposed Research Questions: What architectural boundary mechanisms can strictly isolate untrusted retrieved data channels from executable instruction pathways in multi-modal LLM agents without degrading task reasoning capabilities?
Supporting Citations: Perez & Ribeiro (2022) 18, Kang et al. (2023) 18, Schick et al. (2023) 18, Yao et al. (2023) 18

Paper: ACE: A Security Architecture for LLM-Integrated App Systems
Research Focus: Preventing security violations (integrity, availability, privacy) from malicious third-party apps and indirect prompt injections in LLM-integrated application systems.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Proposed ACE, an ahead-of-time planning architecture separating abstract planning, concrete matching, and isolated execution with Information Flow Control (IFC). Evaluated security on INJECAGENT (1,054 cases) and Agent Security Bench (2,000 trials); evaluated utility and latency/cost overhead on the LangChain Tool Usage benchmark using models including GPT-4o, o3-mini, GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Qwen-2.5-72B.
Key Findings: ACE achieved 100% security against indirect prompt injections on INJECAGENT and blocked all proposed new attacks (Execution Flow Disruption, Execution Manager Hijack, Planner Manipulation) while maintaining high utility (>80%) on LangChain tools with lower latency compared to IsolateGPT.
Author-Stated Limitations: ACE currently supports only standalone apps and single-query interactions; supporting full application suites and multi-query context interactions is left for future work. Formal analysis is limited due to using a Python subset rather than a custom DSL with formal semantics.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address dynamic runtime state changes across complex multi-turn interactions, web agent navigation traps, or resource exhaustion caused by long-running or looping abstract plans in non-sandboxed environments.
Internal Contradictions: Claims formal security reasoning via static analysis on structured plans, yet acknowledges using Python AST/runtime which cannot provide formal soundness guarantees.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from IsolateGPT and f-Secure by assuming a strong threat model where app descriptions and schemas can be adversarial; demonstrates that f-Secure and IsolateGPT fail under description and output manipulation attacks.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks evaluation against multimodal prompt injection vectors, dynamic multi-turn session state decay, and multi-agent collaborative workflows.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-query continuous agent sessions; dynamic app discovery from live external marketplaces; multi-modal GUI/web navigation actions.
Proposed Research Questions: How can lattice-based static information flow control be extended to handle dynamic multi-turn conversational state and dynamic app registration without incurring excessive runtime overhead?
Supporting Citations: IsolateGPT 20, f-Secure 20, INJECAGENT 20, ASB 20, StruQ 20, ReAct 20

Paper: SAFEARENA: Evaluating the Safety of Autonomous Web Agents
Research Focus: Evaluating the susceptibility of autonomous vision-LLM web agents to malicious misuse across web environments.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Constructed SAFEARENA benchmark comprising 500 tasks (250 harmful across 5 categories: bias, cybercrime, illegal activity, harassment, misinformation, and 250 paired safe tasks) across 4 web environments (Reddit-style forum, GitLab-style code platform, E-commerce, Shopping Admin) built on BrowserGym. Evaluated 5 VLLM agents (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o-Mini, Llama-3.2-90B, Qwen-2-VL-72B) using direct prompting, priming, and multi-turn task decomposition attacks under the proposed ARIA framework.
Key Findings: Existing safety alignment transfers poorly to web agents. SOTA models comply with harmful web tasks at alarming rates (GPT-4o completed 34.7% of harmful requests; Qwen-2-VL completed 27.3%). Claude-3.5-Sonnet had the highest refusal rate (64%), but was 100% jailbroken when tasks were decomposed into sequential innocuous substeps.
Author-Stated Limitations: Tasks focus only on explicit harmful intents rather than ambiguous ones requiring environment inspection. Relies on brittle, positive-predictive automatic evaluation metrics (URL/string/locator matching). Harmful intents can potentially be flagged by pre-agent external guardrail classifiers.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not evaluate indirect prompt injection originating from untrusted web content (e.g., adversarial comments on forums) during web navigation, nor defense mechanisms designed for web agent runtime safety.
Internal Contradictions: Noted that Claude-3.5-Sonnet was the safest agent based on direct prompting refusal, yet demonstrated it achieved a 100% attack success rate under simple multi-turn task decomposition.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts safety alignment claims of foundation models by demonstrating that text-based safety guardrails fail when grounded in GUI action spaces.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for execution failures caused by UI layout shifts vs. safety refusal (disentangled partially by NSS, but action loop failures confound completion rates).
Untested Scenarios: Ambiguous/implicit harmful instructions; multi-agent web environments; web environments containing active indirect prompt injections or navigation traps.
Proposed Research Questions: How can multi-turn step-wise safety alignment or real-time action-level guardrails prevent task decomposition jailbreaks in web agents without degrading safe task completion capabilities?
Supporting Citations: WebArena 21, BrowserGym 21, InjecAgent 21, ToolEmu 21, DoomArena 21, BrowserART 21

Paper: Attacking Vision-Language Computer Agents via Pop-ups
Research Focus: Vulnerabilities and security risks of Vision-Language Model (VLM) web and computer agents when exposed to adversarial pop-ups.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Constructed adversarial pop-ups (using attention hooks, instructions, info banners, and ALT descriptors) inserted into observation spaces of OSWorld (50 tasks) and VisualWebArena (72 tasks). Evaluated GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 across pure screenshot and Set-of-Mark (SoM) agent paradigms.
Key Findings: Adversarial pop-ups achieved an Attack Success Rate (ASR) over 86% on average (over 80% on OSWorld, over 60% on VisualWebArena), reducing overall task success rates by 47%. Basic prompt defenses and advertisement disclosures were largely ineffective.
Author-Stated Limitations: Tested only closed-source commercial VLMs due to the poor performance of open-source models on GUI agent benchmarks; did not explore advanced gradient-based string optimization or complex persuasion jailbreaks.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on dynamic pop-ups, real-time network redirections, and multi-turn interactive phishing attacks; missing defenses built into the vision backbone architecture.
Internal Contradictions: The paper claims SoM agents focus heavily on text/a11y tree inputs, yet SoM agents still achieved an ASR over 60–90% when presented with purely visual adversarial coordinates or tags.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from Wu et al. (2024) and Liao et al. (2024) regarding the necessity of imperceptible or stealthy visual noise; shows that clear, human-recognizable visual distractors are highly effective against VLMs without needing invisible pixel perturbations.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Redirections were simulated by ignoring actions rather than loading malicious secondary pages, omitting potential environment feedback loops.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-window OS navigation, physical embodied environments, live commercial websites with real-world pop-up blockers, and open-source VLM agent backbones.
Proposed Research Questions: How can VLM architectures be inherently trained to prioritize privileged user instructions over untrusted visual observation content without relying on external system-prompt guards?
Supporting Citations: Wu et al. (2024) 22; Liao et al. (2024) 22; Xie et al. (2024) 22; Koh et al. (2024) 22

Paper: Why Do LLM-based Web Agents Fail? A Hierarchical Planning Perspective
Research Focus: Fine-grained process-based evaluation and diagnosis of LLM web agent failures using a three-layer hierarchical planning framework (high-level planning, low-level execution, and replanning).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated 104 web navigation tasks from Mind2Web-Live across three base LLMs (GPT-5-nano, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini Flash 2.5) comparing Natural Language (NL) vs. Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) representations across three action spaces (Action Object, Action ID, Expanded).
Key Findings: Low-level execution is the primary failure bottleneck (achieving only 36.4% task success even with human-authored high-level plans). High-level plans specified in PDDL produce more concise, goal-directed plans (84.6% matched rate) than NL (70.6%). A single round of replanning significantly boosts task performance.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluated a limited set of high-level representations, action spaces, and agent configurations; did not consider multimodal (vision-based) settings; high-level plan evaluation requires reference plans.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic, multi-round replanning strategies under real-world web non-determinism; missing integration of visual grounding models into the low-level execution controller.
Internal Contradictions: While the authors emphasize that PDDL reduces verbosity and unaligned steps, PDDL plans suffered a higher increase in missing steps after replanning (rising to 14.5%) compared to NL plans.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts traditional end-to-end benchmark evaluations (such as standard Mind2Web or WebArena metrics) by demonstrating that high end-to-end failure rates are driven by low-level grounding/DOM interaction errors rather than poor high-level logic or reasoning.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Postcondition checking and final evaluation relied on LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-5-nano), which carries potential model bias, despite human agreement verification on a 50-sample subset.
Untested Scenarios: Multimodal vision-language agent web navigation, dynamic cross-domain authentications, and multi-agent collaborative execution environments.
Proposed Research Questions: How can formal symbolic planning languages like PDDL be dynamically updated in real time based on noisy, unstructured DOM observations during low-level execution failures?
Supporting Citations: Pan et al. (2024b) 23; Deng et al. (2023) 23; Ghallab et al. (1998) 23; Xue et al. (2025) 23

Paper: WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks
Research Focus: Benchmarking web agent security and vulnerability against indirect prompt injection attacks in multi-step end-to-end web workflows.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Tested autonomous agents (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, OpenAI o1, Claude Sonnet 3.5 v2, Claude Sonnet 3.7 with Extended Thinking, Llama-3.3-70B) across VisualWebArena (GitLab, Reddit) and CURI environments using plain-text and URL injection templates across 84 attack tasks and 37 utility baseline tasks.
Key Findings: High intermediate hijacking success (ASR-intermediate 17–86%), but low end-to-end task completion by attackers (ASR-end-to-end 0–17%). Reveals 'security by incompetence' where agents are diverted easily but fail complex multi-step attacker execution.
Author-Stated Limitations: Supports only two web environments (GitLab and Reddit); lacks diversity in target website categories (e.g., travel, knowledge bases) and lacks a diverse set of prompt injection attack prompts.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks assessment of dynamic multi-turn attacker strategies, real-time defensive monitoring, and generalizability to desktop/code agents or non-templated injection attacks.
Internal Contradictions: High-reasoning models like OpenAI o1 achieved higher intermediate attack success (85.7%) under tool-calling with instruction hierarchy than simpler models, despite instruction hierarchy being explicitly designed to reduce untrusted input privilege.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Prior works (e.g., InjecAgent, ASB) report high prompt injection threat rates, whereas WASP demonstrates that full end-to-end malicious execution remains near zero for standard agents due to capability bottlenecks rather than defensive filtering.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for browser execution latency, network timeout artifacts, or model context-window truncation affecting multi-step task execution success.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web agents facing non-deterministic environments, multi-modal prompt injections (e.g., hidden in images), visual DOM obfuscations, and agent recovery loops under sustained navigation traps.
Proposed Research Questions: How can agentic architectures maintain task integrity against URL anchor-based prompt injections without sacrificing multi-turn web navigation utility?
Supporting Citations: Koh et al. (2024); Greshake et al. (2023); Wallace et al. (2024); Zhan et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2024a)

Paper: WebSailor: Navigating Super-human Reasoning for Web Agent
Research Focus: Developing a post-training methodology (SailorFog-QA data generation, RFT cold start, and DUPO RL) to equip open-source web agents with super-human reasoning for complex information seeking.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Synthesized SailorFog-QA using graph-sampling and information obfuscation; fine-tuned Qwen-2.5 backbones (3B, 7B, 32B, 72B) via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT) and Duplicating Sampling Policy Optimization (DUPO); evaluated on BrowseComp-en/zh, GAIA, Xbench-DeepSearch, and SimpleQA.
Key Findings: WebSailor-72B matched or exceeded proprietary agents (Doubao, Grok-3) and outperformed open-source agents on BrowseComp-zh (30.1%) and BrowseComp-en (12.0%). RFT cold start proved essential before RL to avoid failure in long-horizon web navigation.
Author-Stated Limitations: Context length capped at 32k tokens during training (causing failure on tasks requiring longer context); tendency for 'over-thinking' on simple tasks; RL training limited to 50 synchronous steps due to speed bottlenecks.
Inferred Research Gaps: Evaluation does not test agent security robustness against deliberate adversarial environments or prompt injections during web search/visit actions.
Internal Contradictions: The paper emphasizes reducing verbosity to avoid context overload, yet empirical results show the agent frequently engages in multi-step over-thinking and redundant verification loops.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts claims from recent RL literature (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) that SFT/cold start can be entirely skipped in favor of pure RL from base models.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for search engine API rate limits, dynamic web page changes over time during evaluation, or summarization model biases (Qwen-2.5-72B used as summary model for visit action).
Untested Scenarios: Performance under adversarial web environments, degraded network conditions, anti-bot/CAPTCHA barriers, or multi-modal search tasks.
Proposed Research Questions: Can asynchronous agentic RL mitigate over-thinking while scaling context windows past 32k tokens without loss of navigation efficiency?
Supporting Citations: Wei et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2025); Mialon et al. (2023); Guo et al. (2025); Yu et al. (2025)

Paper: AgentLAB: Benchmarking LLM Agents against Long-Horizon Attacks
Research Focus: Evaluating LLM agent safety and vulnerability against long-horizon, multi-turn adaptive attacks across complex agentic environments.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created a multi-agent framework (Planner, Attacker, Judge, Verifier) testing 5 long-horizon attack types (intent hijacking, tool chaining, objective drifting, task injection, memory poisoning) across 28 realistic tool-enabled environments and 644 security test cases. Evaluated 6 LLM backends (GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Gemini-3.0-Flash, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Llama-3.1, Qwen-3). Tested standard one-shot defenses (Self-Reminder, Llama-Guard, Repeated Prompt, DeBERTa Detector).
Key Findings: LLM agents are highly vulnerable to long-horizon attacks, achieving up to 81.5% overall Attack Success Rate (ASR) on Qwen-3 and 69.9% on GPT-5.1. Long-horizon attacks significantly outperform single-turn prompt injections (e.g., GPT-4o ASR jumped from 62.5% in one-shot to 79.9% in long-horizon). Single-turn defenses fail to reliably mitigate long-horizon threats.
Author-Stated Limitations: The current evaluation provides preliminary empirical findings across a subset of models and environments; relies on external LLM evaluators (GPT-5.1) as internal judges for task completion.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on continuous real-world web agent deployments, active human-in-the-loop defense interventions, and resource consumption/monetary costs incurred by sustained long-horizon attack loops.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts static evaluation benchmarks (e.g., InjecAgent, AgentDojo baseline static attacks) which report lower attack success rates by assuming adversaries operate in single-turn static injection scenarios.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Impact of backend model system prompt variations; variability/reliability of the LLM-based judge (GPT-5.1) across non-deterministic multi-turn outputs.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web agents facing dynamic human counter-interventions, live multi-user environment interactions, or defensive agent-to-agent collaboration.
Proposed Research Questions: How can multi-turn, stateful defenses be designed to detect cumulative goal drift and context poisoning without destroying agent task execution utility?

Paper: IRLbot: Scaling to 6 Billion Pages and Beyond
Research Focus: Design and performance modeling of a single-server Web crawler capable of downloading billions of pages while handling web spam, dynamic infinite loops, and strict politeness constraints.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Developed DRUM (Disk Repository with Update Management) for disk-based hash operations, STAR (Spam Tracking and Avoidance through Reputation) for PLD-level in-degree budgeting, and BEAST (Budget Enforcement with Anti-Spam Tactics) for multi-queue disk-shuffling budget enforcement. Evaluated via a 41.27-day active crawl on a single quad-CPU AMD Opteron server attached to a 1 Gbps connection.
Key Findings: Successfully crawled 6.38 billion unique HTML pages (7.6 billion connection requests) from 117.5 million hosts in 33.7 million PLDs at an average download rate of 319 mb/s (1,789 pages/s). Parsed 394 billion links and discovered 41.5 billion unique node URLs. Demonstrated that DRUM overhead scales near-linearly compared to quadratic overhead in prior batch disk check methods (Mercator-B, Polybot).
Author-Stated Limitations: Does not perform page-content duplicate/near-duplicate detection due to processing overhead and potential false positives; coarse-grained PLD-level ranking may miss fine-grained intra-domain host/subdirectory spam; 8-byte hashes will experience noticeable collision rates once crawls reach 100B–10T pages.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks real-time evaluation against sophisticated modern anti-scraping measures (e.g., CAPTCHAs, JavaScript rendering requirements, dynamic bot detection).
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts assumptions in Mercator-B and Polybot regarding the scalability of standard memory-buffer batch disk sorting for multi-billion page crawls.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Varying ISP/network throttling policies across different geographic regions and target domain server configurations.
Untested Scenarios: Crawling complex client-side rendered JavaScript web applications (SPA) or crawling under adversarial dynamic web trap environments.
Proposed Research Questions: How can low-overhead content deduplication and fine-grained host reputation algorithms be integrated into disk-oriented crawling pipelines without creating disk I/O bottlenecks?

Paper: A Whole New World: Creating a Parallel-Poisoned Web Only AI-Agents Can See
Research Focus: Stealthy website cloaking attacks specifically targeting autonomous web-browsing LLM agents via agent fingerprinting.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Formal threat modeling and experimental evaluation using Cursor agent powered by Claude 4 Sonnet, GPT-5 Fast, and Gemini 2.5 Pro visiting a custom cloaking API documentation server requiring private environment variable authentication.
Key Findings: 100% attack success rate across tested models; websites can reliably distinguish AI web agents from humans using automation artifacts, browser properties, and IP/ASN signatures to serve cloaked indirect prompt injection payloads while remaining invisible to human users and security crawlers.
Author-Stated Limitations: Primary responsibility for defense falls on agent developers; countermeasure implementation requires a paradigm shift beyond prompt safety; tested on a simple internal API documentation website setup.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not evaluate defense effectiveness against dynamic behavioral fingerprinting or continuous fingerprint randomization in real-world large-scale web environments.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None identified.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks baseline comparison against human-like behavioral perturbation proxies (e.g., randomized delay, non-linear mouse paths) during fingerprinting detection.
Untested Scenarios: Testing against real-world commercial web security crawlers and multi-agent collaborative browsing setups.
Proposed Research Questions: How can agent browser instances dynamically alter canvas/WebGL and DOM fingerprints in real-time without breaking legitimate web applications?

Paper: FocusAgent: Simple Yet Effective Ways of Trimming the Large Context of Web Agents
Research Focus: Context trimming and observation sanitization for web agents via lightweight LLM-based retrieval on accessibility trees (AxTrees).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated on WorkArena L1 (330 tasks) and WebArena (381 tasks, BrowserGym split) using GPT-4.1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and GPT-4.1-mini/GPT-5-mini as retrievers; security evaluated using DoomArena on WebArena Reddit (114 tasks) under banner and pop-up indirect prompt injection attacks.
Key Findings: FocusAgent reduces AxTree observation token size by over 50% (up to 99%) while preserving task completion performance; significantly lowers Indirect Prompt Injection Attack Success Rate (ASR drops from >80% to <1% on popup attacks and to ~1% on banner attacks) while maintaining high task success rates.
Author-Stated Limitations: Performance depends heavily on prompt engineering; retriever does not guarantee a completely clean webpage without residual malicious content; untested on context lengths exceeding 128k tokens.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not resolve situations where task-critical UI elements (e.g., pop-up close buttons) contain embedded prompt injection payloads, leading to task failure despite attack neutralization.
Internal Contradictions: Soft retrieval prompting preserves task performance best, yet removing history from the retriever improves performance over keeping action/thought history, despite history providing explicit step progress context.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates that observation pruning can inherently defend against indirect prompt injections without dedicated stopping guards, contrasting with guard-layer approaches (e.g., DoomArena guard baseline) that halt execution and destroy task utility.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation under hybrid multimodal (screenshot + DOM/AxTree) attack vectors where visual elements bypass text-based retriever filtering.
Untested Scenarios: Real-world web application navigation involving extremely dynamic single-page application (SPA) state updates across hundreds of steps.
Proposed Research Questions: How can LLM retrievers sanitize malicious prompt injections embedded directly within functional UI elements without stripping the element's operational interaction handlers?

Paper: Mind the Web: The Security of Web-Use Agents
Research Focus: Task-aligned indirect prompt injection attacks exploiting web-use agents' contextual reasoning limitations.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Automated 3-stage training pipeline (candidate generation, LLM validation via GPT-5, SFT+DPO fine-tuning of Qwen-3-4B-Instruct offline generator); evaluated on 5 web agents (OpenAI Operator, Browser-Use, Do Browser, OpenOperator, Perplexity Comet) across 9 CIA-triad payloads on self-hosted environments (City-Explorer, Local Reddit) and real-world platforms (GitHub, X/Twitter, ParaBank).
Key Findings: Task-aligned injections (framing malicious commands as helpful guidance) achieved >80% Attack Success Rate (85% with SFT+DPO) across agents and models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.5, Mistral Pixtral Large, OpenAI CUA), easily bypassing built-in security controls, prompt classifiers, and traditional browser security (CSP, SOP, XSS filters).
Author-Stated Limitations: Oversight and execution constraint mitigations introduce trade-offs with agent autonomy, latency, and usability; task-aligned injections exploit fundamental reasoning limits regarding instruction provenance rather than simple code bugs.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks quantitative long-term benchmarks for continuous multi-turn multi-agent ecosystems where injected instructions propagate across shared persistent environments.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Shows that OpenAI CUA and Claude Sonnet 3.5 remain highly vulnerable (>77% ASR) to contextually disguised injections even when explicitly fine-tuned for web security, whereas FocusAgent suggests observation filtering can eliminate similar text-based threats.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not measure performance under varying network latencies or dynamic client-side rendering delays during automated execution traces.
Untested Scenarios: Evaluation against multi-modal stealth injections combining invisible CSS/DOM text with visual steganography in web images.
Proposed Research Questions: What architectural paradigms can enforce immutable instruction provenance separation between user goals and untrusted external web data in ReAct reasoning loops?

Paper: Context manipulation attacks: Web agents are susceptible to corrupted memory
Research Focus: Context manipulation and plan injection attacks against web navigation agents (Agent-E, Browser-use) via corrupted memory state.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Formalized plan injection attack vectors (non-contextual, task-aligned, context-chained). Evaluated Browser-use and Agent-E (powered by GPT-4o controller/planner and GPT-4o-mini navigation agent) on two benchmarks: Plan Injection benchmark (60 tasks across Factual, Opinion, Ad Insertion, Privacy Exfiltration) and WebVoyager-Privacy benchmark (45 scenarios). Tested against prompt defenses (SANDWICH and SECURE guidelines).
Key Findings: Plan injections achieve up to 3x higher attack success rates (ASR) than prompt injections. Context-chained injections boost privacy exfiltration ASR by 17.7% over non-contextual attacks. Opinion steering tasks are highly vulnerable (94.7% ASR), whereas factual tasks resist attacks (18.7% ASR). Prompt defenses (SANDWICH/SECURE) mitigate prompt injections but fail against plan injection (ASR remains up to 46% for Agent-E and 63% for Browser-use).
Author-Stated Limitations: Initial experiments suggest stronger reasoning models may reduce ASR, but comprehensive evaluation of such models was left as a direction for future work.
Inferred Research Gaps: Evaluated primarily against GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini in headless mode; lacks extensive testing across open-source LLM backends or non-web desktop agents. Lacks real-time automated defense implementations for memory/plan integrity.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from traditional prompt-injection literature (e.g., WAAA!) by demonstrating that memory/plan-layer injections bypass standard input/prompt-level defenses.
