Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for variations in system prompts across different production agents or dynamic web latency/rendering differences.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent systems with more than two sub-agents, non-English web navigation tasks, and defensive fine-tuning/memory isolation architectures.
Proposed Research Questions: How can principled memory isolation architectures and semantic inconsistency detectors be designed to provably prevent plan injection in hierarchical agents?
Supporting Citations: Sumers et al. (2023) 31, Patlan et al. (2025b) 31, He et al. (2024) 31, Debenedetti et al. (2024) 31

Paper: Unsafe LLM-Based Search: Quantitative Analysis and Mitigation of Safety Risks in AI Web Search
Research Focus: Quantifying safety risks in AI-Powered Search Engines (AIPSEs) regarding exposure/quoting of malicious URLs and content, and proposing agent-based mitigation.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated 7 production AIPSEs (ChatGPT Search, Perplexity Pro, Copilot, TextCortex, Grok, Doubao, Kimi) using 100 evaluation entries derived from 24,037 malicious URLs (PhishTank, ThreatBook, LevelBlue). Evaluated keyword, natural language, and URL query types. Conducted 2 case studies (online doc spoofing and phishing) and evaluated an agent-based ReAct defense with GPT-4.1 content refinement and URL detectors (HtmlLLM, XGBoost, PhishLLM).
Key Findings: 47% of AIPSE responses contained risky URLs, and 34% directly cited harmful content (Main Risk). URL queries amplified main risk inclusion, whereas natural language queries slightly mitigated risk. AIPSEs outperformed Traditional Search Engines (TSEs) in both utility (NMR score) and safety. Agent-based defense with HtmlLLM-Detector achieved 78.3% defense success rate with an F1 score of 0.822, with a minor ~10.7% information reduction cost.
Author-Stated Limitations: Dataset scale was limited by research resources and lack of automated APIs on AIPSEs, requiring labor-intensive manual evaluation. Phishing website validity is highly time-sensitive.
Inferred Research Gaps: Evaluation relied on non-optimized queries rather than adaptive adversarial SEO; defense mechanisms add inference latency and token overhead via proxy LLM calls.
Internal Contradictions: Claims AIPSEs outperform TSEs in safety despite finding that 47% of AIPSE responses contain risky URLs; however, comparative data shows TSEs return significantly higher counts of malicious URLs overall.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None identified.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Dynamic web changes over time; variations in commercial search backend index snapshots.
Untested Scenarios: Long-term tracking of AIPSE blacklisting response times, multi-lingual performance outside Chinese and English.
Proposed Research Questions: Can real-time webpage visual/HTML verification tools be directly integrated into AIPSE retrieval pipelines to filter malicious content prior to LLM generation?
Supporting Citations: Lewis et al. (2020) 32, Yao et al. (2023) 32, Liu et al. (2024) 32

Paper: WAAA! Web Adversaries Against Agentic Browsers
Research Focus: Establishing a web-focused threat model and attack taxonomy for agentic browsers, treating the agent as a confused deputy susceptible to traditional web social engineering.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Extended See->Act framework across Chromium browser properties, attacker capabilities (markup vs script), and targets. Formalized 20 attacks into 5 failure modes. Tested 18 proof-of-concept attacks on Playwright-MCP (GPT-5) and BrowserOS, and evaluated generalizability of 14 attacks across 4 LLM backends (GPT-5, Kimi-k2p5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen-3.6 Plus). Tested against Perplexity's BrowseSafe detector.
Key Findings: Agentic browsers collapse traditional gadget and script attacker distinctions, reviving 10 traditional web threats in amplified forms. Models are significantly more susceptible to traditional web/scam confusion attacks than to explicit indirect prompt injections. Commercial prompt injection defenses like BrowseSafe completely fail to detect confusion attacks. Identified 5 key failure modes: bridging same-site data, bridging cross-site data, URL hallucination/slop squatting, website attacks on LLMs, and tool misuse.
Author-Stated Limitations: Proof-of-concept implementations excluded testing on live production agent deployments to prevent agents from going rogue on the public web. Evaluated on a snapshot of models/browsers from late 2025.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not provide a fully implemented runtime defense architecture (e.g., explicit HTML trust annotation parser or capability-restricted browser sandbox), leaving defensive proposals as conceptual guidelines.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts input-sanitization-focused agent security papers by demonstrating that prompt-level filtering cannot defend against observationally equivalent web confusion attacks.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Variation in underlying system prompts and non-deterministic LLM reasoning paths across multiple execution steps.
Untested Scenarios: Real-world user study evaluating how human supervisors interact with agentic browser action logs during active social engineering attempts.
Proposed Research Questions: How can explicit HTML trust attributes and origin-aware mediation rules be implemented in browser engines to enforce same-origin boundaries on LLM agents?
Supporting Citations: Zheng et al. (2024) 33, Yao et al. (2023) 33, Akhawe et al. (2010) 33, Barth et al. (2008) 33

Paper: Machine-Readable Ads: Accessibility and Trust Patterns for AI Web Agents Interacting with Online Advertisements
Research Focus: Investigating how semantic markup, placement, media format, and trust patterns influence the perception, actionability, and behavioral safety/trustworthiness of multimodal AI web agents in ad-heavy environments.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Controlled experiments using a React/DOM clone of Tiroler Tageszeitung site across 300 initial baseline runs plus follow-ups (10 tasks x 10 runs x 3 models) using Browser Use framework (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) and pixel-based OpenAI Operator.
Key Findings: Agents exhibit severe satisficing (never scroll past 2 viewports), click side banners only with DOM overlay buttons or off-screen text labels, and succumb to sweepstake paywall traps (GPT-4o and Claude subscribed in 100% of trials; Gemini in 70%). Proposed 5 key web-design principles for agent-readability.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluated on a production clone rather than live domain; commercial LLMs suffer from opacity/version drift; DOM-vs-pixel framework architectural comparisons are indicative; task set limited to single news context; evaluated a small subset of hidden-text strategies; dummy credentials bypassed real payment friction.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of standardized policy-aware metrics for agent consent/financial autonomy; absence of continuous multi-viewport dynamic scrolling models; insufficient investigation into counter-adversarial ad optimization.
Internal Contradictions: None observed within the paper's own experimental claims.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Exhibits contrasting paradigms with generalist agent frameworks like Mind2Web 34 (which emphasize raw DOM sequence action generation without explicit ad safety layers) and WebAgentGuard 35 (which enforces parallel safety verification rather than relying on agent self-restraint).
Missing Controls/Confounders: Impact of live network latency, dynamic real-time personalization, personalized ad-bidding, and anti-bot/CAPTCHA countermeasures.
Untested Scenarios: E-commerce, online banking, and multi-device/mobile platforms; live live-web deployment; adversarial malicious ad-injection attacks.
Proposed Research Questions: How can standardized policy-aware trust metrics be established to quantify agent financial autonomy under deceptive ad patterns? How can agents balance satisficing efficiency with exhaustive depth exploration?

Paper: MIND2WEB: Towards a Generalist Agent for the Web
Research Focus: Building a generalist web agent capable of following high-level natural language instructions across diverse real-world websites and open-ended domain tasks.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created MIND2WEB dataset with 2,350 tasks from 137 real websites across 31 domains. Evaluated MINDACT framework (DeBERTa candidate generation + Flan-T5/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 action selection).
Key Findings: Generalizing across unseen websites and domains is a primary bottleneck (step success rates ~38-40% vs ~52% cross-task). Flan-T5 with multi-choice QA significantly outperforms generation/classification baselines. GPT-4 in-context learning achieves competitive performance.
Author-Stated Limitations: Dataset predominantly English/US-centric; uses offline cached snapshots causing potential false negatives; relies only on textual/DOM context without visual screenshots; lacks dynamic interaction modeling; single upfront task instruction without interactive clarification.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of real-time online evaluation feedback; vulnerability to unexpected dynamic UI popups or adversarial injections; lack of explicit financial or safety boundary checks.
Internal Contradictions: None detected.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Assumes web navigation can be safely modeled as step-by-step action completion, whereas WebAgentGuard 35 shows unconstrained web agents suffer >80% attack failure/prompt injection rates without parallel guardrails.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Live web DOM variability, pop-up interference, network traffic fluctuations, multi-modal alignment.
Untested Scenarios: Real-time execution on live production sites with active authentication, financial transactions, and multi-turn human-in-the-loop interaction.
Proposed Research Questions: How can multi-modal vision-text alignment and dynamic interaction modeling improve generalist web agent task success on unseen domains without sacrificing security?

Paper: WebAgentGuard: A Reasoning-Driven Guard Model for Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks in Web Agents
Research Focus: Detecting indirect prompt injection attacks against multimodal web agents by decoupling safety verification from task execution using a parallel guard agent.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Synthetic dataset generation via GPT-5 (164 topics, 230 UI styles). Two-stage training: reasoning SFT cold-start followed by GRPO reinforcement learning. Benchmark evaluation on constructed in-domain set, PopUp attacks, VPI-Bench, EIA, and WebArena utility.
Key Findings: WebAgentGuard achieves >90% recall on prompt injection detection and reduces attack success rates on Claude and Browser-use agents to near 0%, while introducing zero wall-clock latency (parallel execution) and maintaining agent utility on WebArena.
Author-Stated Limitations: Occasional guard failure cases where the model identifies injected text during thinking but forgets it before final answer generation; reliant on synthetic training datasets.
Inferred Research Gaps: Evaluation limited to static prompt injections; lack of long-context temporal reasoning across multi-step browser interactions where injection spans across multiple distinct pages.
Internal Contradictions: None detected.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates that internal agent self-restraint or system prompting (as assumed in foundational agent frameworks) is ineffective (<20% defense rate), directly opposing reliance on unguardrailed agent frameworks like Mind2Web 34.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Confounding effects of highly dynamic dynamic DOM animations, obfuscated CSS/JS scripts, and multi-agent coordination scenarios.
Untested Scenarios: Live web deployment against active zero-day adversarial prompt injection tactics, non-English adversarial datasets, and extreme context length inputs.
Proposed Research Questions: How can guard models maintain attention persistence over multi-page navigation traces to prevent memory fading in prompt injection detection?

Paper: LASER: LLM Agent with State-Space Exploration for Web Navigation
Research Focus: Modeling web navigation tasks as state-space exploration to allow flexible backtracking and constrained action selection.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Defined 4 high-level states (search, results, item, finish) for WebShop and set permissible actions per state. Evaluated on WebShop (500 test set instructions) and sim-to-real transfer on Amazon.com (100 instructions) using GPT-4-0613 with function calling.
Key Findings: LASER achieves 50.0% success rate on WebShop (outperforming ReAct's 34.0% rerun) and 62.0% on Amazon.com, approaching human expert performance (59.6% WebShop, 65.0% Amazon). Eliminates the need for in-context trajectory examples.
Author-Stated Limitations: Limited to finding target items in e-commerce; does not cover tasks like order tracking or history checking. Requires manual domain annotation of states and generic descriptions.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks generalizability to open-world web tasks without manual state definition; unexamined resource consumption during backtracking loops; untested under adversarial navigation traps or website layout changes.
Internal Contradictions: Claims to avoid costly/unrealistic in-context examples, but relies on manual categorization and generic system prompt/layout annotations for every state.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts ReAct and WebGUM by showing zero-shot state-guided prompting outperforms low-level in-context trajectory demonstrations and fine-tuning on WebShop.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for LLM API cost/latency overhead incurred by multiple backtracking iterations versus single forward passes.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web agents, non-deterministic navigation traps, dynamic web elements, sustained non-progress loops, and non-shopping environments.
Proposed Research Questions: How can high-level states and permissible action spaces be automatically discovered in open-world web navigation to prevent manual annotation overhead?

Paper: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
Research Focus: Guaranteeing the retrieval of Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) malicious payloads under natural user queries in realistic RAG and agentic systems.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Decomposed IPI into trigger and attack fragments using Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) for black-box prefix optimization. Evaluated across 11 BEIR benchmarks, 8 embedding models, and downstream RAG/agent applications (AutoGen, Magentic-One) including email/code execution scenarios.
Key Findings: Unoptimized IPI is almost never retrieved under natural queries. CEM-constructed 10-token triggers achieve near-100% retrieval across benchmarks at ~$0.21 cost. In multi-agent settings, a single poisoned email coerced GPT-4o into exfiltrating SSH keys with up to 80% success rate.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluation restricted to embedding-based retrieval; does not test hybrid pipelines or reranking mechanisms. Trigger transferability is reduced across differing embedding model architectures.
Inferred Research Gaps: Unexplored interaction between optimized triggers and multi-modal rerankers or complex agent memory architectures; lack of robust defenses when triggers are dispersed.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts prior IPI studies (e.g., AgentDojo setups) which assumed malicious text is automatically in-context, showing that unoptimized injections fail at the retrieval stage.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not explicitly benchmark computational overhead of CEM optimization versus white-box gradient attacks when white-box access is available.
Untested Scenarios: Hybrid sparse-dense retrieval systems, secondary visual rerankers, dynamic multi-step search environments with defensive agent filtering.
Proposed Research Questions: Can adaptive reranking mechanisms effectively intercept optimized trigger fragments before context insertion in multi-agent workflows?

Paper: WARD: Adversarially Robust Defense of Web Agents Against Prompt Injections
Research Focus: Developing a robust, low-latency guard model to protect web agents against HTML and visual prompt injections.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Built WARD-Base (177K samples, 719 URLs, 10 platforms) and WARD-PIG datasets. Applied Adaptive Adversarial Attack Training (A3T) with a co-evolving attacker and guard via GRPO. Evaluated on 4 OOD benchmarks (Popup, EIA, VPI, WASP), PIArena, and WebArena utility benchmarks using 0.8B and 2B models.
Key Findings: WARD achieves near-100% recall on OOD benchmarks, maintains <0.5% false positive rate on WebArena, and suppresses attack success rates to near 0% across single/multi-modal injections. Runs in parallel with web agents with negligible added latency.
Author-Stated Limitations: Ineffective against pixel-level environmental adversarial attacks (e.g., WebInject) that lack explicit textual/visual instructions; relies on explicit content threat models.
Inferred Research Gaps: Unexplored robustness against multi-step state-dependent attacks where injections evolve based on agent action history; potential vulnerability to visual-only steganographic injections.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates that standalone text-only or screenshot-only guard models (e.g., BrowseSafe, SnapGuard) fail significantly under multi-modal or guard-targeted (PIG) attacks.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not measure performance degradation when web agents encounter non-English dynamic layouts with heavy localized script variations.
Untested Scenarios: Imperceptible pixel perturbations, multi-turn dynamic interactive injection traps targeting multi-agent loops over prolonged trajectories.
Proposed Research Questions: How can guard models detect contextual mimicry attacks where injected elements appear identical to valid, task-aligned native UI components?

Paper: Attention is All You Need to Defend Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in LLMs
Research Focus: Fine-grained token-level Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) detection and sanitization using internal LLM attention features.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Proposes RENNERVATE, a defense framework incorporating a 2-step attentive pooling detector (pooling response tokens and attention heads) and an injection sanitizer. Evaluated across 5 LLMs (ChatGLM, Dolly, Falcon, LLaMA2, LLaMA3), 6 datasets (FIPI benchmark with 100k instances, MRPC, HSOL, Jfleg, RTE, SST2), and multiple attack types (Naive, Escape Characters, Context Ignoring, Fake Completion, Combined, GCG, Neural Exec, PAIR, TAP).
Key Findings: Achieves 97.88%–99.58% IPI detection accuracy with low false positive rates (0.46%–2.42%) across 5 target LLMs, outperforming 15 commercial/academic baselines. Reduces attack success rate (ASR) to near 0% across various black-box and white-box adaptive attacks while preserving target model utility (win rates near 50% on AlpacaEval2.0).
Author-Stated Limitations: RENNERVATE struggles to fully remove injected-task-specific content (e.g., non-instructional context tied to an injected task), leading to utility degradation in precision-demanding tasks like grammar correction (Jfleg).
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not provide recovery mechanisms for lost clean context beyond token deletion; restricted to single-modality text inputs during inference.
Internal Contradictions: Claims to preserve original prompt utility without model modification, yet utility evaluation reveals severe win-rate drops (e.g., down to ~5% on Jfleg-RTE) when tasks require exact token precision.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts prompt-modification approaches (e.g., Sandwich, Spotlighting) and model-modification approaches (e.g., StruQ) by demonstrating superior defense without altering prompts or fine-tuning model weights.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation relies heavily on synthetic/rewritten datasets (FIPI) rather than real-world dynamic web application environments.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-modal IPI attacks (e.g., image/audio injections) and multi-turn agent interactions where memory accumulates across sessions.
Proposed Research Questions: How can attention-based token sanitization be extended to multi-modal prompt injection defense without degrading vision-language model utility?

Paper: How Much Can We Trust LLM Search Agents? Measuring Endorsement Vulnerability to Web Content Manipulation
Research Focus: Quantifying endorsement corruption in web-search LLM agents under adversarial web content manipulation (Generative Engine Optimization/GEO attacks).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces SearchGEO, an evaluation framework featuring a 3-layer/5-mode attack taxonomy (Hidden DOM, Snippet-Page Divergence, Forged Authority, Synthetic Consensus, Citation Chain), a hybrid search proxy caching real Google search results, a 44-query suite across 4 high-stakes domains (health, finance, legal, consumer IT), and an auxiliary agent-skill install probe. Evaluates 13 LLM backends over 6,000 cases.
Key Findings: Vulnerability varies drastically by model choice (ASR ranges from 0.0% on Claude-Sonnet-4.6 to 31.4% on Gemini-3-Flash). Source diversity (multi-source synthetic consensus) drives attack success, whereas simple source repetition does not. In agent-skill probes, robust models show opposite failure modes: Claude over-rejects clean ecosystems (80% false rejection), while GPT over-trusts fabricated skills (94% ASR).
Author-Stated Limitations: Uses a static hybrid search proxy rather than live web search engines (30% of cached results expose snippet-only content), meaning live ranking dynamics and SEO competition are not fully modeled.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks longitudinal measurement of cumulative belief/preference drift over multiple search sessions.
Internal Contradictions: Claude-Sonnet-4.6 is ranked as the most robust model on the main benchmark (0.0% ASR), but in the skill-installation probe it fails completely due to excessive over-refusal (80% false rejection rate on benign inputs).
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts traditional prompt injection safety evaluations by proving that agents can be completely hijacked via evidence manipulation without using any explicit imperative instructions or jailbreak prompts.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Did not control for backend pre-training corpus exposure to specific search result domain structures.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-step complex research workflows involving autonomous browser interactions or live multi-turn web search loops.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web search agents distinguish between genuine multi-source consensus and coordinated synthetic SEO campaigns at the evidence layer?

Paper: RecurGuard: Runtime Monitoring for Reasoning-Token Consumption Attacks
Research Focus: Real-time runtime detection and early termination of reasoning-token consumption (unbounded consumption / slowdown) attacks on reasoning LLMs.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Proposes RECURGUARD, an online streaming trace monitor tracking Recurrence Rate (RR), Volume Growth (VG), and Task-Conditioned Progress (TP) over 64-word reasoning chunks. Evaluated on DS-R1-Qwen-7B, DS-R1-Llama-8B, Qwen3-8B, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.7 against OverThink, ExtendAttack, and 4 adaptive stress tests (C1-C4) across SQuAD, HumanEval, GSM8K, and CNN/DailyMail datasets.
Key Findings: RECURGUARD achieves 99% TPR on OverThink and 92% TPR on ExtendAttack with near 0% FPR on benign tasks, halting generation early to save ~92% of output tokens. Under adaptive stress tests, topical attacks (C1) maintain 11.9x token amplification with a 50% joint miss rate, whereas full semantic evasion (C4) forces attack amplification to collapse from 22.8x down to 2.2x.
Author-Stated Limitations: Requires exposed, non-empty reasoning traces. Inapplicable when APIs hide reasoning traces (e.g., Claude Opus 4.7) and less sensitive on provider-summarized thinking blocks (e.g., Claude Sonnet 4.5). Topical CSP attacks (C1) remain an unaddressed boundary for semantic monitors.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not evaluate logit-level entropy signals or defense performance under white-box gradient-based attacks against the sentence encoder.
Internal Contradictions: States that token-length baselines are ineffective due to high FPR on code generation (69%-80%), yet length baselines outperform semantic monitors against topical adaptive attacks (C1) catching 94%-99% of instances.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Challenges standard input-side safety classifiers (e.g., Llama Guard 3) by demonstrating a 0% detection rate against reasoning consumption attacks because prompts lack policy-violating text.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation of closed-API models (Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.7) used small sample sizes (N=30 and N=3) compared to open-weight models.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-turn tool-augmented agentic workflows where reasoning traces span across tool calls.
Proposed Research Questions: How can task-conditioned runtime monitors defend against topically aligned reasoning-consumption attacks without increasing false positive rates on long-form synthesis?

Paper: Go-Browse: Training Web Agents with Structured Exploration
Research Focus: Fully unsupervised and scalable synthetic data collection for web agents via graph-based structured exploration.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Presents Go-Browse, which uses an outer loop for global URL coverage (building a URL graph G=(V,E)) and an inner loop with NavExplorer, PageExplorer, FeasibilityChecker, and Solvers for local page exploration and task sampling. Evaluated by collecting Go-Browse-WA (~10K successful, ~17K failed trajectories across 100 WebArena URLs) and fine-tuning Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. Evaluated on WebArena and Online-Mind2Web.
Key Findings: Go-Browse-7B achieves 21.7% overall success rate on WebArena, outperforming sub-10B SOTA NNetNav-7B by 2.9% and beating GPT-4o mini by 2.4%. It excels in deeper page navigation (higher maximum URL depth) and demonstrates that prefixed trajectory sampling enables weaker open models to bootstrap high-quality local task-solving data.
Author-Stated Limitations: Data collection was limited to 5 WebArena domains (100 URLs); did not fine-tune on the ~39K unsuccessful trajectories (e.g. via RL/DPO); limited to 7B model size; risk of LLM prompt/model bias propagating to agents.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation against active adversarial/malicious web environments (e.g., navigation traps, prompt injection); unassessed behavior under dynamic or changing web DOM structures; reliance on static URL graph definitions which fail on single-page web applications (SPAs) where URLs do not change with state transitions.
Internal Contradictions: The paper argues that instruction-first task generation causes agents to hallucinate infeasible tasks due to static observation constraints, but Go-Browse relies heavily on an inner loop composed of instruction-first task proposers (NavExplorer/PageExplorer) anchored to static URL observations.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Go-Browse claims web agents perform poorly without direct domain interaction data and that learning from synthetic tutorials fails to transfer. However, Synatra (Ou et al.) demonstrates that indirect internet knowledge can be synthesized effectively into direct demonstrations without environment rollouts.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Fails to control for total computational budget (API tokens/GPU hours) between Go-Browse and baseline exploration methods during data collection; lacks a control ablation isolating the VLM-as-a-judge filtering accuracy versus raw agent execution success.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web pages containing prompt injections, dynamic single-page web applications (SPAs) without explicit URL changes, anti-bot/CAPTCHA mechanisms, and environments requiring sustained multi-session memory or state recovery after errors.
Proposed Research Questions: How can graph-based exploration agents adapt to dynamic Single-Page Applications (SPAs) where interaction states change without URL mutations? Can unsuccessful exploration trajectories be leveraged via off-policy RL to improve navigation recovery from traps?

Paper: Overthinking Loops in Agents: A Structural Risk via MCP Tools
Research Focus: Structural overthinking attacks where malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools induce infinite cyclic execution loops in tool-using LLM agents, causing extreme resource and latency inflation.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Implemented 14 malicious MCP tools (across Text Repetition, Iterative Refinement, and Distraction categories) added to normal tool registries (ToolRet and Qwen-Code settings). Evaluated across 6 LLMs (Kimi-K2-Thinking, MiniMax-M2, Qwen3-Thinking, Qwen3-Coder, DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-4.6/4.7) on benchmarks (AIME2025, GPQA Diamond, HumanEval, CodeElo). Tested decoding-time defense NoWait.
Key Findings: Malicious MCP tools induce structural overthinking loops causing up to 142.4x token amplification and 27.5x latency amplification in coding agents (Qwen-Code), and up to 971x on individual task instances. Severe task accuracy degradation occurred in reasoning/coding tasks (e.g., HumanEval success dropped from 30.5% to 3.0% on Qwen3-Coder). Mixed registries (normal + attack tools) often cause higher token amplification than attack-only registries. Decoding-time concision controls (NoWait) fail to prevent structural loops.
Author-Stated Limitations: Benchmark evaluation restricted to science, math, and code domains; focused on tasks solvable within default budgets to isolate attack effects; excluded proprietary commercial APIs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini) due to Terms of Service constraints; did not systematically test structural defenses like graph cycle detection or strict depth constraints.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic runtime graph analysis defenses to detect cyclic dependency in tool metadata; unexamined interaction between multi-agent setups where loop induction in one agent cascades across an agent network; unassessed economic cost impact under dynamic API rate-limiting.
Internal Contradictions: Authors emphasize that attack tools rely on 'trivial logic' without 'sophisticated adversarial engineering', yet also claim that these tools are 'strategically designed' to exploit complex agent control flows and verification checkpoints.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While prior efficient reasoning literature (e.g., Wang et al., 2025a) shows that decoding-time reflection suppression (like NoWait) mitigates inference overthinking, this paper proves NoWait is completely ineffective against tool-induced overthinking because the cost stems from repeated system calls rather than token length per turn.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks baseline controls evaluating standard system timeouts or simple context-window sliding mechanisms that might naturally truncate or break structural loops; does not decouple token amplification caused by tool output length versus model reasoning length.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent orchestration architectures with cross-agent verification; registries protected by automated tool description summarization or static code analysis filters; live deployment environments with dynamic rate limits and automated budget kill-switches.
Proposed Research Questions: Can runtime tool-call dependency graphs detect and break structural overthinking cycles before budget exhaustion without degrading complex multi-step reasoning tasks? How do multi-agent coordination frameworks propagate or suppress tool-induced cyclic loops?

Paper: VisualWebArena: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Realistic Visually Grounded Web Tasks
Research Focus: Benchmarking autonomous multimodal web agents on realistic, visually grounded tasks requiring visual processing, text interpretation, and web navigation.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces VisualWebArena with 910 tasks across 3 self-hosted web environments (Classclassifieds, Shopping, Reddit), including 25.2% tasks with image inputs and 17.1% requiring OCR. Evaluated SOTA text-only LLMs (GPT-4, Gemini-Pro, LLaMA-2-70B, Mixtral-8x7B), caption-augmented LLMs, and multimodal VLMs (GPT-4V, Gemini-Pro, CogVLM, IDEFICS-80B, GPT-4o). Evaluated a novel Set-of-Marks (SoM) visual prompting interface against accessibility tree inputs.
Key Findings: SOTA multimodal agents significantly outperform text-only agents, with GPT-4V + SoM reaching 16.37% success rate (and GPT-4o reaching 19.78%), compared to 7.25% for text-only GPT-4. Human performance is 88.70%. SoM prompting improves element grounding and navigation efficiency on visually dense sites (Classifieds, Reddit). Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and long-horizon execution remain major failure bottlenecks for VLMs.
Author-Stated Limitations: Current models fall far short of human performance (16.4% vs 88.7%); benchmark uses binary reward metrics rather than continuous progress scales; open-source VLMs (IDEFICS-80B, CogVLM) perform poorly (<1% SR); agents suffer from failure modes like getting stuck in loops, undoing successful steps, and giving up prematurely.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation of agent robustness against adversarial visual elements (e.g., visual prompt injections, deceptive banners, or hidden elements); no analysis of dynamic video/animation inputs on web pages; absent metrics for resource usage/computational efficiency during VLM navigation trajectories.
Internal Contradictions: The paper highlights that SoM prompting simplifies the action space and boosts performance on visually complex sites (Classifieds/Reddit), yet Table 3 shows that for Gemini-Pro, SoM slightly decreases overall success rate (5.71%) compared to standard multimodal inputs (6.04%).
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While standard web benchmarks like WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) demonstrate that accessibility tree text representations are sufficient for complex web navigation, VisualWebArena proves that text-based DOM/accessibility trees fail completely (dropping GPT-4 SR from 12.75% to 7.25%) when visual information is omitted.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for spatial rendering variability (e.g., viewport dimensions or browser zooming) across different VLM backbones, which severely affects SoM bounding box coordinates and OCR accuracy; lacks ablation isolating image resolution effects on VLM success.
Untested Scenarios: Visually dynamic or non-static environments (e.g., streaming media, canvas-based applications, or dynamic pop-ups); anti-bot visual challenges (CAPTCHAs); multi-tab coordination across visually complex non-standard interfaces.
Proposed Research Questions: How can vision-language agents improve fine-grained OCR capabilities on low-resolution web elements to close the performance gap on visually grounded tasks? What execution-tracking memory mechanisms can prevent VLM agents from repeatedly executing cyclic loop actions on visual interfaces?

Paper: BrowseSafe: Understanding and Detecting Prompt Injection Within AI Browser Agents
Research Focus: Empirical evaluation of prompt injection detection fragile points in real-world HTML browser environments and proposing a fast, multi-layered detection defense (BrowseSafe).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created BrowseSafe-Bench with 14,719 HTML samples (11 attack types, 9 injection strategies, 5 distractor types, 3 linguistic styles, 5 domains) sampled from production usage. Evaluated over 20 open- and closed-weight LLMs/classifiers (including GPT-5, Sonnet 4.5, Qwen3 fine-tuned) using token lengths up to 80k without truncation.
Key Findings: General reasoning frontier models outperform specialized safety classifiers (e.g., PromptGuard-2 F1 ~0.36 vs Sonnet 4.5 ~0.86). Benign distractor elements cause a ~10-point accuracy drop (90.5% to 81.3%). Visible content manipulation evades detection at nearly twice the rate of hidden metadata injection (69-75% vs 87-92%). Multilingual attacks are the hardest to detect (76.0% accuracy). Fine-tuning Qwen3-30B (BrowseSafe) achieves an F1 of 0.904 with <1s latency.
Author-Stated Limitations: Training set contains low multilingual coverage (only 184 samples). The benchmark excludes non-textual/vision-based prompt injection attacks (e.g., adversarial images). Standard classifiers struggle when evaluating novel, unseen injection strategies (F1 drops to 0.788 in generalization ablations).
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic, multi-turn stateful evaluation where browser agents execute actions across complex navigation traps, sustained non-progress loops, or adaptive multi-step attacks. Reliance on single-pass tool output detection rather than full agent action trajectory safety monitoring.
Internal Contradictions: Authors claim PromptGuard-2 performs poorly due to low recall (0.213-0.221) and low F1 (0.35-0.36) 46, yet later argue it is 'worth considering the effort to finetune' because of CPU latency benefits and efficacy in narrow-scope environments 46, contradicting its reported failure as a viable defense.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: BrowseSafe finds that small specialized safety classifiers fail compared to large general-purpose LLMs 46, whereas IsolateGPT 47 demonstrates that architectural process isolation combined with deterministic non-LLM operators eliminates cross-app data exfiltration without needing large reasoning LLMs at the chokepoint.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks evaluation of adaptive adversaries who dynamically adjust prompt injections based on knowledge of the Qwen3 detector or chunking window boundaries. Fails to control for vision-language multimodal interaction vectors.
Untested Scenarios: Multimodal visual prompt injections (pop-ups, adversarial images), multi-agent collaborative workflows, long-term stateful memory manipulation, and real-time interactive browser environments with continuous DOM updates.
Proposed Research Questions: How can real-time prompt injection detectors maintain high recall against unseen context-aware visible content rewrites without relying on high-latency general reasoning LLMs? Can architectural trust boundaries mitigate browser agent hijacking when semantic detectors are completely bypassed?

Paper: ISOLATEGPT: An Execution Isolation Architecture for LLM-Based Agentic Systems
Research Focus: Designing an execution isolation architecture (hub-and-spoke) to prevent third-party LLM applications from compromising other apps or stealing sensitive system/user data.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Implemented a hub-and-spoke system using process isolation (seccomp, setrlimit) in Python/LangChain/LlamaIndex. Evaluated against VanillaGPT across 1,598 attack scenarios (extending InjecAgent) and 4 LangChain benchmark categories (single app, multi-app, multi-app collaboration, no apps) using OpenAI GPT-4.
Key Findings: IsolateGPT eliminates cross-app data exfiltration and unauthorized behavior manipulation by design via process sandboxing, deterministic non-LLM operators, and an Inter-Spoke Communication (ISC) protocol. Performance overhead is under 30% for 75.73% of tested queries, while maintaining identical utility/correctness compared to VanillaGPT.
Author-Stated Limitations: Relies on manual user consent/permission dialogs for raw text inter-app communications due to lack of automated natural language sanitization. System does not prevent prompt injection within the scope of a single app (only stops cross-app propagation). High latency overhead when dealing with numerous (>10) apps due to serial hub planning.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address adversarial web agents navigating complex, dynamic web environments (focuses on static API tools/apps). Lacks mechanisms to prevent resource exhaustion, sustained loops, or denial-of-wallet attacks driven by malicious tool outputs.
Internal Contradictions: Authors claim that user fatigue is minimized by a multi-tiered permission model (permanent, session, one-time) 47, but acknowledge that permanent permissions cannot be applied to irreversible or raw-text sharing actions 47, forcing frequent user intervention during realistic multi-app tasks.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: IsolateGPT claims a 20.2% attack success rate on VanillaGPT across InjecAgent-based benchmarks 47, whereas 'Silent Failures in Agentic Security Evaluation' 48 demonstrates that InjecAgent-style benchmarks contain critical harness defects (e.g., identity-based scoring, undelivered payloads) that artificially inflate reported attack success rates from 1.2% up to 21.7% or 62.8%.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation assumes benign user decision-making during permission warnings, failing to account for user habituation and blind permission clicking in realistic deployments.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web agents executing multi-step navigation, prompt injection embedded in external untrusted web pages (IPI via browsing), and dynamic multi-agent network topologies.
Proposed Research Questions: How can process isolation architectures automatically validate natural language data streams between isolated agent spokes without degrading user experience through permission dialogs? What is the resilience of hub-and-spoke architectures against adaptive attacks that exploit the hub's intent-planning LLM?

Paper: Silent Failures in Agentic Security Evaluation: A Validated Harness for Tool-Call Mediation Under Indirect Prompt Injection
Research Focus: Auditing and correcting fundamental measurement defects in agentic indirect prompt injection (IPI) evaluation harnesses to ensure valid benchmarking of tool-call chokepoint defenses.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Audited existing IPI evaluation harnesses and identified four major defect classes. Built a validated, open evaluation harness featuring machine-checkable payload placement, argument-level attacker predicates, per-scenario sandboxed environments, and full trace persistence. Evaluated gpt-5.6-terra, llama3.1:8b, gemma4:12b, and qwen2.5-coder:7b across 95 core scenarios.
Key Findings: Discovered four defect classes: D1 (silent payload non-delivery, 91% dropped), D2 (scoring success by tool identity instead of arguments), D3 (conflating environment errors/incapacity with false rejections), and D4 (lack of audit trails). On identical traces, tool-identity scoring inflated ASR from 1.2% to 21.7%. Correcting D1 and D2 dropped Llama-3.1-8B's reported ASR from 62.8% to 0%. Overturned the reported 'tool-binding barrier' of Gemma-4-12B, showing it was an artifact of environment mismatch.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluated on a single tool domain with 5 mock tools; larger multi-domain environments were not tested. Benchmark suite size (43 attack scenarios) is statistically underpowered to detect minor defense performance differences on highly robust frontier models. Evaluation used static prompt injections rather than adaptively optimized attacks.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks continuous multi-turn interactive browser testing, resource consumption tracking, or defense evaluation against dynamic, multi-stage adaptive attackers who alter strategy upon encountering chokepoint vetoes.
Internal Contradictions: Author states that static evaluation showing 0% ASR on small models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B) must not be interpreted as model safety or robustness 48, yet highlights the 62.8% to 0% drop as a primary finding overturning prior assumptions about small model vulnerabilities.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts InjecAgent 48 and IsolateGPT's benchmark evaluations 47 by proving that their reported attack success rates are largely measurement artifacts resulting from tool-identity scoring and undelivered payloads.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate adaptive, multi-turn prompt injections tailored specifically to bypass argument-matching regexes and LLM-Judge prompt policies.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent networks, complex multi-turn web browsing with dynamic DOM shifts, adaptive IPI payloads, and resource exhaustion/denial-of-wallet attacks.
Proposed Research Questions: How do chokepoint defenses perform when subjected to automated, adaptive indirect prompt injections designed with full knowledge of argument-sanitization rules? What metrics beyond ASR/FRR are required to evaluate security in long-horizon, stateful web agents?

Paper: Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting
Research Focus: Defending large language models against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks (XPIA) by improving the model's ability to distinguish safe system instructions from unsafe external data.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated Spotlighting prompt engineering techniques (delimiting, datamarking, and encoding) on synthetic datasets of 1,000 documents across GPT-family models (text-davinci-003, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4) using summarization, Q&A, and NLP benchmarks (SQuAD, SuperGLUE, IMDB).
Key Findings: Spotlighting significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from >50% to <2% in many settings; encoding works best for high-capacity models like GPT-4 without harming NLP benchmark performance, whereas datamarking preserves task performance across models.
Author-Stated Limitations: Encoding degrades performance on lower-capacity models like GPT-3.5-Turbo due to decoding hallucinations; simple delimiting can be easily subverted if system prompts leak; mechanism behind why spotlighting works lacks complete theoretical understanding.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on open-source weights/models or non-GPT architectures; no testing on multimodal inputs (vision/audio) or interactive multi-step web agent environments; reliance on simple keyword payload attack triggers.
Internal Contradictions: None noted.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Hines et al. claim system prompt defenses (safety instructions) have negligible/modest effect on ASR, whereas Wu et al. demonstrate that system safety prompts completely fail or perform worse in complex multimodal web agent settings.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation relies primarily on a synthetic dataset with uniform simple keyword payloads ('canary'), omitting diverse dynamic adversarial payloads.
Untested Scenarios: Interactive multi-turn tool-using agents, vision-language agents, multi-modal web navigation, adaptive dynamic adversarial counter-spotlighting.
Proposed Research Questions: How effective is spotlighting when applied to vision-language models receiving mixed visual/textual streams, and can adaptive attackers defeat datamarking using dynamic tokenization manipulations?

Paper: Dissecting Adversarial Robustness of Multimodal LM Agents
Research Focus: Evaluating the adversarial robustness of multimodal language model agents against targeted environmental attacks in realistic web navigation environments.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created VWA-Adv (200 targeted adversarial web tasks in VisualWebArena); proposed the Agent Robustness Evaluation (ARE) framework using agent graphs; evaluated frontier black-box models (GPT-4o, GPT-4V, Claude-3-Opus, Gemini-1.5-Pro) across base, captioner-augmented, reflexion, and tree-search agent architectures using text injection, white-box, and black-box CLIP image attacks.
Key Findings: Frontier multimodal agents can be hijacked with attack success rates up to 67% using imperceptible perturbations to a single image (<5% of page pixels); scaling inference-time compute via reflexion or tree search introduces critical vulnerabilities when evaluators or value functions are compromised.
Author-Stated Limitations: Attacks serve only as a lower bound of risks; evaluation is limited to web environments (VisualWebArena) rather than OS or mobile environments; evaluated a fixed set of existing agent algorithms.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not evaluate long-horizon multi-goal sustained attacks, resource exhaustion, or navigational loop traps in pure text/citation graphs.
Internal Contradictions: None noted.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Wu et al. show that adding reflection/evaluator components can increase overall vulnerability (ASR increases from 31% to 36%), contradicting general assumptions that reflection uniformly enhances agent performance and self-correction in benign/adversarial settings.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Attacks were evaluated on pre-filtered tasks where the benign model succeeded, which may skew the baseline distribution compared to unfiltered real-world task streams.
Untested Scenarios: Operating system desktop agents, multi-agent cooperative networks under joint environmental attacks, and defense combinations involving cryptographic provenance.
Proposed Research Questions: Can agent architectures isolate evaluator and value function components into unprivileged execution environments to prevent adversarial influence propagation?

Paper: How Adversarial Environments Mislead Agentic AI?
Research Focus: Investigating environmental deception in tool-using AI agents via Adversarial Environmental Injection (AEI), establishing two orthogonal attack surfaces: breadth (epistemic drift) and depth (navigational loops/policy collapse).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Developed POTEMKIN, an MCP-compatible Model-in-the-Tool evaluation harness; conducted 11,000+ task runs across 5 frontier base agents (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Llama-3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSeek-V3) and 5 post-2025 frontier models (GPT-5.2, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3.5, Kimi-K2.5) on citation graph topologies (Semantic Scholar dataset).
Key Findings: Discovered the Robustness Schism: epistemic robustness to content poisoning does not predict navigational robustness to structural traps (transfer AUC ~0.55-0.58); depth attacks induce trap entry rates up to 96% and waste 44-73% of step budgets; agents exhibit the 'Punishment of Honesty', penalizing scientific hedging on true claims at 2.1x the rate of confident claims.
Author-Stated Limitations: Empirical scope focused primarily on citation-graph-based agent tasks; defense evaluations limited to lightweight runtime filters (perplexity filtering, spotlighting); model snapshot evaluations cannot anticipate future architectural changes.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not evaluate depth attacks on visual web interfaces (e.g., VisualWebArena DOM graphs) or complex multi-tool API orchestration chains.
Internal Contradictions: None noted.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Zhan et al. find that spotlighting prompt defenses cause a 25–29 percentage point utility degradation on clean inputs, whereas Hines et al. claim spotlighting transformations (datamarking) yield negligible detrimental impacts on task performance.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Unconditional vs. conditional engagement metrics must be controlled; unengaged runs (agents failing to call tools) falsely appear robust if not isolated.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent graph navigation, real-time dynamic graph updates with adversarial counter-defense adaptation, and hardware-enforced tool sandboxing.
Proposed Research Questions: How can agent planning algorithms incorporate topological cycle detection to prevent navigational loop traps without degrading search performance on complex decision graphs?

Paper: AI Agent Traps (Franklin et al., 2026)
Research Focus: Taxonomy and framework of environmental security threats ("Agent Traps") targeting autonomous web-browsing AI agents across six architectural layers.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Conceptual taxonomisation and literature synthesis across 123 referenced works covering adversarial machine learning, web security, and multi-agent systems.
Key Findings: Identifies 6 threat categories: Content Injection (perception), Semantic Manipulation (reasoning), Cognitive State (memory/learning), Behavioural Control (action), Systemic (multi-agent dynamics), and Human-in-the-Loop traps.
Author-Stated Limitations: Systemic and Human-in-the-Loop traps remain largely theoretical; many trap categories lack standardized benchmarks; legal/accountability gaps remain unresolved.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks direct empirical validation or experimental implementation of the proposed systemic multi-agent attacks (e.g., tacit collusion, interdependence cascades) on contemporary LLM agent frameworks.
Internal Contradictions: None identified; theoretical claims align with cited sub-domain literature.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts claims from Bhagwatkar et al. (2025) regarding firewall completeness: Franklin et al. highlight that input/output filtering alone cannot prevent RAG/latent memory poisoning or systemic multi-agent traps.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate performance or safety trade-offs (e.g., latency, token cost, utility degradation) when implementing proposed ecosystem or training mitigations.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent cascade dynamics under real-time financial or competitive market settings; direct exploitation of human overseers through automated approval fatigue.
Proposed Research Questions: How do correlated model architectures accelerate interdependence cascades in open virtual agent economies?

Paper: Identifying AI Web Scrapers Using Canary Tokens (Seiden et al., 2026)
Research Focus: Empirical identification and mapping of real-time web scraping User-Agents serving production AI chatbots using canary tokens.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Deployed 20 synthetic websites with dynamic canary tokens across 3 access conditions (online, offline, robots.txt disallowed) and evaluated 22 production AI chatbots over several months.
Key Findings: 18 of 22 chatbots were mapped to scrapers; chatbots heavily rely on third-party search engines (e.g., Googlebot, Bravebot) or generic browser User-Agents; robots.txt and site takedowns fail to prevent cached content retrieval.
Author-Stated Limitations: Small dataset of websites (20 sites); single geographic vantage point (US university network); match score heuristics ignore single-token hits, potentially causing false negatives.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not test non-textual modalities (images, audio, video) or long-term pre-training data scraping pipelines beyond real-time inference retrieval.
Internal Contradictions: None identified; empirical token matches consistently support findings.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts standard web governance assumptions (and official publisher disclosures) that robots.txt policies or taking sites offline effectively opt out content from AI chatbot availability.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Unable to fully control for search engine indexing lag versus active intentional disregard of robots.txt directives by AI scrapers.
Untested Scenarios: Varying geographic IP locations, complex TLS/browser fingerprinting anti-bot evasion, and multimodal canary token injections.
Proposed Research Questions: Can canary token attribution be preserved and verified when data propagates through multi-party retrieval supply chains?

Paper: Indirect Prompt Injections: Are Firewalls All You Need, or Stronger Benchmarks? (Bhagwatkar et al., 2025)
Research Focus: Evaluation of modular agent-tool boundary firewalls (Minimizer & Sanitizer) against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) attacks and critique of existing security benchmarks.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Tested Tool-Input (Minimizer) and Tool-Output (Sanitizer) firewalls using LLM prompts across four public benchmarks: AgentDojo, Agent Security Bench (ASB), InjecAgent, and Tau-Bench across multiple LLMs (GPT-4o, Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen3). Identified and fixed benchmark design flaws.
Key Findings: Tool-Output Firewall achieves 0% or lowest Attack Success Rate (ASR) across benchmarks without reducing task utility; existing benchmarks (ASB, AgentDojo) suffer from forced tool injections, missing task context, and brittle scoring metrics.
Author-Stated Limitations: Sanitizer alone relies on static/fixed prompt filters; Current benchmarks utilize rigid, context-agnostic attack prompts that fail to model adaptive real-world adversaries.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address stateful attacks targeting long-term memory (e.g., latent memory poisoning) or multi-agent communication channels outside the immediate tool-call boundary.
Internal Contradictions: Minimizer firewall reduces ASR but significantly degrades task utility on certain suites due to over-aggressive argument redaction, partially conflicting with the universal efficacy claim of the combined firewall approach.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Claims complete defense against tool-based IPIs using simple firewalls, whereas Franklin et al. (2026) show that advanced IPIs (e.g., steganographic payloads, dynamic cloaking, persona hyperstition) subvert standard text-based output sanitizers.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate adaptive adversaries who format malicious instructions specifically to bypass the Sanitizer's system prompt instructions.
Untested Scenarios: Adaptive multi-turn attacks where injected payloads are split across multiple consecutive tool outputs or non-textual tool response formats.
Proposed Research Questions: How can Tool-Output Sanitizers defend against adaptive prompt injections designed specifically to manipulate the Sanitizer model's evaluation logic?

Paper: Beyond Max Tokens: Stealthy Resource Amplification via Tool Calling Chains in LLM Agents
Research Focus: Stealthy multi-turn economic Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks on LLM agents operating at the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool layer to maximize resource consumption while preserving task correctness.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Text-only edits to MCP tool server responses optimized via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS); evaluated on 6 target LLMs (Qwen-3-32B, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Llama-DeepSeek-70B, Mistral Large, Seed-32B, GLM-4.5-Air) using ToolBench (105 tools, 261 queries) and BFCL (80 tools, 203 queries) benchmarks on a simulated qwen-agent harness.
Key Findings: Extends trajectory lengths beyond 60,000 tokens, inflates token budgets by up to 658x, increases energy consumption by 100–560x, raises peak GPU KV-cache usage to 35–74%, halves throughput of concurrent benign workloads, and evades PPL filters, self-monitoring, and trajectory safety judges (Qwen-Guard-3, Llama-Guard-3).
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluation conducted in a controlled agent simulator with stubbed tool payloads, restricted to single-tool single-turn benchmark subsets, and focuses primarily on structured numeric calibration sequences rather than exploring all long-form text patterns.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation under multi-tool multi-step long-horizon agent workflows, real-world non-stubbed networked tool environments, and dynamic agent architectures with non-fixed system prompts or active anti-loop defenses.
Internal Contradictions: Claims the attack preserves task correctness without altering payload semantics, yet introduces artificial multi-turn delay arguments and calibration sequences that modify tool feedback semantics during intermediate steps.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts classic DoS approaches (e.g., Engorgio, P-DoS, Auto-DoS) which rely on white-box/black-box single-turn prompt injection and cause noticeable off-task verbosity or task failure; directly contrasts with Overthink by moving the long-output trigger from RAG/thinking steps to tool-calling steps across multiple turns.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for the impact of varying system prompt instructions across different agent frameworks or the effect of real network latency and rate limits on tool execution loops.
Untested Scenarios: Performance under multi-agent collaboration setups, real-time tool execution environments with live API calls, dynamic tool selection among multiple available servers, and against behavioral rate-limiting defenses.
Proposed Research Questions: How can agent runtimes effectively detect protocol-compliant but semantically redundant tool-calling loops without harming legitimate multi-step task execution?
Supporting Citations: Kumar et al. (2025) 55, Dong et al. (2025) 55, Zhang et al. (2025c) 55, Zhang et al. (2025a) 55

Paper: Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs
Research Focus: Fine-tuning LLMs with Retriever-Aware Training (RAT) to generate accurate API calls, handle documentation updates at test time, obey constraints, and reduce argument hallucinations.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Fine-tuned LLaMA-7B (Gorilla) using self-instruct datasets across ~1,600 APIs from TorchHub, TensorFlow Hub, and HuggingFace (APIBench); evaluated zero-shot and with retrievers (BM25, GPT-Index, Oracle) using an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) subtree matching metric.
Key Findings: Gorilla outperforms GPT-4 and Claude in writing accurate API calls while significantly reducing argument hallucination; RAT enables adaptation to test-time API documentation updates and user constraints (e.g., parameter limits, accuracy thresholds).
Author-Stated Limitations: Limited execution testing of the generated supporting code (only tested on a sample of 100 outputs); heavily relies on retrieval quality when using external retrievers (imperfect retrievers degrade accuracy).
Inferred Research Gaps: No evaluation of multi-step tool execution sequences, stateful multi-turn agent interactions, or resilience to malicious or adversarial tool documentation.
Internal Contradictions: States that AST subtree matching evaluates functional correctness, yet acknowledges that 6% of AST-verified correct calls failed when executed end-to-end due to bugs in generated supporting code.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates that fine-tuning with retrieval outperforms standard in-context prompting for API calling, challenging claims that zero-shot/few-shot prompting on frontier models (e.g., GPT-4) is sufficient for tool usage.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for potential data contamination or overlap between self-instruct training data generation (via GPT-4) and evaluation prompts.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-turn tool execution chains, stateful session interactions, handling malformed/adversarial API documentation, and real-time execution in interactive environments.
Proposed Research Questions: How does Retriever-Aware Training perform when exposed to untrusted or maliciously poisoned API documentation in agent context?
Supporting Citations: Schick et al. (2023) 55, Zhou et al. (2022) 55, Patil et al. (2025) 55

Paper: LoopTrap: Termination Poisoning Attacks on LLM Agents
Research Focus: Formalizing Termination Poisoning attacks that inject prompts into retrieved context to corrupt an agent's internal progress evaluation, preventing termination and inducing unbounded execution loops.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Systematic evaluation of 10 attack strategies across 8 LLM agents (Gemini-3-Pro, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-R1, Kimi-K2-Thinking, GLM-5, Grok-4, Claude Sonnet 4.5) on 60 GAIA benchmark tasks. Introduced LoopTrap for automated profiling (4 behavioral dimensions) and adaptive trap synthesis.
Key Findings: LoopTrap achieves an average step amplification of 3.57x (peak 25x) and token overhead of 3.93x; reveals model-specific vulnerability profiles along authority compliance, phased progression, verification thoroughness, and recursion susceptibility.
Author-Stated Limitations: Profiling schema is limited to 4 behavioral dimensions derived from 10 strategies; evaluation uses simulated tool environments without real external service calls; focused primarily on single-agent architectures.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of testing against active defense systems or runtimes with explicit anti-loop mechanisms; unexamined impact on multi-agent messaging networks.
Internal Contradictions: Claims the attack does not alter final output or task success, yet some prolonged execution paths lead to tool errors or altered trajectory conclusions in complex tasks.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts traditional indirect prompt injection literature that assumes attacker goals are limited to output manipulation or data exfiltration, showing that agent control flow itself is an effective attack vector.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate the effect of strict runtime execution timeouts or hard token/cost budget caps enforced at the agent framework level during the empirical study.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent coordination loops with inter-agent message poisoning, dynamic real-time web browsing environments, and environments with anti-prompt-injection input filtering.
Proposed Research Questions: Can sandboxed progress signal verification modules effectively detect termination poisoning without introducing false positives in legitimately complex tasks?
Supporting Citations: Greshake et al. (2023) 55, Mialon et al. (2024) 55, Yao et al. (2023) 55, Debenedetti et al. (2024) 55

Paper: An Illusion of Progress? Assessing the Current State of Web Agents
Research Focus: Rigorously evaluating frontier web agents on realistic, unconstrained online environments to reveal benchmark over-optimism and develop reliable automatic trajectory evaluation.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Constructed Online-Mind2Web (300 online tasks across 136 real-world websites across 12 domains and 3 difficulty tiers). Evaluated 6 web agents (SeeAct, Browser Use, Agent-E, Claude Computer Use 3.5/3.7, OpenAI Operator) via human annotation, and introduced WebJudge (LLM-as-a-judge with key screenshot filtering) validated on AgentRewardBench (1,302 trajectories).
Key Findings: Reported ~90% success rates on benchmarks like WebVoyager are inflated due to shortcut solutions (e.g., simple Google Search solves 51%) and unreliable evaluators. On Online-Mind2Web, most agents achieve ~30% success, while top agents (Claude 3.7, Operator) reach 56.3% and 61.3%. WebJudge achieves ~85-87% agreement with humans.
Author-Stated Limitations: WebJudge computational cost/latency scales with trajectory length; reliance on static threshold parameters for key screenshot selection; exclusion of Google Search during evaluation limits natural user strategies.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address agent resilience against deliberate adversarial web traps or dynamic anti-bot mechanisms during long-horizon navigation.
Internal Contradictions: Operator achieved highest success rate (61.3%) but exhibited the lowest efficiency score (2.6x human steps, taking up to 44 minutes), highlighting a stark conflict between task completion and operational resource cost.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts WebVoyager self-reported agent benchmark scores (e.g., Browser Use reported 89% on WebVoyager vs 30% verified on Online-Mind2Web).
Missing Controls/Confounders: Varying context window limits across agent frameworks; potential web structure changes during live evaluation pass.
Untested Scenarios: Web navigation under real-world dynamic CAPTCHAs, bot protections, or non-deterministic payment/checkout flows.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agents improve long-horizon planning and numeric/temporal constraint adherence without sacrificing execution efficiency?

Paper: LoginTrap: Uncovering Task-Agnostic Phishing-Style Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks against LLM-based Web Agents
Research Focus: Task-agnostic phishing-style indirect prompt injection attacks (LoginTrap) targeting the login authentication boundary of LLM-based web agents to cause sensitive information leakage.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluation across 80 cloned webpages from Mind2Web (5 domains: Travel, Service, Information, Shopping, Entertainment), 1,175 user tasks, 4 LLM backbones (GPT-4o, Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-V3.2), and 3 web agent architectures (Browser-Use, LiteWebAgent, Skyvern) using a fuzzing-inspired generation pipeline with shadow evaluator models and MCTS seed selection; maximum 5 interaction steps per task.
Key Findings: LoginTrap achieved an average end-to-end Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 86% and Login Entry Rate (LER) of 93% across LLM backbones, and an average ASR of 79% across agent architectures; 100% Page Exploitability Rate (PER) was reached across all backbones, demonstrating that task-agnostic login inducement is a general and persistent risk across different model families and architectural paradigms.
Author-Stated Limitations: Incomplete form filling, early termination, or returning to the original task by certain models (e.g., GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3.2) caused larger gaps between LER and ASR; a small number of webpages remained unexploited under LiteWebAgent and Skyvern within the attempt budget.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on complex multi-factor authentication (MFA) or OAuth/SSO login flows; limited scope to a maximum step budget of 5 steps; lack of real-time adaptive defense mechanisms specifically reasoning about the task-necessity of authentication.
Internal Contradictions: High LER (initial login path entry) does not always convert directly into high ASR (actual sensitive credential leakage) due to execution interruptions, showing a friction point between task plan revision and full form completion.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts traditional prompt injection studies (e.g., WASP, AgentDojo) that assume attacks require knowledge of the user task or specific agent prompt templates to succeed, proving that task-agnostic page-context injections alone are sufficient.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Impact of pre-existing authenticated browser states/session cookies; variation in visual rendering encodings (e.g., Set-of-Mark vs raw screenshots); baseline behavior on genuine dynamic authentication workflows vs controlled local test environments.
Untested Scenarios: Real-world web environments with CAPTCHAs, two-factor authentication (2FA/MFA), dynamic JavaScript obfuscation, cross-domain SSO popups, or long-horizon agent trajectories (>5 steps).
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agents dynamically verify whether an authentication request is structurally necessary for a benign user task before engaging in form submission? What runtime defense mechanisms can prevent credential leakage when login flows are induced by page-level context?
Supporting Citations: Mind2Web 59, Browser-Use 59, Skyvern 59, LiteWebAgent 59

Paper: Measuring What the Crawler Sees: Discovery Curves, Core Persistence, and Shell Dynamics in Longitudinal Web Crawls
Research Focus: Mathematical urn modeling and closed-form parameter recovery (coverage, churn, core/shell decomposition) for longitudinal web crawling across different web scale archives.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Longitudinal analysis comparing two archives with contrasting architectures: Common Crawl (2020–2025 monthly snapshots at domain granularity) and German Academic Web (GAW, 2013–2019 biannual snapshots at URL granularity); fitting single-component and two-component urn models to pairwise containment g(Δt) and discovery curves U(s, T).
Key Findings: Single-component homogeneous urn models fail because pairwise containment (recurrence-weighted) and discovery curves (fresh-discovery-weighted) yield contradictory parameter fits; introducing a two-component urn model with a persistent core fraction (κ ≈ 0.4 for Common Crawl domain level, κ ≈ 0.06 for GAW URL level) reconciles the cross-source disagreement and successfully parameterizes life expectancy, sampled time, and hidden time.
Author-Stated Limitations: A residual disagreement on shell coverage c∂ remains, indicating that the shell itself is non-homogeneous; the model does not include a URL rebirth mechanism (short dormancies fold into hidden time); parameter fitting relies on scalar summaries rather than full rank-resolved rank dynamics.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of fine-grained continuous rank-resolved rigidity profiles μ(r) across harmonic-centrality thresholds; absence of real-time adaptive crawling policy evaluations using the recovered parameters.
Internal Contradictions: Independent fits of the single-component urn model on containment vs discovery curve produce divergent values for survival α and coverage c on the exact same dataset.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Challenges traditional single-urn or simple capture-recapture web sampling models by proving that web crawling datasets inherently manifest a two-component core/shell structure.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Operator policy shifts over time (e.g., changing host budgets, harmonic centrality cutoffs, crawl schedule gaps during 2021-2022); web content anti-crawling/blocking measures.
Untested Scenarios: Evaluation on real-time dynamic web content changes, streaming web archives, or web agent traversal patterns.
Proposed Research Questions: How can crawler operators map scalar core fractions (κ) to continuous harmonic-centrality rank profiles to optimize web budget allocation? How do rank dynamics and diffusion affect long-term URL hidden time?
Supporting Citations: Paris 59, Heritrix/GAW 59, Common Crawl stats 59

Paper: The Hidden Dangers of Browsing AI Agents
Research Focus: End-to-end security evaluation, vulnerability assessment, and MAESTRO-based threat modeling of open-source LLM-based autonomous browsing agents, focusing on Browser Use.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: White-box security assessment of Browser Use (v0.1.44), static code analysis, proof-of-concept exploit development for domain restriction bypass (CVE-2025-47241) and prompt-injection-based credential exfiltration; threat mapping across all 7 MAESTRO layers.
Key Findings: Browser Use suffers from a critical FQDN validation flaw (CVE-2025-47241, CVSS 9.3) caused by naive URL parsing with Basic Auth syntax allowing allowlist bypass, and is highly vulnerable to prompt injection via appended HTML web content that can exfiltrate sensitive credentials and canary tokens.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluation focused primarily on the open-source Browser Use framework due to proprietary closed-source constraints of commercial agents; model size impact on adversarial robustness remains empirically inconclusive.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of empirical benchmark evaluations testing formal analyzers or planner-executor isolation across large-scale real-world web agent task sets.
Internal Contradictions: The built-in credential handling mechanism (replacing sensitive credentials with canary tokens during inference) acts as an ineffective workaround because appended raw HTML content can induce the agent to output or navigate to attacker-controlled endpoints carrying those tokens.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates that relying on surface-level input sanitization or simple domain allowlists fails to secure browsing agents, contradicting claims that prompt masking alone provides sufficient privacy.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Variations in LLM backend robustness (e.g., comparing smaller fine-tuned models vs GPT-4o); impact of multi-tab state isolation.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent collaborative mesh environments (MCP/A2A) with active adversarial agent nodes under realistic load.
Proposed Research Questions: To what extent can formal security analyzers with hard constraint enforcement mitigate prompt injection without reducing web agent task completion rates?
Supporting Citations: Browser Use 59, WebVoyager 59, MAESTRO 59, CVE-2025-47241 59

Paper: Autonomy Comes with Costs: Detecting Denial-of-Service Vulnerabilities Caused by Resource Abusing in LLM-based Agents
Research Focus: Detecting Denial-of-Service (DoS) vulnerabilities caused by resource exhaustion and improper resource management in LLM-based agents.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Static analysis to locate resource-consuming operations and identify resource lifecycles (short-lived, long-lived, full-lifecycle); directed grey-box fuzzing (AgentDoS) leveraging LLMs for prompt generation/mutation; evaluated on 20 open-source LLM agent web applications.
Key Findings: Discovered 36 zero-day DoS vulnerabilities in 16 agents (15 assigned CVE IDs); AgentDoS achieved 95.2% lifecycle identification accuracy, 100% precision, and 94.7% recall, significantly outperforming AgentFuzz.
Author-Stated Limitations: Requires source code access (white-box/grey-box static analysis) and cannot be directly applied to black-box commercial agents like OpenAI GPTs or Coze without adaptation.
Inferred Research Gaps: Black-box resource consumption testing for proprietary agents using side-channel signals (e.g., latency, error codes) remains unexplored.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; claims regarding AgentDoS performance align with the empirical benchmark results.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None detected.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation relies on hardware constraints imposed via Docker containers (minimum specs like 4GB RAM, 10GB disk); varying real-world cloud autoscaling/quota conditions were not evaluated as controls.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-modal prompt inputs, multi-agent collaborative workflows, and black-box commercial LLM agent platforms.
Proposed Research Questions: How can side-channel indicators be used to guide black-box resource-exhaustion fuzzing in proprietary LLM agent platforms?

Paper: SecAlign: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Preference Optimization
Research Focus: Defending LLMs and LLM-integrated systems against prompt injection attacks using preference optimization.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Formulates prompt injection defense as a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) task using prompt-injected inputs with secure/insecure output pairs; evaluated on 5 open-weight models (Llama and Mistral variants) across 6 optimization-free/optimization-based attacks and multiple utility/security benchmarks.
Key Findings: SecAlign reduces attack success rates (ASR) to <10% for strong optimization-based attacks (e.g., GCG, AdvPrompter) and 0% for optimization-free attacks while preserving model utility.
Author-Stated Limitations: Only applies when instruction and data parts are explicitly separated by delimiters; less effective when injections occur at the start/middle of data rather than the end; cannot defend against jailbreaks or multi-turn/multi-modal injections.
Inferred Research Gaps: Robustness against adaptive prompt injections in complex multi-turn web-agent workflows and un-delimited data contexts remains unaddressed.
Internal Contradictions: None detected.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None detected.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate performance under real-world prompt templates where instruction-data boundaries are fluid or implicit.
Untested Scenarios: Defending against multi-turn indirect prompt injections in autonomous web/GUI agents.
Proposed Research Questions: Can preference-optimization defenses be extended to multi-turn agent execution traces without explicit data delimiters?

Paper: The Impact of Crawl Policy on Web Search Effectiveness
Research Focus: Evaluating the impact of web crawler link-based selection policies on web search retrieval effectiveness (maxNDCG).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduced maxNDCG metric using human relevance judgment pooling across 10,570 queries; conducted large-scale crawling simulations (1 billion and 100 million page scale) comparing PageRank, Indegree, Trans-Domain Indegree, and domain-budgeting policies over single and multiple iterations.
Key Findings: PageRank is the most effective and stable selection policy across multiple crawl iterations; Trans-Domain Indegree performs well initially but suffers from instability and high churn across iterations; domain limits based on entry points improve efficiency.
