Author-Stated Limitations: The sandbox method relied on static snapshots and did not capture real-time dynamic web changes during multi-iteration crawls; spam and content freshness were not factored into the evaluation metric.
Inferred Research Gaps: Integration of web crawl selection policies with modern semantic vector search and neural retrieval effectiveness remains unstudied.
Internal Contradictions: None detected.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None detected.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Search engine index freshness and duplicate/near-duplicate page filtering were not controlled in the maxNDCG calculation.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web pages designed specifically to manipulate crawl selection policies in modern AI agent web navigation contexts.
Proposed Research Questions: How do traditional link-graph crawl selection policies impact the retrieval context quality for modern RAG-based Web LLM agents?

Paper: Luo and Chen (2026) - One Polluted Page Is Enough: Evaluating Web Content Pollution in Generative Recommenders
Research Focus: Evaluating search-augmented LLM recommender vulnerability to Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and web content pollution.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces FORGE benchmark (225 real products across 15 categories). Tested 12 commercial/open-weights LLMs under controlled local content rewrites (entity replacement, passage injection, full synthesis) across Chinese and English web search contexts.
Key Findings: All 12 LLMs are vulnerable; top-3 replacement yields up to 73.8% fooled rate, while a single rank-1 polluted page yields up to 27%. Reasoning capability amplifies vulnerability (+9 to +18 pp) by generating spurious social proof. Standard defenses like skepticism prompting backfire on closed-source models (+24 pp).
Author-Stated Limitations: Attack design is unoptimized entity replacement (lower bound); dose-response and trace analyses restricted to open-weights subset; Local Life scenario fixed geographically to Shenzhen; frozen static web retrieval snapshot (2026-04).
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic, multi-turn adversarial web navigation evaluation; missing evaluation of non-English/multi-region GEO mechanics; absence of active retrieval-time grounding defenses.
Internal Contradictions: Authors note skepticism prompting is intended to reduce reliance on unfamiliar brands, yet empirical testing shows it increases vulnerability across closed-source models by forcing deeper engagement with planted entities.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts long-context QA findings (e.g., Liu et al., 2024a) which demonstrate a U-shaped 'lost in the middle' curve; FORGE demonstrates a strict, pure primacy effect where only rank-1 placement significantly fools models.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Controlled density of injected text versus surrounding authentic text in passage injection (A2 vs A3); uncontrolled pretraining brand familiarity bias across open vs. closed models.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-turn conversational web navigation traps; real-time live web injection (unsimulated); adversarial SEO combined with indirect prompt injections.
Proposed Research Questions: How can retrieval-time source-credibility weighting and cross-document agreement filters be integrated into search-augmented LLMs without destroying legitimate recommendation utility?

Paper: Chen et al. (2026) - The Compliance Trap: Diagnosing How AI Agents Consume Conflicting Memory
Research Focus: Diagnosing how autonomous web agents consume retrieved memory across multi-step action trajectories when presented with conflicting guidance.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Formulates Entry-Propagation-Recovery (E-P-R) framework. Evaluates 5 LLM agent backbones (Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, Gemini-3) across WebArena (77 memory-sensitive tasks) and MemTrapBench (231 custom long-horizon tasks) under early, persistent, and late memory injection schedules.
Key Findings: Identifies the 'compliance trap': agents exhibit high, scale-independent compliance (~65%) to conflicting memories. Stronger models suffer higher absolute damage (up to -26 pp) because compliance drops performance to a uniform low floor, erasing baseline capability. Trajectory-level recovery exists (55-80%) but fails to translate to task success due to irreversible environmental changes.
Author-Stated Limitations: Long-horizon evaluation restricted to web-browsing environments; no novel memory architecture or training-time mitigation proposed.
Inferred Research Gaps: Unexplored resilience of agents in non-web environments (OSWorld, terminal/shell execution); lack of real-time conflict-detection mechanisms before action execution.
Internal Contradictions: Agents frequently execute trajectory-level realignment actions (55-80% recovery rate) after adopting conflicting memory, yet final task success remains near zero (1.3%), showing a disconnect between action-level self-correction and task-level state recovery.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts claims from self-correction benchmarks (e.g., Reflexion, Shinn et al., 2023) by demonstrating that internal reasoning and verbal feedback fail to correct trajectory deviations without external environment feedback.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Impact of action-history length versus context window degradation on memory compliance; potential bias from hand-authored vs LLM-generated memory structure.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent memory sharing environments; adversarial memory poisoning in multi-session enterprise tools.
Proposed Research Questions: How can control policies detect memory-state conflicts at the 'Entry' phase before irreversible UI/environment actions are committed?

Paper: Drouin et al. (2024) - WorkArena: How Capable are Web Agents at Solving Common Knowledge Work Tasks?
Research Focus: Measuring the capability of LLM-based web agents to automate knowledge work tasks in enterprise software systems (ServiceNow).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces WorkArena (33 tasks, 19,912 instances across 6 functional categories) and BrowserGym (OpenAI Gym web environment with multimodal observations and Playwright action space). Evaluates GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, and Llama3-70B zero-shot agents with up to 15 steps per task.
Key Findings: Current web agents exhibit a severe performance gap on enterprise software. GPT-4o achieves 42.7% overall success, outperforming Llama3-70B (17.9%) and GPT-3.5 (6.1%). Tasks requiring complex UI interaction (such as list filtering) yield a 0% success rate across all models due to non-standard HTML widgets and large context DOMs.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluated agents capped at 15 steps per episode (insufficient for complex workflows without multi-action mode); benchmark lacks long-horizon compositional tasks across multiple enterprise apps.
Inferred Research Gaps: Evaluation lacks adversarial robustness testing, memory poisoning, navigation traps, or recovery from invalid UI state changes.
Internal Contradictions: Enabling 'think history' (memory of previous chain-of-thought outputs) was expected to assist multi-page tasks but empirically degraded performance on WorkArena and MiniWoB by causing agents to rigidly adhere to early erroneous decisions.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates that text-only AXTree representation with GPT-4o outperforms multimodal vision-augmented setups (GPT-4o-V with Set-of-Mark), contrasting with findings on benchmarks like WebVoyager (He et al., 2024) where visual grounding provided significant gains.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Confounding effect of context truncation (due to 8K/16K window limits on Llama3/GPT-3.5 vs 128K on GPT-4o) on agent reasoning quality.
Untested Scenarios: Agent execution under adversarial prompt injection, corrupted enterprise database states, or dynamic authorization changes.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agent architectures maintain long-context DOM understanding and overcome non-standard UI controls without collapsing into repetitive action loops?

Paper: ANDROIDWORLD: A Dynamic Benchmarking Environment for Autonomous Agents
Research Focus: Dynamic interactive environment and benchmarking for autonomous agents controlling mobile operating systems (Android).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created 116 programmatic tasks across 20 Android apps using dynamically generated parameters and system-state reward mechanisms via ADB. Evaluated baseline M3A agent variants, SeeAct, and humans across models (GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemma 2 27B) using single-seed and multi-seed robustness setups.
Key Findings: Best agent (M3A with GPT-4 Turbo text/accessibility tree) achieved a 30.6% success rate on AndroidWorld vs. 80.0% human performance. Multimodal SoM visual input did not consistently improve text-only performance. Performance varies significantly across random parameter seeds (26.3%–33.2%). Adapting desktop web agent SeeAct to mobile yielded inferior performance.
Author-Stated Limitations: Relies exclusively on open-source F-Droid apps and built-in system apps (no login-requiring or popular commercial apps). Excluded 12 MiniWoB++ tasks due to emulator rendering, touch compatibility, or real-time constraints. LLM-generated task definitions require manual human review due to field errors and hallucinated parameters.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on complex, multi-account commercial apps with dynamic network dependencies; absence of adversarial or malicious UI traps (e.g., pop-up traps, dynamic web prompts, or system security alerts).
Internal Contradictions: Claims M3A uses ReAct and Reflexion-style dynamic updates and reflection, yet error analysis reveals agents frequently fail to recover from simple grounding or mistyping errors and loop indefinitely until the step cap.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Directly contradicts desktop web benchmark findings (e.g., WebArena, VisualWebArena) where multimodal visual groundings (SoM) significantly outperform text-only representations; on Android native apps, accessibility tree text-only input yielded higher success rates.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Uncontrolled LLM temperature/sampling non-determinism during multi-step runs across evaluation trials; lack of isolation controls for dynamic system background states or OS latency delays.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial UI environments (e.g., malicious pop-ups, phishing prompts, dark patterns); long-horizon workflows requiring sustained multi-app memory or user re-authentication.
Proposed Research Questions: How can mobile autonomous agents maintain state memory across multi-app workflows without relying on explicit text prompt context windows? How robust are OS-level agents when confronted with dynamic adversarial navigation traps or deceptive UI elements?

Paper: Detection of Crawler Traps: Formalization and Implementation—Defeating Protection on Internet and on the TOR Network
Research Focus: Formalizing, detecting, and escaping dynamic crawler traps deployed by websites to impede automated bots.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Formulated information-theoretic distance metrics (e.g., Dottyback, Handfish, Shark, Archerfish) based on word distributions and bi-grams. Tested metrics on a custom 13-source dataset (6,500 total pages) spanning regular websites (Wikipedia, StackOverflow, CPAN) and active crawler traps (notEvil, Poison, Tarantula) using confidence interval overlapping analysis and robust trimmed k-means clustering.
Key Findings: Custom distances (Dottyback, Handfish, Shark) significantly outperformed standard state-of-the-art information distances (Jensen-Shannon, Hellinger, Bhattacharyya) in separating regular web pages from crawler traps, achieving near-zero overlapping rates under high confidence thresholds.
Author-Stated Limitations: The study focused primarily on developing discriminating information distances; full operational real-time bot integration, classifier selection, and online escaping execution were left for future work.
Inferred Research Gaps: Evaluated text/HTML content distribution static differences but did not evaluate modern interactive JavaScript-driven dynamic traps, AJAX application state loops, or adversarial visual traps.
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Assumes crawler traps are designed primarily to consume network bandwidth and lock web crawlers into infinite content loops, whereas general crawling literature (e.g., Olston & Najork) highlights that many traps are accidental (e.g., infinite calendar interfaces) or designed for SEO link manipulation.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation used a relatively small set of 4 crawler trap implementations; lacked controls for highly dynamic non-trap websites (e.g., live sports feeds, social media streams) that exhibit high content churn.
Untested Scenarios: Real-time, online navigation through complex web applications where traps dynamically adapt content based on detected crawler behavior or user-agent signatures.
Proposed Research Questions: Can information-theoretic distance metrics detect dynamic JavaScript/AJAX-based crawler traps on mobile web environments in real time without causing significant latency degradation?

Paper: Web Crawling
Research Focus: Comprehensive survey of the science, architecture, algorithms, and challenges of web crawling.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Systematic literature survey covering crawler architecture, batch and incremental crawl ordering algorithms, politeness policies, duplicate/mirror detection, web spam/cloaking countermeasures, and deep web crawling techniques.
Key Findings: Optimal crawl scheduling depends heavily on objective functions (e.g., uniform resource allocation outperforms proportional allocation under binary freshness, whereas age-based freshness requires continuous scaling with change rates). Highly scalable crawlers require specialized disk-based streaming data structures (e.g., Mercator DUE, IRLbot BEAST).
Author-Stated Limitations: Identifies broad open research gaps including lack of parameter tuning frameworks, absence of page retirement/deletion policies, disconnect between theoretical crawl ordering models and disk-bound architecture realities, and undeveloped deep web extraction paradigms.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address modern LLM-driven web agents, dynamic multi-modal UI interaction traps, or complex client-side single-page applications (SPAs).
Internal Contradictions: None identified.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Frames crawler traps as an architectural and resource allocation challenge to be managed via domain budgets and heuristics (e.g., IRLbot BEAST), whereas security-oriented literature (e.g., David et al.) treats crawler traps as discrete, adversarial protection mechanisms requiring dynamic distance-based classification to escape.
Missing Controls/Confounders: N/A (Survey paper).
Untested Scenarios: Crawling autonomous agent environment interfaces, handling dynamic OAuth/CAPTCHA security barriers, and managing client-side state storage across complex web applications.
Proposed Research Questions: How can continuous incremental crawl scheduling strategies be adapted to prioritize dynamic UI action spaces for autonomous agent navigation?

Paper: EvoCrawl: Exploring Web Application Code and State using Evolutionary Search
Research Focus: Automated black-box web application vulnerability crawling and state exploration using evolutionary search and dynamic dependency tracking.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Combines a Page Collection Module (PM) and an Evolutionary Search Module (ESM) using a genetic algorithm with fitness functions (rewarding form submissions, filled inputs, file uploads, JS events, and penalizing invisible elements) and dynamic browser dependency tracking. Evaluated against BlackWidow, JAK, and CrawlJAX on 10 modern web applications (WordPress, HotCRP, Dokuwiki, Drupal, Humhub, Opencart, phpBB, ImpressCMS, Kanboard, GitLab) over 24-hour test sessions. Includes custom IDOR (IVD) and XSS (XVD) detectors.
Key Findings: Achieved an average code coverage increase of 59% over BlackWidow and submitted POST HTML forms 5× more frequently. Identified 8 zero-day vulnerabilities (IDOR and XSS) across WordPress, HotCRP, Kanboard, ImpressCMS, and GitLab.
Author-Stated Limitations: Fitness function weights require manual parameter tuning; relies on page URLs as crawling seeds which causes redundancy on duplicate/similar pages.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not evaluate performance or resilience against adversarial web agents, navigation traps, infinite loop traps, or resource consumption attacks during crawling.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; claimed coverage improvements and form submission rates are corroborated by detailed empirical tables and code-coverage logs across all 10 benchmarks.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None declared within the scope of the examined corpus.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks evaluation under adversarial web navigation traps or hostile client-side DOM manipulations.
Untested Scenarios: Real-world dynamic multi-tenant web environments with live user traffic, complex multi-factor authentication flows, or adversarial navigation traps.
Proposed Research Questions: How can evolutionary crawlers defend against malicious web pages designed to trap web agents in infinite state loops or exhaust computational budgets?
Supporting Citations: BlackWidow 71, Enemy of the State 71, JAK 71, CrawlJAX 71

Paper: The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research
Research Focus: Standardized gym environment and ecosystem (BrowserGym & AgentLab) for evaluating and benchmarking autonomous LLM/VLM web agents across diverse tasks.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Unified 6 popular web agent benchmarks (MiniWoB++, WebArena, VisualWebArena, WorkArena L1-L3, WebLINX, AssistantBench) into an OpenAI Gym-compliant interface with structured observations (DOM, AXTree, screenshots, Set-of-Marks) and high-level action primitives. Evaluated 6 SOTA LLMs/VLMs (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, o1 Mini, Llama-3.1 70B, Llama-3.1 405B) across all benchmarks using parallelized execution.
Key Findings: Claude-3.5-Sonnet achieved state-of-the-art performance across almost all benchmarks (e.g., 39.1% success on WorkArena L2 compared to 8.5% for GPT-4o), except on vision-specific tasks where GPT-4o performed better. Open-weights model Llama-3.1 405B outperformed GPT-4o Mini on multiple benchmarks.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluations are subject to stochasticity and non-determinism in live websites; risk of database collision when multiple agents operate concurrently on shared backends; potential rate limits and API costs; vulnerability to robot detection/CAPTCHAs on open-web benchmarks.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not systematically benchmark agent resilience against deliberate adversarial web traps, prompt injections, or malicious state manipulation designed to exhaust resources or derail execution.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; benchmarking tables and individual task execution logs in AgentXRay validate performance claims.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None declared within the scope of the examined corpus.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks controlled benchmarking for security boundaries, prompt injection resilience, or computational resource exhaustion bounds during web navigation.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web pages containing prompt injections, navigation loops, or dynamic anti-agent mechanisms.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agent benchmarking ecosystems integrate real-time security and adversarial robustness stress tests alongside functional task completion metrics?
Supporting Citations: MiniWoB Shi et al., 2017, WebArena Zhou et al., 2024b, VisualWebArena Koh et al., 2024a, WorkArena Drouin et al., 2024, AssistantBench Yoran et al., 2024, WebLINX Lù et al., 2024

Paper: When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents
Research Focus: Detection and analysis of Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs)—a structural execution failure where agent feedback paths repeatedly trigger model calls, tools, or handoffs without an effective bound.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Developed IAL-SCAN, a static analysis tool that abstracts agent code into a framework-independent Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to model explicit and framework-induced feedback paths (e.g., retries, tool dispatch, delegation), and evaluates bound coverage over feedback paths. Evaluated on 6,549 real-world Python LLM agent repositories across 8 frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, Semantic Kernel), followed by manual verification and comparison with LLM/coding agent baselines.
Key Findings: IAL-SCAN identified 74 potential findings, confirming 68 true IAL failures across 47 real-world projects (91.9% precision). The dominant impacts identified were API cost exhaustion (95.6%) and model denial of service (95.6%). Unbounded retry feedback and tool-call iterations were the leading failure patterns.
Author-Stated Limitations: Static analysis over-approximates dependencies leading to potential false positives; limited to Python repositories and 8 supported frameworks; limited capability to infer dynamic external state bounds or natural-language stopping conditions.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not evaluate runtime defense or dynamic mitigation strategies for stopping infinite loops live during execution without terminating legitimate long-running agent tasks.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; reported static metrics, ablation results, and LLM pruning sensitivity experiments are internal consistent.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: None declared within the scope of the examined corpus.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks dynamic runtime execution verification for statically flagged loops where external API rate limits or external side-effects might break loops out-of-band.
Untested Scenarios: Dynamic dynamic injection of adversarial tool outputs specifically designed to trigger static or dynamic IALs in autonomous web/desktop agents.
Proposed Research Questions: What dynamic runtime guardrails can reliably detect and break infinite agentic loops in real-time without introducing false-positive task terminations?
Supporting Citations: AutoGen Wu et al., 2023, LangChain/LangGraph LangChain, 2026, CrewAI CrewAI, 2026, OpenAI Agents SDK OpenAI, 2026, ReAct Yao et al., 2023

Paper: EIA: Environmental Injection Attack on Generalist Web Agents for Privacy Leakage
Research Focus: Privacy risks and indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities in generalist web agents operating on compromised web environments.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated SeeAct framework across 3 LMM backbones (GPT-4V, LlavaMistral7B, LlavaQwen72B) on 177 action steps with PII from Mind2Web. Evaluated Form Injection (FI) and Mirror Injection (MI) strategies across 8 injection positions (P+∞ to P-∞), stealthiness (zero vs. low opacity), traditional malware detection tools (VirusTotal), functional integrity (ASRpt), and defensive system prompts.
Key Findings: Standard EIA achieves up to 70% Attack Success Rate (ASR) in leaking specific user PII at an action step via Mirror Injection at P+1 (using GPT-4V). Zero-opacity EIA fails to leak full user requests (0% ASR) because the action generation stage relies solely on screenshots; Relaxed-EIA (low opacity α=0.2) increases full request leakage ASR to 16% on GPT-4V. EIA evades VirusTotal, preserves functional integrity, and bypasses defensive system prompts.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluations were conducted offline on static action steps adapted from Mind2Web dumps rather than real-time interactive environments; exploration was limited to single-element injection per webpage rather than multi-point or multi-turn compositional injections.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on dynamic, multi-turn web sessions; missing defenses that effectively balance visual/DOM data filtering with maintaining web agent task execution performance.
Internal Contradictions: Authors assert that setting CSS opacity to zero makes injections completely invisible, but acknowledge that zero-opacity DOM elements still disrupt layout flow by occupying physical DOM layout space (creating unusual white space) unless additional manual CSS adaptation is applied.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: EIA relies on DOM/HTML manipulation which relies on structured text context, whereas pixel-space vision attacks like WebInject demonstrate that HTML injection can be completely bypassed by applying imperceptible raw pixel perturbations directly rendered to the screenshot.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation did not control for web browser viewport layout shifts, dynamic CSS media queries, or multi-screen resolution variations across target user environments.
Untested Scenarios: Testing EIA against agents utilizing Set-of-Mark visual grounding, multi-agent cooperative web navigation setups, or live real-time web environments with active anti-bot/CAPTCHA controls.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agent architectures decouple functional element understanding from unverified text/DOM instructions without degrading navigation accuracy?
Supporting Citations: Zheng et al., 2024 (SeeAct); Deng et al., 2023 (Mind2Web); Greshake et al., 2023b; VirusTotal, 2023; Wallace et al., 2024

Paper: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
Research Focus: Systematic formalization and benchmark evaluation of prompt injection attacks and defenses across LLM-Integrated Applications.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Formalized prompt injections using a task-decoupling framework (target task vs. injected task). Evaluated 5 attack methods (Naive, Escape Characters, Context Ignoring, Fake Completion, and Combined Attack) across 10 LLMs (including GPT-4, PaLM 2, Llama-2, Vicuna) and 7 natural language processing tasks (49 task combinations, 10,000 paired samples). Benchmarked 10 defenses (5 prevention-based, 5 detection-based) using ASV, MR, PNA, FPR, and FNR metrics.
Key Findings: Combined Attack outperforms single attack strategies across all models and tasks, achieving an average ASV of 0.75 on GPT-4. Attack success positively correlates with LLM model size (Pearson correlation 0.63-0.64). Existing prevention defenses fail to stop attacks or severely degrade baseline task utility (e.g., Paraphrasing drops baseline PNA by 0.14). Known-answer detection achieves low FNR for specific syntax overwriting but fails against context-switch attacks (e.g., on grammar correction tasks).
Author-Stated Limitations: Attacks evaluated were restricted to heuristic string manipulation rather than gradient/optimization-based search; evaluation of known-answer detection was restricted to a single fixed prompt template; black-box closed models prevented perplexity calculation.
Inferred Research Gaps: Absence of post-detection recovery mechanisms to reconstruct clean data context; lack of fine-tuning paradigms that train non-instruction models to execute specific tasks without adhering to embedded instructions.
Internal Contradictions: The paper assumes the backend LLM maintains complete integrity, yet demonstrates that instruction-following capabilities inherent to larger backend LLMs directly facilitate security degradation under indirect prompt injection.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While Liu et al. show that text-based delimiters (like triple quotes or XML tags) fail to isolate data context in LLM text applications, WebInject demonstrates that structural DOM and vision-based isolation face distinct security failures due to cross-layer non-differentiable rendering mappings.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Did not control for system prompt role-ordering variations across different LLM API provider implementations.
Untested Scenarios: Optimization-based adversarial suffix attacks combined with prompt injection heuristics; evaluation on interactive agentic tool-use tasks.
Proposed Research Questions: Can fine-tuning strategies effectively decouple instruction execution capabilities from data context processing without sacrificing zero-shot task generalization?
Supporting Citations: Greshake et al., 2023b; Perez & Ribeiro, 2022; Willison, 2022; Jain et al., 2023; Piet et al., 2024

Paper: WebInject: Prompt Injection Attack to Web Agents
Research Focus: Adversarial pixel-level visual prompt injection attacks against multimodal large language model (MLLM) web agents via webpage source code modifications.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Formulated finding human-imperceptible raw pixel perturbations (l_infinity bound epsilon=16/255) as a constrained optimization problem targeting specific agent actions across multiple monitors. Approximated non-differentiable webpage-to-screenshot ICC profile mappings using U-Net neural networks and applied differentiable interpolation for image resizing. Evaluated across 10 webpage datasets (5 real, 5 synthetic), 5 MLLM agents (UI-TARS, Phi-4, Llama-3.2, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3), 5 monitor configurations, and 10 target actions.
Key Findings: WebInject achieves an overall Attack Success Rate (ASR) exceeding 0.96-0.97 across all 5 MLLMs, outperforming webpage-based text injection baselines (ASR <= 0.345) and direct screenshot perturbation attacks (ASR = 0.000 due to non-differentiable browser/monitor rendering pipelines). The attack remains effective against semantically equivalent user prompt variations (ASR ~0.88-0.95) and generalizes across multiple target monitor profiles.
Author-Stated Limitations: Assumes attacker capability to modify target webpage source code (not applicable to highly secure sites like Amazon); did not evaluate transferability to closed-source MLLMs (e.g., GPT-4V) due to computational constraints.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation under dynamic user browsing behaviors like scrolling, zooming, or responsive layout recalculations; lack of robust defense benchmarks against visual-space universal perturbations in MLLMs.
Internal Contradictions: The threat model assumes the attacker has no knowledge of user interaction history and uses random shadow histories for optimization, yet claims near-deterministic attack control over complex multi-step web agent trajectories.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Liao et al. (EIA) state that invisible HTML elements with zero opacity effectively manipulate agent action grounding, whereas WebInject proves that pure HTML injections yield poor attack success rates on vision-first MLLMs compared to direct raw pixel visual perturbations.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Did not account for dynamic browser-side image compression, anti-aliasing rendering variations, or OS-level display scaling factors.
Untested Scenarios: Attack performance against closed-source commercial visual web agents (e.g., OpenAI Operator, Claude Computer Use) and defensive visual adversarial training.
Proposed Research Questions: How can MLLM web agents detect visual adversarial noise in screenshots without introducing heavy computational overhead to real-time action generation?
Supporting Citations: Zheng et al., 2024; Liao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Aichberger et al., 2025; Ronneberger et al., 2015

Paper: AWE: Adaptive Agents for Dynamic Web Penetration Testing
Research Focus: Autonomous web penetration testing targeting injection-class vulnerabilities using a specialized memory-augmented multi-agent architecture.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated on the 104-challenge XBOW benchmark and tested on DVWA across 5 vulnerability categories (Reflected XSS, Stored XSS, DOM XSS, Basic SQLi, Blind SQLi) comparing Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, and Gemini 2.0 Flash against MAPTA.
Key Findings: Achieved 51.9% solve rate on XBOW (versus MAPTA's 76.9%), but outperformed MAPTA on injection classes: XSS (87% vs 57%) and Blind SQLi (66.7% vs 33.3%). Delivered a 98% reduction in token usage (1.12M vs 54.87M), 63% lower cost ($7.73 vs $21.38), and 4.4x faster average execution time (53.1s vs 190.8s).
Author-Stated Limitations: Restricted to injection-centric vulnerabilities (excluding business logic, authentication, or protocol-level attacks); limited multi-step planning across dependent attack chains; relies on heuristic context abstractions; sensitive to underlying LLM model reasoning variability.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks systemic resilience/containment when facing dynamic counter-defenses or adversarial navigation traps; unaddressed resource consumption and behavior under sustained non-progress.
Internal Contradictions: None observed.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Exhibits lower overall benchmark solve rate (51.9%) compared to generalist frameworks like MAPTA (76.9%) due to strict specialized domain scope, despite claiming superior performance on specific targeted injection vulnerabilities.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not explicitly control for real-world dynamic network latent delays or adaptive Web Application Firewall (WAF) rate-limiting blocks during time-bounded runs.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-step complex chaining (e.g., Default Credentials -> IDOR -> Escalation); protocol-level desynchronization/request smuggling; sustained non-progress under navigation loops.
Proposed Research Questions: How can specialized injection agents be dynamically combined with high-level generalist agents to resolve multi-step chain attacks without losing token efficiency?

Paper: A Survey on Autonomy-Induced Security Risks in Large Model-Based Agents
Research Focus: Systematic review and taxonomy of autonomy-induced security vulnerabilities across perception, memory, planning, tool usage, and multi-agent interaction in LLM agents, proposing the R2A2 cognitive framework.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Qualitative literature survey and taxonomy development structuring agent autonomy across five levels (L1–L5) and formalizing agent decision-making under Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs).
Key Findings: Higher autonomy shifts AI security risks from epistemic outputs to behavioral/environmental harm. Identifies failure modes including memory poisoning, tool misuse, recursive misalignment, and emergent deception; presents R2A2 to balance autonomy, controllability, and robustness.
Author-Stated Limitations: Lack of scalable formal verification methods for policies conditioned on symbolic language inputs; scarcity of standardized full-stack runtime evaluation environments; potential failure of CMDP approximations under non-stationary real-world environments.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of empirical benchmark validation for the proposed R2A2 theoretical framework against live adversarial web agents or real-world exploitation environments.
Internal Contradictions: None observed.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Advocates for complex introspective reflection and constraint filtering layers for risk control, which contrasts with empirical findings in penetration testing literature (e.g., AWE) showing that expansive generalist reasoning increases latency, costs, and failure rates.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate performance under strict resource or API budget constraints.
Untested Scenarios: Empirical testing of R2A2 in high-stakes multi-agent penetration testing or live competitive web environments.
Proposed Research Questions: Can R2A2's CMDP constraint filtering be lightweight enough to run in real-time continuous agent loops without triggering prohibitive token overhead?

Paper: Talk is (Not) Cheap: A Taxonomy and Benchmark Coverage Audit for LLM Attacks
Research Focus: Data-informed 507-leaf taxonomy and 4x6 Target x Technique matrix audit assessing collective coverage of LLM attack benchmarks across 932 arXiv papers (2023–2026).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Automated LLM extraction (Gemini 3.1 Pro / Claude Opus 4.6) and human spot-check validation on 932 papers yielding 2,521 unique attack groups. Audit of 6 public benchmarks: HarmBench, InjecAgent, AgentDojo, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and StrongREJECT.
Key Findings: Primary benchmarks collectively cover at most 25% of the 4x6 threat matrix with zero overlapping cells among HarmBench, InjecAgent, and AgentDojo. Entire categories—Service Disruption (100% gap) and Model Internals—are completely unevaluated by existing public benchmarks.
Author-Stated Limitations: Corpus restricted to English arXiv papers from Promptfoo database; pipeline extraction recall (89.4%) is frequency-dependent and misses less-established attacks; potential paper selection bias.
Inferred Research Gaps: Unaddressed evaluation infrastructure for measuring resource consumption, infinite reasoning loops, and denial-of-wallet attacks against dynamic web/LLM agents.
Internal Contradictions: None observed.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Highlights that benchmarks heavily focus on safety/alignment bypass (jailbreaking), whereas multi-agent and system-focused studies identify indirect prompt injection and tool hijacking as the predominant real-world threat vectors.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not include non-English literature or proprietary/commercial red-teaming benchmark suites.
Untested Scenarios: Standardized benchmark evaluations measuring per-request resource accounting (latency, token amplification, API cost) under Denial-of-Service prompt attacks.
Proposed Research Questions: How can standardized metrics for Service Disruption (e.g., token amplification ratio, latency ratio) be integrated into existing dynamic agent testbeds?

Paper: AGENTREWARDBENCH: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
Research Focus: Evaluating the capability of LLM judges and rule-based evaluation functions to accurately assess web agent navigation trajectories across diverse environments against human expert judgments.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluation of 12 LLM judges (including Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, Llama 3.3, Qwen2.5-VL, AER-C, AER-V, NNetNav) across 1,302 trajectories generated by 4 web agents on 5 benchmarks (WebArena, VisualWebArena, AssistantBench, WorkArena, WorkArena++). Trajectories were annotated by 6 human experts for Success, Side Effects, and Repetition Cycles.
Key Findings: No single LLM judge excels across all benchmarks. Current LLM judges fail to exceed 70% overall precision (GPT-4o judge peak precision 69.8%), frequently overestimating success by trusting misleading agent thought traces or missing task constraints. Conversely, official benchmark rule-based evaluations severely underreport success rates (recalls down to 55.9%) due to brittle exact-string/URL match requirements.
Author-Stated Limitations: The benchmark relies on expert annotators whose shared domain knowledge may not reflect general user preferences. Certain environments/tasks required workarounds (e.g., replacing search engines in AssistantBench), and complex tasks (Level 3 WorkArena++) had to be excluded due to low base agent performance.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation methods that can operate dynamically when environment states cannot be preserved; reliance on static screenshot/accessibility tree snapshots rather than interactive environment state queries; insufficient capability of judges to ground visual reality against agent reasoning.
Internal Contradictions: Including both accessibility trees and visual screenshots as multi-modal input to the simplified LLM judge yielded lower precision (62.1%) than including screenshots alone (64.5%), contradicting the assumption that providing richer multimodal context improves judgment accuracy.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Rule-based evaluation ranks Qwen2.5-VL above GPT-4o on WebArena and WorkArena++, whereas expert human annotators prefer GPT-4o over Qwen2.5-VL across all benchmarks (showing over 14% higher true success rate on VisualWebArena).
Missing Controls/Confounders: Confounding effect of agent self-reported reasoning traces on judge models (judges susceptible to sycophancy/hallucinated reasoning); failure to control for variations in screenshot rendering resolution across web environments.
Untested Scenarios: Evaluating LLM judges under active adversarial environments (e.g., UI elements containing prompt injections), multi-agent collaborative workflows, or real-time continuous trajectory evaluation during inference (online reward modeling).
Proposed Research Questions: How can LLM judges be architected to independently verify task outcomes against visual ground truth without being misled by an agent's internal chain-of-thought? Can hybrid evaluation metrics combine flexible LLM visual checking with rule-based deterministic checks to optimize both precision and recall?

Paper: Breaking Agents: Compromising Autonomous LLM Agents Through Malfunction Amplification
Research Focus: Investigating security vulnerabilities of LLM agents against malfunction-inducing attacks (inducing infinite loops or executing incorrect/irrelevant actions) rather than overtly harmful/policy-violating actions.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluating attack strategies (Prompt Injection, Adversarial Perturbations like GCG/SCPN/VIPER, Adversarial Demonstrations) across direct input, intermediate outputs, and agent memory. Evaluated on an LLM Agent Emulator (144 test cases, 36 toolkits, >300 tools) using GPT-3.5-Turbo/GPT-4/Claude-2, as well as two implemented agents (Gmail Agent, CSV Agent) in single-agent and multi-agent network topologies.
Key Findings: Malfunction-inducing attacks via prompt injection are highly effective, inducing failure rates exceeding 80% (e.g., up to 88.1% on Claude-2, 90% on Gmail agent). Advanced multi-agent attacks propagate across different agent types (CSV agent infecting downstream Gmail agent with ~80% ASR). Standard LLM self-examination/policy checks fail to detect these benign-looking malfunction attacks (0% detection rate on policy checks).
Author-Stated Limitations: Large-scale evaluations relied on an LLM-emulated sandbox framework rather than fully deployed real-world tools for all 300+ tools. Practical case studies were limited to two implemented agents (Gmail and CSV). Only three core LLM model families were systematically evaluated.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of robust input-sanitization frameworks designed specifically for tool outputs and external API data streams; absence of defensive architectural controls to break execution loops without relying on LLM self-reflection.
Internal Contradictions: Adversarial demonstrations were completely ineffective when placed in user prompts (0% ASR due to ReAct reasoning filtering them out), but gained minor success when injected directly into core LLM system messages.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While safety benchmarks evaluate agent safety via explicit policy-violating prompts, this paper demonstrates that agents can be completely incapacitated through benign, policy-compliant action requests that bypass standard safety filters entirely.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Uncontrolled variation in ReAct framework prompt structures across different agent frameworks; baseline hallucination/randomness rates of core LLMs confounding the measured attack success rates.
Untested Scenarios: Attack resistance in multi-modal vision-web agents; impact of dynamic context-window truncation or memory-summarization mechanisms on attack persistence.
Proposed Research Questions: How can deterministic execution monitors be integrated into LLM agent frameworks to detect and break infinite action loops without degrading autonomous task reasoning? Can tool-output parsing schemas isolate untrusted intermediate data from model instruction channels?

Paper: Odysseys: Benchmarking Web Agents on Realistic Long Horizon Tasks
Research Focus: Benchmarking multimodal computer-use agents on realistic, multi-site, long-horizon web navigation workflows derived from actual human browsing histories.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Curated 200 long-horizon tasks (easy, medium, hard) across 22 domains from 2,380 human Chrome browsing journeys. Evaluated frontier models (Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini) and open-weight models (Qwen-3.5 series, UI-TARS-1.5-7B) in Ubuntu desktop VMs with Google Chrome. Implemented fine-grained rubric-based evaluation (1,225 rubrics total, ~6.1 per task) and introduced Trajectory Efficiency metrics.
Key Findings: Frontier models struggle with long-horizon execution: peak perfect task completion was 44.5% (Opus 4.6) and dropped sharply on hard tasks (11.0%). Single binary trajectory-level judging is inaccurate compared to rubric-based evaluation, which achieves substantially higher human agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.788–0.849 vs 0.508). Trajectory efficiency is extremely low across all models (peak 1.15%). Extending step budgets from 100 to 200 steps improved Opus 4.6 (44.5% -> 76.5%) but failed to help open-weight models like Qwen-3.5-9B (which flatlined at ~1.3%).
Author-Stated Limitations: Tasks are evaluated on the live internet, leading to potential site drift/dynamism over time. Human browsing journeys required heavy LLM filtering and manual rewriting. Experiments restricted models to a 100-step default budget due to high execution cost (~$2.50 / 30 mins per task for Opus 4.6).
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of sub-agent decomposition mechanisms for high-fanout tasks (e.g., gathering data from 30 separate venues); absence of explicit state-tracking memory structures to prevent agents from over-researching without producing requested final deliverables.
Internal Contradictions: GPT-5.4 achieved higher trajectory efficiency (1.15%) than Opus 4.6 (1.06%) despite having lower overall task completion accuracy (33.5% vs 44.5%), caused by GPT-5.4 batching multiple UI actions per LLM call while Opus executed strictly one action per turn.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While previous web agent benchmarks (WebArena, Mind2Web) report near-saturation scores using short single-site tasks, Odysseys reveals that state-of-the-art frontier models drop to near-zero success on realistic hard multi-site tasks.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Temporal instability of live web pages during evaluation runs; variable network latency and unannounced UI updates on external commercial websites.
Untested Scenarios: Evaluating multi-agent collaboration or specialized sub-agent hierarchies on multi-site long-horizon tasks; testing agent resilience against live web popups, cookie banners, or anti-bot verification traps during extended browsing sessions.
Proposed Research Questions: How can computer-use agents balance exploration and task synthesis to avoid infinite data-gathering loops on broad tasks? What architectural or prompting scaffolds enable effective multi-action turn batching without increasing action execution error rates?

Paper: SnapGuard: Lightweight Prompt Injection Detection for Screenshot-Based Web Agents
Research Focus: Lightweight, pre-action prompt injection detection for screenshot-based web agents without relying on full-page VLM semantic inference.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Dual-branch multimodal representation analysis: (1) Visual Stability Indicator (VSI) measuring gradient variance (threshold set at FPR=0.05, VSI=4450); (2) Textual Signal Extraction via Contrast-Polarity Reversal (CPR), Pytesseract OCR, and Action-Oriented Pattern Detection (APD). Evaluated on 948 benign and 2,185 malicious samples across 8 attack configurations (EIA, WebInject, Pop-up, WASP, VWA-emb, VWA-shot, VPI-BU, VPI-CU) and compared against 10 baselines (Embedding-I/T, JailGuard, LLaVA-1.5, GPT-4o, KAD, PromptGuard, DataSentinel, PromptArmor).
Key Findings: SnapGuard achieves an average F1 score of 0.75 (TPR 0.66, FPR 0.09) and AUC of 0.742, outperforming GPT-4o-prompt (F1 0.71) while operating 8× faster (1.81s vs. 14.50s) with 0 MB GPU memory overhead. Demonstrates high robustness against visual noise (Gaussian noise up to σ=1.0) and maintains effectiveness across different OCR/VLM text extraction backends.
Author-Stated Limitations: Primary computational bottleneck remains in text extraction (CPR+OCR accounts for 98.8% of runtime, 1.788s out of 1.810s). Does not cover post-detection mitigation strategies, multi-turn dynamic temporal page interactions, or joint co-optimization with agent policies.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks evaluation against multi-step dynamic attacks, continuous interaction trajectories, or adaptive visual adversaries specifically fine-tuned to spoof the VSI gradient variance metric or bypass static APD rule taxonomies.
Internal Contradictions: None identified within the paper.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Text-centric defenses (e.g., KAD, PromptArmor) show near-zero detection performance (F1 0.05 - 0.45) on screenshot-based prompt injection scenarios compared to their reported high effectiveness on structured HTML/text inputs.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate performance under varying screen resolutions, mobile rendering viewports, or complex canvas/WebGL dynamic web components.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-turn dynamic state sequences, real-time interactive execution pipelines, and adaptive adversarial attacks targeting VSI and APD logic directly.
Proposed Research Questions: How can lightweight visual stability metrics be adapted to distinguish intentional visual web styling variations from stealthy adversarial gradient perturbations in multi-turn web agent interactions?

Paper: WebRollback: Enhancing Web Agents with Explicit Rollback Mechanisms
Research Focus: Explicit multi-step rollback and search mechanisms for web agents navigating dynamic online environments.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces WebRollback using an Action Module, Critique Module (evaluates state and outputs binary continue/back decisions), and Rollback Module (selects specific historical state index and records experience). Tested on Mind2Web-Live (42 test cases) and WebVoyager (342 test cases) using zero-shot LLMs (Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, GPT-4o) and fine-tuned 8B/7B models. Evaluated using GPT-4o auto-evaluator across max step budgets (8 to 32).
Key Findings: Explicit Rollback outperforms greedy OneWay and BestFirst search strategies across zero-shot and fine-tuning setups (e.g., Qwen2.5-72B achieves 51.90% full success on WebVoyager vs 49.56% OneWay and 47.95% BestFirst). Reduces unnecessary state switches (2.1 switches on WebVoyager vs 4.3 for BestFirst) and significantly lowers the struggle-ratio (7% vs 19% for OneWay).
Author-Stated Limitations: Rollback relies on a simple URL redirection mechanism via Playwright, which fails on non-revertible or high-stakes real-world actions (e.g., financial payments, sending emails). Experiments were restricted to web navigation tasks and fine-tuning was limited to ~7B model scales due to compute constraints.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address state reconstruction for client-side web application state changes (e.g., unsubmitted multi-page form entries, DOM mutations) that are not captured or restored purely by URL redirection.
Internal Contradictions: None identified within the paper.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: BestFirst value-guided search algorithms (Koh et al., 2024) induce frequent, inefficient state switching in complex web environments due to noisy intermediate state evaluations.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for network latency delays or server-side session state timeouts during multi-step backward URL navigations.
Untested Scenarios: High-stakes non-reversible action pipelines, dynamic single-page web applications (SPAs) without distinct URL state shifts, and adversarial web navigation traps.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web agents effectively maintain and verify state checkpoints in dynamic single-page applications where URL redirection cannot accurately restore DOM state?

Paper: WebWalker: Benchmarking LLMs in Web Traversal
Research Focus: Benchmarking and executing vertical web traversal for complex, multi-layered information seeking.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Constructed WebWalkerQA dataset comprising 680 human-verified QA pairs across 4 domains (conference, organization, education, game) in Chinese and English, categorized by difficulty (easy, medium, hard) and source width (single-source vs multi-source across up to 1,373 subpages). Developed WebWalker, a multi-agent framework comprising an Explorer Agent (ReAct-based, HTML button action space) and a Critic Agent (incremental memory management and stopping judge). Evaluated across 9 LLM backbones (including GPT-4o, Qwen-Plus, Qwen2.5 series) and compared against ReAct, Reflexion, and commercial/open-source RAG baselines.
Key Findings: WebWalkerQA poses a significant challenge; top-performing WebWalker with GPT-4o achieves only 37.50% overall accuracy. WebWalker consistently outperforms ReAct and Reflexion baselines. Standard commercial and open-source RAG systems struggle with deep web information (Tongyi leads commercial RAG at 40.73%; Naive RAG achieves 20.73%). Integrating WebWalker into RAG systems significantly boosts performance across all difficulty levels.
Author-Stated Limitations: Dataset size is limited to 680 human-verified QA pairs. Action space is constrained exclusively to text-based HTML button clicks via DOM parsing, excluding visual modalities (screenshots) and multi-action browser operations. WebWalker uses zero-shot prompting without agent fine-tuning.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks defensive checks against malicious web content, prompt injections embedded within traversed subpages, or navigation loops caused by adversarial web page structures.
Internal Contradictions: None identified within the paper.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates that horizontal open-domain RAG retrieval fails on multi-layered web traversal QA tasks where information is buried across deep subpages.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for real-time web structural changes between initial dataset annotation crawling and live experiment execution.
Untested Scenarios: Web traversal in visual/screenshot-centric environments, interactive web forms requiring text inputs, and execution under adversarial or dynamic anti-scraping web defenses.
Proposed Research Questions: How can multi-agent web traversal frameworks maintain execution integrity and memory safety when encountering adversarial prompt injection traps during deep website exploration?

Paper: AdvAgent: Controllable Blackbox Red-teaming on Web Agents
Research Focus: Developing an automated, controllable black-box red-teaming framework using reinforcement learning to generate invisible HTML adversarial prompt injections against multimodal web agents.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Tested against SeeAct (powered by GPT-4V and Gemini 1.5 backends) on 440 tasks across 4 domains (Finance, Medical, Housing, Cooking) from Mind2Web. Evaluated step-based Attack Success Rate (ASR), controllability across target arguments, transferability, and resistance to standard prompt defenses (Sequence enclosure, Instruction defense, Sandwich defense).
Key Findings: Achieved 97.5% average ASR against GPT-4V SeeAct and 99.8% against Gemini 1.5 SeeAct. The two-stage training paradigm (SFT + DPO) significantly boosted performance compared to SFT alone (from 69.5% to 97.5%). Existing prompt-based defenses provided limited protection, leaving agents vulnerable with ASRs exceeding 88.8%.
Author-Stated Limitations: Requires obtaining offline feedback from victim agents before prompt optimization (lacks real-time online optimization). Evaluation relies on step-based ASR rather than end-to-end task completion due to current agents' low end-to-end success rates.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation in live dynamic web environments with real-time DOM updates or multi-step session states; failure to explore counter-defenses operating at the vision rendering layer rather than text/HTML prompt layer.
Internal Contradictions: Claims to maintain stealthiness via non-rendered attributes (e.g., aria-label), but ablation experiments reveal that shifting injection position prior to target element drastically reduces ASR in certain domains (e.g., down to 26.0% in Finance), indicating structural sensitivity that conflicts with claims of effortless transferability across positions.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While white-box gradient methods like GCG achieve high attack rates on standard aligned LLMs (Zou et al., 2023), they completely fail (0.0% ASR) when transferred to black-box web agents, contradicting assumptions that open-source VLM transfer attacks generalize to complex web workflows.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Did not control for backend VLM temperature settings or model version updates during API calls; lacked baseline controls evaluating benign task completion degradation caused by injected HTML modifications.
Untested Scenarios: Real-time interactive web applications with dynamic WebSockets or virtual scrolling; multi-turn dynamic dialogs requiring sustained non-progress recovery; multi-agent collaborative environments.
Proposed Research Questions: How can real-time online reinforcement learning adapt adversarial prompters during live user sessions? Can visual-grounding-level defenses detect HTML-invisible text injections before action generation?
Supporting Citations: Zheng et al., 2024 (SeeAct) 86; Deng et al., 2024 (Mind2Web) 86; Rafailov et al., 2024 (DPO) 86; Zou et al., 2023 (GCG) 86.

Paper: Webscraper: Leverage Multimodal Large Language Models for Index-Content Web Scraping
Research Focus: Creating an autonomous MLLM-based web scraping framework (Webscraper) for dynamic index-and-content web architectures using visual navigation and specialized custom parsing/merging tools.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Built on Anthropic's Computer Use (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) integrated with GPT-o3-mini for HTML parsing. Evaluated on 6 mainstream news websites (30 runs each to establish 95% CI stability) and 2 e-commerce platforms (Momo, Amazon) using ROUGE-L (threshold >= 0.8) and exact URL match for Correctness.
Key Findings: Webscraper (Prompt + Tool) substantially outperformed zero-shot Computer Use baseline across all news and e-commerce sites (e.g., achieving up to 82% average correctness on PTS news vs 18% baseline). Outsourcing parsing to GPT-o3-mini preserved context window and increased robustness.
Author-Stated Limitations: Limited strictly to index-and-content web architectures; fails on virtual scrolling or WebSocket streaming. Visual grounding can falter during complex navigation (e.g., inaccurate clicks after zooming). LLM code generation occasionally produces buggy parsing scripts on inconsistent HTML.
Inferred Research Gaps: High monetary cost and latency of multi-LLM orchestration (Claude + GPT-o3-mini) per scraping task; absence of real-time anti-bot/CAPTCHA evasion mechanisms; vulnerability to adversarial HTML manipulations or prompt injections embedded in scraped pages.
Internal Contradictions: Promotes cost efficiency via automated script generation, yet the architecture relies on running proprietary high-cost LLMs (Claude 3.7 Sonnet + GPT-o3-mini) iteratively per website evaluation, which introduces significant token cost prior to script synthesis.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Assumes web content is trusted and static for parsing, whereas Kaya et al. (2026) demonstrate that 13% of e-commerce sites contain untrusted user-generated content that exposes MLLM/LLM tools to indirect prompt injection.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks baseline comparison against traditional automated web scraping drivers (e.g., Playwright/Selenium with heuristic wrappers) regarding execution speed and API cost efficiency.
Untested Scenarios: Scraping websites behind authentication/login walls, CAPTCHAs, or anti-scraping Cloudflare checks; handling non-English dynamic layouts with non-standard DOM structures.
Proposed Research Questions: Can MLLM navigation trajectories be compiled into deterministic Playwright scripts in a one-shot execution to eliminate runtime LLM costs? How can visual scraping agents detect indirect prompt injection traps embedded in DOM elements?
Supporting Citations: Anthropic, 2024 (Computer Use) 87; Lin, 2004 (ROUGE) 87; Müller & Žunič, 2024 (Browser Use) 87.

Paper: When AI Meets the Web: Prompt Injection Risks in Third-Party AI Chatbot Plugins
Research Focus: Empirical security study analyzing prompt injection vulnerabilities (direct via network history tampering and indirect via web scraping/RAG) across 17 third-party AI chatbot plugins deployed on 10,000+ public websites.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Audited 7 WordPress and 10 generic plugins across Common Crawl datasets (Aug 2024 & Apr 2025). Performed black-box POST request tampering on live sites and controlled local simulations across 11 commercial LLMs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini) evaluating 3 attack tasks (System Prompt Extraction, Task Hijacking, Tool Hijacking) under various prompt hardening styles and RAG insertion modes.
Key Findings: 8 plugins (used by 8,000+ sites) fail to verify conversation history integrity in POST requests, enabling adversaries to inject forged system/assistant messages and boosting attack success by 3–8x. 15 plugins indiscriminately scrape untrusted third-party content (e.g., user reviews), creating persistent indirect prompt injection risks (found active in 13% of audited e-commerce chatbots). System prompt hardening failed to prevent Tool Hijacking attacks.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluations rely on a simulated e-commerce setup and static datasets; cannot safely probe live custom developer tools without risking unintended persistent side effects on target sites. Manual sampling was limited to 5 queries per chatbot.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of automated dynamic taint-tracking tools capable of tracing user-generated content (UGC) directly into LLM context windows without developer intervention; lack of standard protocols for authenticating client-side conversation state in stateless web protocols.
Internal Contradictions: Demonstrates that hardened system prompts reduce Task Hijacking (e.g., prohibiting coding reduced success to 0% for user injections), but observed that for Tool Hijacking, hardened system prompts actually increased attack success rates in certain models (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet), showing that system-level prompt hardening can paradoxically degrade tool-level security.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Assumes standard LLM instruction hierarchy (Wallace et al., 2024) protects system-level instructions, whereas actual plugin implementations bypass role boundaries by inserting retrieved RAG data as system messages, breaking theoretical safety guarantees.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Did not evaluate the impact of network latency or browser-side web application firewalls (WAFs) on blocking tampered HTTP POST requests in the wild.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial tool hijacking targeting multi-step agentic workflows where tools perform state-changing financial transactions or database deletions; interactions with open-weight local LLMs (e.g., Llama-3).
Proposed Research Questions: How can cryptographically signed state tokens prevent client-side history forging in stateless HTTP web chatbots? Can automated HTML parsing classifiers (e.g., UGCBuster) sanitize untrusted user reviews prior to RAG indexing without dropping domain context?
Supporting Citations: Wallace et al., 2024 (Instruction Hierarchy) 88; Greshake et al., 2023 (Indirect Prompt Injection) 88; Liu et al., 2024 (Prompt Injection Benchmarking) 88.

Paper: ToolHijacker: Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection in LLM Agents
Research Focus: Prompt Injection Attacks targeting the tool selection phase (retrieval and selection) in LLM agents within a no-box threat model.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Presents ToolHijacker, an optimization approach dividing malicious tool description into subsequence R (optimized via gradient-free LLM generation or gradient-based HotFlip for retrieval) and subsequence S (optimized via tree-of-attack search or multi-term loss gradient descent for selection). Tested on MetaTool and ToolBench datasets across 8 LLMs (including GPT-4o, Llama-3, Claude-3.5) and 4 retrievers, evaluating against 7 baseline attacks and 6 defenses.
Key Findings: ToolHijacker achieves high Attack Success Rates (ASR) up to 99.6% and Attack Hit Rates (AHR) up to 100% in a no-box setup. It significantly outperforms manual prompt injection baselines and existing automated attacks (JudgeDeceiver, PoisonedRAG). Existing prevention defenses (StruQ, SecAlign) and detection defenses (known-answer, DataSentinel, perplexity-based) fail to reliably mitigate the attack (e.g., PPL misses 90% of gradient-based attacks).
Author-Stated Limitations: Optimizing subsequence S via gradient-based methods requires notable compute (~8 GPU-hours on NVIDIA A800). Gradient-based token-level optimizations can degrade textual readability, making them partially detectable by windowed perplexity (PPL-W) detectors compared to gradient-free methods.
Inferred Research Gaps: The attack assumes static single-step tool selection rather than multi-step tool execution feedback loops. The study does not evaluate adaptive defenses explicitly designed to sanitize retrieved tool metadata or joint attacks that simultaneously target tool selection and subsequent tool execution payloads.
Internal Contradictions: None identified. Results consistently support the failure of current defense mechanisms against both gradient-free and gradient-based variants under no-box constraints.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Differs from standard prompt injection literature (e.g., Liu et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2024) by demonstrating that indirect prompt injections can succeed without explicit, human-readable adversarial instructions or prompt delimiters, bypassing traditional perplexity filters.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate the effect of real-time multi-agent oversight or human-in-the-loop validation mechanisms on tool selection.
Untested Scenarios: Joint, multi-stage attacks where a hijacked tool document dynamically alters its secondary payload during tool calling/execution; environments with active structural prompt-isolation architectures.
Proposed Research Questions: How can LLM agent architectures enforce secure tool selection when tool descriptions are dynamically retrieved from untrusted open marketplaces? Can multi-agent verification or intent-grounding defenses prevent tool selection hijacking without sacrificing task efficiency?

Paper: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
Research Focus: Synergizing verbal reasoning traces and task-specific actions in LLMs for decision-making and knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluates ReAct (Reason + Act) via few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on four benchmarks: HotpotQA (multi-hop QA), FEVER (fact verification), ALFWorld (embodied text game), and WebShop (web navigation/shopping). Compared against Standard prompting, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Act-only baselines, and RL/imitation learning methods.
Key Findings: ReAct reduces hallucination and error propagation compared to CoT on knowledge tasks by interacting with external environments (e.g., Wikipedia API). On decision-making tasks, ReAct outperforms imitation/reinforcement learning baselines by 34% on ALFWorld and 10% on WebShop with 1-2 in-context examples. Combining ReAct and CoT-SC achieves state-of-the-art prompting performance.
Author-Stated Limitations: Few-shot prompting is constrained by context window length. Structural constraints in ReAct can reduce reasoning flexibility, occasionally causing repetitive action-thought loops. Non-informative search results can derail reasoning trajectories.
Inferred Research Gaps: ReAct relies on fixed, heuristic API interactions and simple prompt templates; it lacks formal safety bounds or policy compliance mechanisms when interacting with noisy or untrusted environments.
Internal Contradictions: While ReAct reduces fact hallucination relative to CoT, its tight structural coupling of thought-action steps leads to higher pure reasoning error rates (47% vs 16% on HotpotQA failure cases).
Cross-Paper Contradictions: ReAct demonstrates that few-shot prompting can outperform RL/IL models (like BUTLER) trained on thousands of trajectories, contrasting with classic RL findings emphasizing the necessity of extensive task-specific training.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for potential prompt injection or malicious adversarial observations present in external environment search returns.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial or untrusted environments where search returns contain prompt injections or navigation traps designed to manipulate internal thoughts.
Proposed Research Questions: How can ReAct reasoning traces be made resilient against manipulative or deceptive external environment inputs? How can dynamic decoding algorithms (e.g., tree search) prevent infinite thought-action looping?

Paper: ST-WebAgentBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Safety and Trustworthiness in Web Agents
Research Focus: Systematic evaluation of Safety and Trustworthiness (ST) policy adherence in autonomous web agents alongside task completion.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Introduces ST-WEBAGENTBENCH with 375 web automation tasks across 3 applications (GitLab, ShoppingAdmin, SuiteCRM) and 3,057 policy constraints across 6 orthogonal ST dimensions (User Consent, Boundary, Strict Execution, Hierarchy, Security & Robustness, Error Handling). Evaluates three SOTA open web agents (AWM, WorkArena-Legacy, WebVoyager) using new metrics: Completion Under Policy (CuP), Partial CuP (pCuP), and Risk Ratio.
Key Findings: Current web agents exhibit severe safety gaps: average completion rate drops from 24.3% (raw CR) to 15.0% when enforcing policy adherence (CuP). Approximately 38% of successful task completions violate at least one safety/organizational policy. Agent compliance decays drastically under higher policy loads (CuP drops from 18.2% with 1 active policy to 7.1% with ≥5 policies). Violations are heavily concentrated in User Consent (permission skipping) and Strict Execution (hallucinated data/deletions).
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluates only 3 open agents sharing a GPT-4o backbone; excludes proprietary computer-use stacks (Claude, Gemini). Tasks are limited to English language and enterprise web applications. Robustness checks focus primarily on prompt injection rather than the complete cyber threat landscape.
Inferred Research Gaps: The benchmark relies on pre-defined static policy templates in prompt context; it does not explore dynamic policy generation or real-time guardrail enforcement architectures capable of runtime intervention.
Internal Contradictions: Agents with higher raw task completion capabilities (e.g., AWM with 46.9% Partial CR) exhibit significantly higher safety policy breach rates (e.g., 37 user consent violations), demonstrating that current capability optimization directly undermines policy compliance.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts the implicit assumption of standard web agent benchmarks (e.g., WebArena, Mind2Web) that task completion rate is a sufficient indicator of real-world agent readiness and utility.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluations do not isolate LLM backbone alignment fine-tuning from agent controller prompt engineering when measuring policy violation rates.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent collaborative environments with conflicting user roles; non-English enterprise web workflows; adaptive adversarial prompt injections during live web navigation.
Proposed Research Questions: How can autonomous web agent controllers enforce non-negotiable organizational policy hierarchies without degrading overall task planning efficiency? What architectural guardrails can prevent web agents from skipping user confirmation steps during irreversible actions?

Paper: VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents
Research Focus: Evaluating vulnerabilities of Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) and Browser-Use Agents (BUAs) against Visual Prompt Injection (VPI) attacks across dynamic web platforms.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created VPI-Bench (306 interactive test cases across Amazon, Booking.com, BBC, Messenger, Email). Evaluated 8 agent implementations across CUA (Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) and BUA frameworks (GPT-5, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3). Measured Attempted Rate (AR) and Success Rate (SR) using a 3-LLM majority voting judge.
Key Findings: BUAs executed malicious instructions without resistance at rates up to 100%. CUAs showed higher resistance but remained highly vulnerable (up to 51% SR). System prompt defenses provided virtually no protection, while model fine-tuning and framework defense layers offered only partial mitigation.
Author-Stated Limitations: Assumes users delegate tasks to agents without active supervision, whereas real human users might detect visually injected pop-ups/emails and intervene.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not test multi-agent setups or defense techniques that disguise malicious prompts from humans while remaining detectable by screenshot-based vision agents.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; empirical execution rates and behavioral classifications logically align with stated threat model parameters.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Exhibits contrasting paradigms with WebDancer and YURASCANNER regarding agent trust models; while WebDancer and YURASCANNER treat web content as passive environment observations, VPI-Bench demonstrates that visual web content acts as an untrusted adversarial input vector.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks human-in-the-loop intervention baselines to measure real-world user detection rates of visual injections.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-modal audio/video prompt injections, non-English interface injections, and multi-agent collaborative task execution under injection conditions.
Proposed Research Questions: How can operating systems enforce privilege gating for AI agent-initiated actions versus human-initiated actions to prevent unauthorized system file modifications?
Supporting Citations: Anthropic (2025), Zhang et al. (2024), Debenedetti et al. (2024), Wang et al. (2025d)

Paper: WebDancer: Towards Autonomous Information Seeking Agency
Research Focus: Building end-to-end autonomous information-seeking web agents using a data-centric synthesis pipeline and a two-stage SFT + on-policy RL training paradigm.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Synthesized two datasets (CRAWLQA via web crawling and E2HQA via easy-to-hard question rewriting). Created short/long CoT trajectories via ReAct. Trained Qwen-2.5 (7B/32B) and QwQ-32B using SFT followed by DAPO RL. Evaluated on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and BrowseComp benchmarks.
Key Findings: WebDancer outperformed vanilla ReAct baselines across model scales, with QwQ-32B reaching 51.5% average on GAIA and 47.9% on WebWalkerQA. SFT is essential for cold-start instruction following; RL expands reasoning trajectory length and action space exploration.
Author-Stated Limitations: Limited to two basic web actions (search, visit/click); high rollout computational costs during RL; data underutilization during RL due to stability limits (only ~5,000 pairs used out of 100K+); brittleness of transferring long-CoT reasoning patterns from LRMs to smaller instruction LLMs.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address security vulnerabilities or adversarial inputs (such as visual/textual prompt injections) during open-web trajectory exploration.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; experimental figures and trajectory statistics directly support claims of performance gains via DAPO RL.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Assumes web environments provide accurate/truthful information for answering questions, directly contrasting with VPI-Bench's findings that web interactions expose agents to adversarial visual prompt injections.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks evaluation against web pages containing noisy, dynamic, or adversarial script elements during the RL rollout phase.
Untested Scenarios: Open-domain long-form synthesis/research tasks, dynamic browser interaction with sandbox environments, and real-time adversarial environment manipulation.
Proposed Research Questions: How can on-policy RL algorithms be optimized to train long-horizon agents on noisy or non-stationary web environments without policy degradation?
Supporting Citations: Yao et al. (2023), Yu et al. (2025), Mialon et al. (2023), Wu et al. (2025)

Paper: YURASCANNER: Leveraging LLMs for Task-driven Web App Scanning
Research Focus: Autonomous black-box web application scanning for deep-state vulnerability detection using task-driven LLM exploration.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Modeled scanner as a goal-based agent using GPT-4 via a three-part prompt architecture (Sensors, Bridge, Actuators). Extracted CRUD task catalogs from depth-1 web crawls. Tested against 20 modern containerized web applications (e.g., Redacted, Moodle, GitLab, Dolibarr) using the Black Widow XSS injection engine over 4-hour evaluation runs.
Key Findings: YURASCANNER successfully completed/partially executed 61.3% of valid tasks. Discovered +55.2% more forms and +35.2% more URLs compared to state-of-the-art crawlers (Black Widow, BFS, Random BFS). Identified 12 new zero-day XSS vulnerabilities in deep application states (up to 15 steps deep).
Author-Stated Limitations: Task generation can produce invalid tasks due to ambiguous context/hallucinations (23% invalid tasks); execution depends heavily on task ordering (missing state errors account for 75% of failures); state-changing tasks (like deleting users) can lock the scanner out of subsequent tasks.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks multi-role/multi-session context switching and dynamic state recovery mechanisms when destructive tasks invalidate the environment.
Internal Contradictions: None detected; empirical task execution metrics and vulnerability counts match across tabular datasets and narrative sections.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Assumes full autonomous execution authority over web forms without considering environmental prompt injection risks evaluated in VPI-Bench.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Did not benchmark compute/API cost trade-offs between open-source local LLMs (e.g., Llama 3) and GPT-4 during full vulnerability scans.
Untested Scenarios: Complex single-page applications (SPAs) reliant heavily on WebSocket interactions or multi-factor authentication workflows.
Proposed Research Questions: How can LLM-driven scanners automatically infer and maintain complex state dependencies to prevent environment lockout during state-destructive scanning tasks?
Supporting Citations: Eriksson et al. (2021), Stafeev & Pellegrino (2024), Doupé et al. (2012), Deng et al. (2024)

Paper: The Task Shield: Enforcing Task Alignment to Defend Against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
Research Focus: Introducing a test-time defense framework (Task Shield) that enforces 'task alignment' by dynamically extracting actionable instructions from user inputs, agent plans, and tool outputs, and scoring whether each action contributes to user goals.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated on the AgentDojo benchmark across 4 task suites (Travel, Workspace, Banking, Slack) using GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-3.5-turbo. Tested against 3 indirect prompt injection attack types (Important Instructions, Injecagent, Ignore Previous). Compared performance (Clean Utility, Utility under Attack, ASR) against 4 baselines (Tool Filter, Repeat Prompt, Delimiting, PI Detector).
