Key Findings: Task Shield reduces the ASR of the strongest attack (Important Instructions) from 47.69% to 2.07% on GPT-4o while preserving high utility (69.79%). 2) Input Shielding (filtering tool outputs) provides the single strongest cost-benefit trade-off, lowering ASR significantly at lower latency than full two-way verification. 3) Explicitly echoing user goals back to the LLM agent during feedback prevents context drift in multi-turn dialogues.
Author-Stated Limitations: Relies on a powerful defender LLM (weaker defenders like GPT-3.5-turbo cause lower clean utility); introduces noticeable computational overhead/latency per turn; evaluated on a single benchmark (AgentDojo) using synthetic conversations without testing open-source model backbones.
Inferred Research Gaps: High susceptibility to 'denial-of-service via misalignment' where benign complex tasks are misclassified as misaligned (false positives) and repeatedly blocked; unaddressed attacker strategies specifically crafted to manipulate the defender LLM's ContributesTo scoring prompt.
Internal Contradictions: The paper claims Task Shield avoids rigid binary judgments by using a fuzzy score 95 (Definition in 4.1 & B.1), yet enforces a hard zero-threshold decision rule where any instruction with an aggregate score S(e) = 0 is flagged as misaligned and blocked.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Task Shield asserts that prompt injections are effectively mitigated at the tool/input level via semantic alignment checks, whereas CELLMATE (Meng et al.) demonstrates that UI and tool-level checks suffer from a fundamental 'semantic gap' and are vulnerable to TOCTOU and branch steering attacks unless enforced at the browser/HTTP layer.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate against adaptive attackers who possess full knowledge of the Task Shield system prompt and attempt to craft injections designed to trick the instruction extraction step.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent workflows where instructions originate from intermediate secondary autonomous agents; open-ended real-world web environments (e.g., WebArena, OSWorld); execution environments with streaming tool outputs.
Proposed Research Questions: Can adaptive prompt injections bypass task alignment defenses by phrasing malicious directives as necessary preparatory or intermediate steps that score above the zero-threshold ContributesTo filter?

Paper: CELLMATE: Sandboxing Browser AI Agents
Research Focus: Proposing a browser-level, agent-agnostic sandboxing framework (CELLMATE) that enforces deterministic security policies at the HTTP request layer to eliminate the 'semantic gap' and prevent prompt injection side-effects.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Implemented CELLMATE as a Chrome extension with dynamic DOM monitoring, fast authorization lookup tables, and an automated LLM-based policy selector/instantiator. Evaluated policy selection accuracy across 209 web tasks (retail, travel, version control) using GPT-5.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Claude-Opus-4-5. Tested end-to-end attack blocking on GitLab tasks from WASP using 12 emulated browser automation attack scripts. Measured runtime and memory overhead.
Key Findings: Interposing at the HTTP layer bridges the semantic gap inherent in low-level UI primitives (clicks, typing), neutralizing TOCTOU and branch steering attacks regardless of UI pathways. 2) Modern frontier LLMs achieve over 94% accuracy in predicting required domains and selecting minimal required policies. 3) CELLMATE blocked 100% of the 12 emulated exfiltration and destruction attacks on GitLab with modest latency overhead (7.25%–15.0%).
Author-Stated Limitations: Single-turn focus (multi-turn dynamic permission accumulation left for future work); does not track data-flow or control-flow causality (cannot prevent data exfiltration if the request itself is permitted by policy); does not handle WebSockets traffic; relies on web developers to manually author agent sitemaps.
Inferred Research Gaps: Unaddressed vulnerability to 'in-policy abuse' where an injected prompt tricks an agent into taking harmful actions within the strictly allowed scope (e.g., posting offensive comments when issue commenting is allowed); lack of automated tools for static sitemap extraction across non-Rails frameworks.
Internal Contradictions: The paper assumes that user prompts provide trusted intent for policy generation, but acknowledges that underspecified or ambiguous prompts cause policy selection to fail closed, severely degrading utility for open-ended agent operations.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: CELLMATE assumes that low-level UI actions cannot be reliably sandboxed without inspecting HTTP requests, contradicting UI/action-level verification approaches like Task Shield's Action Shield or vision-based guardrails in OSWorld.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks evaluation against dynamic prompt injections that adaptively alter their exfiltration technique to fit inside pre-approved HTTP endpoints.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-tab browser agent navigation where context and authentication states cross domain boundaries; real-time streaming WebSocket web applications (e.g., Slack, collaborative document editors).
Proposed Research Questions: How can browser-level sandboxes combine HTTP request filtering with data-flow tracking to prevent in-policy data exfiltration without breaking legitimate multi-step agent interactions?

Paper: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
Research Focus: Dynamic evaluation framework for measuring prompt injection attacks and defenses on tool-calling LLM agents across stateful environments.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created 97 user tasks, 629 security test cases, 74 tools across 4 environments (Workspace, Slack, Travel, Banking). Evaluated 10 LLMs (closed/open-source like GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3 70B) under diverse prompt injections and 5 defense paradigms.
Key Findings: SOTA LLMs fail at many tasks even without attacks (benign utility < 66%). More capable models are easier to attack (inverse scaling). Baseline generic attacks succeed < 25% overall, but tailored attacks reach higher rates (e.g., Slack suite ASR 92%). Simple tool filtering defense lowers targeted ASR to 6.84%.
Author-Stated Limitations: Evaluates relatively simple attacks and defenses; relies on manual specification of tasks and utility criteria; lacks multimodal support (text/images); lacks complex continuous multi-task persistence without state reset.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic adaptive red-teaming where attacks automatically iterate against specific defenses in real-time; narrow coverage of multi-modal, agent-to-agent interactions, or state persistent non-progress traps.
Internal Contradictions: None noted; results consistently demonstrate utility-security trade-offs and report error bars across configurations.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: AGENTVIGIL 98 shows that automated MCTS-guided fuzzing achieves a 71% attack success rate on AgentDojo, contradicting AgentDojo's initial finding that attacks succeed in less than 25% of cases and demonstrating that handcrafted baseline attacks significantly underestimate adversary capabilities.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Tool documentation format variations across different provider APIs; context window degradation in multi-turn execution.
Untested Scenarios: Multimodal (vision-language) prompt injections; long-term persistent agent memory hijacking across multi-session workflows.
Proposed Research Questions: How can dynamic adaptive attack generation be integrated directly into benchmark execution loops to prevent static baseline underestimation?

Paper: AGENTVIGIL: Automatic Black-Box Red-teaming for Indirect Prompt Injection against LLM Agents
Research Focus: Automatic black-box optimization framework (fuzzing) for discovering indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities in multi-step LLM agents.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Combines initial prompt template corpus, MCTS-based seed selection (UCB1), LLM-based semantic mutators, and coverage-guided seed scoring. Evaluated on AgentDojo (142 fuzz / 173 test tasks) and VWA-adv (99 fuzz / 100 test tasks) across o3-mini, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, QwQ-32B, and real-world WebArena environments.
Key Findings: Achieves 71% ASR on AgentDojo (vs. 38% handcrafted baseline) and 70% ASR on VWA-adv (vs. 36% baseline). Demonstrates strong transferability to unseen tasks (65% on o3-mini test) and unseen models (67% on Gemini-2-flash-exp). Successfully redirects web agents in real-world setups to arbitrary/phishing URLs.
Author-Stated Limitations: High computational cost due to iterative fuzzing and MCTS search; lower transferability against specific model families like Claude-3.5-Sonnet.
Inferred Research Gaps: Optimization relies heavily on discrete textual prompt mutations rather than multi-modal trigger search or systemic execution path manipulation; limited evaluation on defense-in-depth isolation architectures.
Internal Contradictions: None identified; reported results clearly detail fuzzing vs. test set performance and transferability across multiple backbones.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Achieves high attack success rates against defenses like 'delimit' (49% ASR) and 'repeat' (74% ASR when optimized adaptively), contradicting earlier prompt injection defense literature claiming input delimiters and prompt sandwiching provide robust protection.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Helper LLM bias in prompt mutation generation; varying latency and stochasticity of black-box commercial LLM API endpoints during search iterations.
Untested Scenarios: Sustained non-progress navigation traps; multi-agent collaborative workflows where injections propagate across agent boundaries.
Proposed Research Questions: Can MCTS-based seed selection be adapted to discover visual and multimodal indirect prompt injection triggers with minimal query budgets?

Paper: AutoWebGLM: A Large Language Model-based Web Navigating Agent
Research Focus: Development and training of an efficient 6B open web navigation agent (ChatGLM3-6B backbone) capable of complex real-world web browsing.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Custom HTML simplification algorithm (HTML Pruner) + OCR parser. Multi-stage training: Curriculum Learning (SFT on ~10k web recognition/operation traces), Reinforcement Learning (DPO + SFT loss on 13k contrastive error pairs), and Rejection Sampling Finetuning (RFT on MiniWoB++ & WebArena). Created AutoWebBench (bilingual EN/ZH benchmark). Evaluated on AutoWebBench, Mind2Web, MiniWoB++, and WebArena.
Key Findings: AutoWebGLM 6B outperforms GPT-4 and LLaMA2-70B across web benchmarks (e.g., 89.3% on MiniWoB++, 18.2% on WebArena, 59.5% average on Mind2Web). RFT and DPO significantly reduce operational hallucinations and repetition loops.
Author-Stated Limitations: Falters on advanced visual web apps (maps, video, complex animations); occasional operational errors (44% hallucinations, 28% poor graphical recognition, 20% context misinterpretation, 8% pop-up interruptions).
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks explicit adversarial robustness evaluations against web-embedded indirect prompt injections or malicious navigation traps.
Internal Contradictions: None identified; comprehensive ablation studies validate the incremental contributions of curriculum learning, DPO, and RFT stages.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: AutoWebGLM achieves an 18.2% success rate on WebArena using a 6B parameter model with text-focused HTML pruning, whereas prior generalist models like GPT-4 or LLaMA2-70B achieved significantly lower scores (<15% and <1.2% respectively) without specialized web-interaction training pipelines.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Network latency and dynamic website state alterations during real-world evaluation passes.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web contexts containing indirect prompt injections, malicious pop-ups, or phishing traps designed to hijack web navigation agents.
Proposed Research Questions: How resilient is a curriculum-trained web agent like AutoWebGLM when encountering adversarial prompt injections embedded within webpage HTML/DOM elements?

Paper: WorkArena++: Towards Compositional Planning and Reasoning-based Common Knowledge Work Tasks
Research Focus: Benchmarking web agents on complex, multi-step knowledge work tasks requiring compositional planning, reasoning, and retrieval.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: 682 tasks evaluated across 5 skill categories in 2 difficulty levels (L2 explicit, L3 via ticket/knowledge base) on ServiceNow platform. Tested closed-source (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-v) and open-source models (Llama3-70b, Mixtral-8x22b) alongside 15 human evaluators across 98 task instances.
Key Findings: Humans achieved a 93.9% success rate, while state-of-the-art AI web agents failed almost completely (GPT-4o scored 3.0% on L2, 0.0% on L3; open-source models scored 0.0% across both). Multi-modal vision (GPT-4o-v) provided marginal utility in chart reading.
Author-Stated Limitations: Confined to the ServiceNow platform without cross-application/external software interactions. Does not evaluate security, safety, or adversarial robustness. Limited task horizon enforced by a 50-step limit.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation for agents operating under long-horizon multi-application workflows or handling unexpected system exceptions dynamically.
Internal Contradictions: Lllama3-70b context-length ablation showed no significant performance variation between 13k and 130k tokens, contradicting expectations that long-context capacity aids complex enterprise web task execution.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Not in source
Missing Controls/Confounders: Human baseline evaluation cohort had prior exposure bias (75% were ServiceNow employees or affiliated researchers).
Untested Scenarios: Robustness against malicious prompt injection or interface navigation traps embedded within enterprise knowledge bases.
Proposed Research Questions: How can specialized fine-tuning on ground-truth observation/action traces bridge the gap between human and LLM web agent performance on multi-step enterprise workflows?
Supporting Citations: Drouin et al. (2024) WorkArena L1 & BrowserGym, Zhou et al. (2023) WebArena

Paper: Prismata: Confining Cross-Site Prompt Injection in Web Agents
Research Focus: Defending autonomous web agents against Cross-Site Prompting (XSP) and indirect prompt injections by enforcing dynamic least-privilege policies at the DOM level.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Presents Prismata, a transparent defense layer utilizing action gating, Biba-inspired integrity parsing, and mechanical confinement. Empirical analysis on 5,664 DOMs (Common Crawl and Mind2Web); evaluation in WebArena using gpt-5.4-mini against Shortcut, Fake Completion, Ignore Instruction, WASP, and adaptive stress test attacks.
Key Findings: Prismata reduces average attack success rate (ASR) from 85.5% to 0.7% while boosting task completion under attack from 4.5% to 23.0% and preserving baseline utility (26.6% TSR vs 29.9% baseline). Residual risk paths where attacker content appears on critical paths without preceding structural cues account for only 0.1% (and 0.017% on standard-compliant sites).
Author-Stated Limitations: Protects against privilege-exceeding XSP attacks, but not in-scope attacks like fake product reviews. Operates primarily on textual/DOM modalities (does not cover pure visual/image perturbation attacks). Relies on the accuracy of underlying labeling LLMs.
Inferred Research Gaps: Does not address non-textual/multimodal visual prompt injections; performance on sites lacking standard HTML structural cues (e.g., custom canvas/shadow DOM heavy UI) remains unverified.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Evaluates pop-up attack templates where Prismata achieves high DSR (>88%), whereas SecureWebArena reports Pop-up attacks achieve 76.67% to 100% vulnerability across all tested LVLM agents without structural DOM defenses.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation relies heavily on gpt-5.4-mini as the base agent model; does not extensively benchmark across vision-first or GUI-grounded native LVLM architectures.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial visual perturbations, image-based prompt injections, multimodal UI environments, and complex multi-agent collaborative browser workflows.
Proposed Research Questions: How can Biba integrity models and DOM-based critical path isolation be extended to multimodal vision-language agents operating on raw pixel/screenshot observations?

Paper: SecureWebArena: A Holistic Security Evaluation Benchmark for LVLM-based Web Agents
Research Focus: A holistic benchmark for evaluating LVLM-based web agent security across user-level and environment-level threats using a multi-layered evaluation protocol.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: 330 adversarial tasks generating 2,970 trajectories across 6 web environments (Shopping, Classifieds, ShoppingAdmin, Wikipedia, GitLab, Reddit) evaluating 9 representative LVLMs across 6 attack vectors (Jailbreak, DP Injection, Pop-up, AdInject, Distract, IP Injection). Multi-stage evaluation of Internal Reasoning (RVR), Behavioral Trajectory (BCR), and Task Outcome (PDR).
Key Findings: Modern LVLMs are universally vulnerable to subtle attacks, with Pop-up attacks showing highest effectiveness (76.67%–100% PDR). GUI-grounded models resist textual injections better but remain vulnerable to visual pop-ups/ads. Different models exhibit distinct failure modes (e.g., GPT-5 fails in reasoning alignment while UI-TARS-1.5 suffers perceptual salience failure).
Author-Stated Limitations: Sim-to-real gap due to controlled web simulations without live network latencies/dynamic updates; does not capture non-evaluated emerging composite attack vectors; findings may not generalize to all proprietary frameworks.
Inferred Research Gaps: Evaluates model vulnerabilities without testing system-level structural defenses (like DOM filtering/isolation layers) to determine if system boundaries mitigate observed LVLM weaknesses.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates near total agent failure under Pop-up attacks across all LVLMs, contrasting with Prismata's findings where system-level structural confinement neutralizes Pop-up attacks to ~0% ASR.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate system-level defense layers or DOM sanitization tools alongside raw LVLM agent evaluations.
Untested Scenarios: Performance under defensive mediation software (e.g., Prismata, CaMeL) or multi-agent isolation architectures.
Proposed Research Questions: Can multi-layered reasoning evaluation protocols automatically trigger fallback or quarantine modes in web agents before unsafe actions are executed?

Paper: A Systematic Survey of Security Threats and Defenses in LLM-Based AI Agents: A Layered Attack Surface Framework
Research Focus: Architectural security threats, temporal attack dynamics, and defense coverage gaps across the LLM-based agent stack.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Systematic literature review (PRISMA-inspired SoK) analyzing a 116-paper corpus (2021–2026); proposed the Layered Attack Surface Model (LASM, L1–L7) and a 4-class temporality dimension (T1–T4); formal mathematical proof sketch for Defense Non-Transferability (Theorem 1).
Key Findings: Under-studied high-risk zone {L5, L6, L7} × {T3, T4} accounts for only 6.3% of literature assignments (EF1); all surveyed L4 tool execution attacks reduce to principal trust inversion (EF2); 7 of 28 LASM-temporality grid cells have zero defense coverage (EF3); zero surveyed benchmarks evaluate T3 or T4 delayed/drift threats (EF4).
Author-Stated Limitations: Search terms under-sample non-'agent'-prefixed work; 20-citation threshold excludes recent preprints; single-author layer/temporality coding without formal inter-rater reliability assessment; systematic exclusion of unindexed industry/red-team reports.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of standardized multi-session benchmarks for delayed cross-session attacks (T3/T4); absence of formal information-theoretic upper bounds for steganographic multi-agent collusion detection; lack of adoption-ready ABOM schemas and certified logging protocols.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Disagrees with OWASP Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS type-centric categorizations, proving that attacks sharing the same OWASP label (e.g., LLM01 or LLM07) map to different architectural layers and require non-overlapping defense controls.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation metrics lack false-positive rate reporting alongside true-positive mitigation rates; missing adaptive adversary threat models in benchmark evaluations.
Untested Scenarios: Longitudinal agent behavior monitoring across thousands of turns; non-session-bounded weight-level backdoor trigger detection; cross-session memory auditing under dynamic multi-agent topologies.
Proposed Research Questions: How can multi-session replay environments be standardized to benchmark T3/T4 cross-session attacks? Can information-theoretic lower bounds be established for detecting steganographic agent collusion across arbitrary output encodings?

Paper: Commercial LLM Agents Are Already Vulnerable to Simple Yet Dangerous Attacks
Research Focus: Empirical security and privacy vulnerabilities of commercial and open-source web and scientific LLM agents.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Red-teaming evaluations on commercial agents (Anthropic Computer Use, MultiOn) and scientific discovery agents (ChemCrow, PaperQA); testing a 4-step web attack pipeline (Reddit/Google redirection to malicious sites) and database/safeguard bypasses.
Key Findings: Achieved 10/10 attack success in stealing credit card info, downloading/executing malicious files, and sending authenticated phishing emails when agents land on malicious posts via trusted platforms (Reddit); direct links without trusted platform redirection failed (0/10); PaperQA retrieved fabricated malicious documents in 100/100 trials when queried for optimal chemical synthesis; ChemCrow provided nerve gas synthesis steps when queried via IUPAC nomenclature or indirect references.
Author-Stated Limitations: Unable to perform full statistical success rate recordings on MultiOn due to the product being disabled/offline during testing; focused primarily on black-box evaluation without internal agent access.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of structural boundary controls for visual/computer-use web agents navigating untrusted DOM structures; absence of context-aware safety filters that evaluate action intent rather than output text toxicity alone.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts standard LLM safety evaluations (e.g., HarmBench) by demonstrating that aligned models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) fail safety constraints in >90% of instances when embedded in tool-use/web pipelines.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Missing domain whitelist/blacklist controls on browser navigation; missing mandatory human-in-the-loop authorization gates for high-risk tools (file execution, email sending, payment submission).
Untested Scenarios: Performance of agents under strict domain whitelisting and digital credential verification; robustness against multi-modal/image-based prompt injections.
Proposed Research Questions: How can web browser extensions isolate tool permissions and prompt contexts when navigating untrusted external websites? What context-aware filtering mechanisms can distinguish legitimate credit card submission from unauthorized data exfiltration?

Paper: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
Research Focus: Self-supervised learning for language models to autonomously discover, invoke, and incorporate external API tool outputs.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Self-supervised API annotation and filtering based on weighted cross-entropy token prediction loss on a CCNet subset using GPT-J (6.7B); evaluated across 5 APIs (Calculator, Q&A, Wikipedia Search, MT, Calendar) on downstream benchmarks (LAMA, ASDiv, SVAMP, MAWPS, WebQS, NQ, TriviaQA, MLQA, TEMPLAMA, DATESET).
Key Findings: Toolformer (6.7B) achieved zero-shot downstream performance outperforming larger models like GPT-3 (175B) and OPT (66B) on math and LAMA benchmarks (e.g., ASDiv 40.4 vs GPT-3 14.0; SQuAD 33.8 vs GPT-3 26.8); tool-use capability is an emergent property appearing around 775M parameters; fine-tuning with API calls maintained core language modeling perplexity on WikiText and CCNet.
Author-Stated Limitations: Inability to use tools in a chain (using one tool's output as another's input); lack of interactive, multi-turn tool usage (e.g., iterative search query refinement); sensitivity to input prompt wording; high sample-inefficiency during dataset generation; failure to account for computational costs of API calls.
Inferred Research Gaps: Absence of security boundaries or input sanitization on API call returns, creating direct exposure to principal trust inversion and indirect prompt injection.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Demonstrates strong zero-shot tool usage without human demonstrations, contrasting with human-annotation-heavy approaches (e.g., WebGPT) or task-specific few-shot prompting (e.g., ReAct).
Missing Controls/Confounders: Missing verification/trust-labeling on returned API strings before context injection; missing authorization checks for high-privilege API execution.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial evaluation of API responses (e.g., poisoned search results or malicious calculator outputs); multi-step chained API execution pipelines.
Proposed Research Questions: How can self-supervised tool-learning frameworks be extended to learn tool authentication and output sanitization invariants alongside functional usage?
Supporting Citations: Schick et al. (2023) 106

Paper: BackdoorAgent: A Unified Framework for Backdoor Attacks on LLM-based Agents
Research Focus: Unified, stage-aware evaluation and benchmarking of backdoor attacks and trigger propagation across LLM-based agent workflows (Planning, Memory, Tools).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created BackdoorAgent framework with stage-specific hooks and trajectory logging across 4 tasks (Agent QA, Code, Web, Drive). Benchmarked 7 representative backdoor attacks against closed-source (Claude, Gemini, GPT) and open-source (DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen) LLM backbones.
Key Findings: Triggers injected at a single stage persist across intermediate states (e.g., GPT backbone trigger persistence: 43.58% planning, 77.97% memory, 60.28% tool). High attack success rate (ASR) frequently coexists with high task accuracy (ACC). Probability-based single-step LLM backdoor defenses fail to generalize to agent trajectories.
Author-Stated Limitations: Experiments do not fully capture the complete diversity of real-world agent architectures, execution environments, and complex deployment scenarios with adaptive adversaries.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic, trajectory-level runtime defenses designed to track multi-step contextual propagation of triggers across agent memory and feedback loops.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Evaluates backdoor susceptibility in static/controlled environments, whereas real-world web settings introduce dynamic DOM/content shifts that may alter trigger persistence.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not evaluate defense performance against adaptive adversaries who dynamically modify trigger strength or format during runtime.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-agent workflows where backdoor triggers propagate across multiple interacting autonomous agents.
Proposed Research Questions: How can trajectory-aware defenses effectively distinguish benign reasoning/tool feedback from delayed, multi-step backdoor activation?

Paper: It’s a TRAP! Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark for Web Agents
Research Focus: Evaluating autonomous web agents' susceptibility to social-engineering prompt injection attacks using psychological persuasion techniques and interface variations.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Developed TRAP benchmark with a 5-D modular attack space (630 injection variants) across 6 website clones from REAL (Amazon, Gmail, Google Calendar, LinkedIn, DoorDash, Upwork). Evaluated 6 frontier models (GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 3.7, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek-R1, LLaMA 4 Maverick, GPT-OSS-120B) using a single-click redirection metric.
Key Findings: Agents were compromised in ~25% of tasks on average (13% for GPT-5 up to 43% for DeepSeek-R1). Button-based injections are ~3.5x more effective than hyperlinks (77.5% vs 22.5%). Contextual tailoring increases ASR up to 5.6x. Injections breaking strong models transfer widely to weaker models (up to 90%).
Author-Stated Limitations: Focuses on 6 website clones, textual injections, and a single-click redirection metric without assessing post-redirection agent behaviors, multi-modal image injections, or dynamic persuasion interactions.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation on defensive interventions or agent-side prompt filtering mechanisms targeting interface-level social engineering elements.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Relies on single-click redirection as the primary ASR metric, whereas benchmarks like WebChoreArena and WebArena focus on end-to-end task completion metrics.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not isolate whether button-based injection dominance is driven by visual parsing biases or structural token formatting differences in AXTree representations.
Untested Scenarios: Multimodal visual/image-based prompt injections integrated into dynamic website interfaces.
Proposed Research Questions: Can UI-level architectural constraints or DOM-filtering guards neutralize button-based persuasion attacks without degrading agent navigational capabilities?

Paper: WebChoreArena: Evaluating Web Browsing Agents on Realistic Tedious Web Tasks
Research Focus: Benchmarking web browsing agents on labor-intensive, tedious, and cognitively demanding web tasks requiring massive memory, calculations, and long-term memory.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created WebChoreArena with 532 human-curated tasks across 4 WebArena environments (Shopping, Shopping Admin, Reddit, GitLab) and Cross-site tasks. Evaluated frontier LLMs (GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o) using BrowserGym and AgentOccam frameworks.
Key Findings: Current state-of-the-art LLM agents struggle on tedious web chores; even GPT-5 achieved below 50% overall accuracy (48.3% top score), while GPT-4o dropped from 42.8% on WebArena to 3.4-6.8% on WebChoreArena. Human performance reached only 50.2% due to task complexity/tediousness.
Author-Stated Limitations: Trade-off between controlled diagnostic precision and real-world web variability; excludes API-based interactions and relies primarily on outcome-based rather than trajectory-based evaluation.
Inferred Research Gaps: Insufficient memory architectures and state tracking mechanisms in agents to handle multi-page data collection, counting, and arithmetic reasoning without accumulating state degradation.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Excludes the map domain due to low reproducibility and API issues, whereas other web benchmarks include navigation/geospatial tasks.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for execution step budgets when comparing agents with explicit scratchpad/calculator tools versus unaugmented agents.
Untested Scenarios: Agents operating with direct DOM execution scripts or custom memory compression algorithms over extended multi-day session horizons.
Proposed Research Questions: What persistent memory structures allow web agents to perform multi-step data aggregation and counting without suffering step-budget exhaustion or memory degradation?

Paper: GPT-4V(ision) is a Generalist Web Agent, if Grounded
Research Focus: Evaluating LMMs (GPT-4V) as generalist web agents across diverse web tasks and comparing visual grounding techniques.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated SeeAct framework on Mind2Web dataset (137 websites, 31 domains) using offline metrics (Element Accuracy, Operation F1, Step SR) and live web online evaluation tool across 90 tasks using Playwright.
Key Findings: GPT-4V with oracle grounding achieves a 51.1% task success rate on live websites, substantially outperforming text-only models. Element grounding remains a major bottleneck; combining HTML structure with visuals performs best among tested grounding techniques.
Author-Stated Limitations: Substantial gap (20-30%) between current grounding methods and oracle grounding; high hallucination in image annotation/SoM prompting on complex webpage screenshots; high cost and context usage.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of robust automated error-recovery mechanisms when dynamic web elements fail to load or shift layout during execution.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts SoM/Image Annotation effectiveness findings in object-centric vision tasks when applied to complex web GUIs.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not explicitly control for real-time dynamic web content changes or network latency during online live-site evaluations.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web environments, malicious prompt injections embedded in webpages, and multi-tab state tracking.
Proposed Research Questions: How can hybrid visual-DOM representations be architected to eliminate the 20-30% gap with oracle grounding without relying on human intervention?

Paper: GUIDE: Interpretable GUI Agent Evaluation via Hierarchical Diagnosis
Research Focus: Interpretable and robust evaluation of GUI agents using a hierarchical trajectory decomposition and diagnosis framework.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated GUIDE framework on 3 benchmarks: an industrial e-commerce dataset (932 trajectories), AGENTREWARDBENCH (1,302 web trajectories), and AndroidBench (120 tasks/480 trajectories).
Key Findings: GUIDE achieved 95.80% accuracy on e-commerce, 89.21% precision on AGENTREWARDBENCH, and 94.9% accuracy on AndroidBench. Trajectory decomposition prevents context overload and performance degradation on long-horizon tasks.
Author-Stated Limitations: Relies on LLM reasoning without domain-specific fine-tuning, leading to occasional misjudgments where implicit business/domain knowledge is required.
Inferred Research Gaps: Inability to dynamically verify live environment state changes post-hoc without relying entirely on recorded trajectory screenshots and logs.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Contradicts single-call holistic evaluator paradigms (e.g., WebJudge, AgentTrek) by demonstrating that single-call evaluations collapse on longer trajectories.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for potential non-deterministic outputs from underlying LLM evaluators (e.g., Gemini-3.0-flash / o4-mini) across temporal API updates.
Untested Scenarios: Evaluations under active adversarial prompt injections or intentionally misleading GUI agent trajectory logs.
Proposed Research Questions: How can lightweight domain-knowledge preambles be dynamically synthesized to prevent misclassification in domain-specific workflows?

Paper: Untrusted Content Masking for Web Agents with Security Guarantees
Research Focus: Defending web agents against prompt injection attacks via DOM-based untrusted content masking and type-directed privilege separation.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated Untrusted Content Masking (UCM) on 10 custom website environments (100 tasks) and WebArena GitLab suite (41 task templates) across frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6, GPT-5.4) and strengthened WASP attacks.
Key Findings: UCM achieves 0% Attack Success Rate (ASR) against prompt injections while fully preserving task utility. Cost overhead is moderate (1.05x to 1.84x). Automated trust boundary inference from sanitized DOM achieves high F1 scores (0.84-0.99).
Author-Stated Limitations: Does not protect against data-flow attacks (e.g., single-value corruption, selection hijacking) or active-content vulnerabilities like XSS without additional downstream policy enforcement.
Inferred Research Gaps: Unaddressed vulnerability when websites utilize obscure or non-standard HTML rendering frameworks that obscure structural DOM boundaries.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Challenges the necessity of replacing the ReAct loop with strict plan-then-execute architectures (Piet et al.) to achieve control-flow security guarantees.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not account for performance under real-time dynamic DOM modifications generated by complex JavaScript web apps at runtime.
Untested Scenarios: Websites with heavily obfuscated DOM structures or anti-scraping/bot-detection mechanisms that alter DOM trees dynamically.
Proposed Research Questions: How can multi-candidate parallel querying be formalized to systematically detect and mitigate data-flow selection hijacking in masked environments?

Paper: A Framework for Studying AI Agent Behavior: Evidence from Consumer Choice Experiments
Research Focus: Investigating how LLM-powered software agents make decisions in web-based consumer choice environments when exposed to psychological nudges, price gaps, ratings, and order manipulations.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Used ABXLAB (a man-in-the-middle web intervention platform derived from Agent-Lab and WebArena) on OneStopMarket across 17 SOTA LLMs (over 80,000 trials, 2.5B tokens). Evaluated binary forced choice (2AFC) product selection under original, matched rating (MR), matched rating & price (MRaP) conditions, explicit user profile preferences, and human baselines (30 participants).
Key Findings: LLM agents exhibit strong, systematic biases dwarfing human responses (e.g., preference shifts up to 90+ pp for ratings, order, or nudges vs. ~4-10 pp in humans). When ratings/prices are matched, simple nudges (e.g., Wirecutter top pick, BOGO) dominate agent choices (+10 to +60 pp). Explicit user profiles act like binary threshold switches suppressing competing attributes.
Author-Stated Limitations: Focuses on binary forced choices with controlled textual nudges rather than larger/multimodal choice sets; restricted to one domain (e.g., consumer shopping on OneStopMarket); pairing and filtering rules simplify real-world heterogeneity.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks investigation into multi-step interactive navigation traps or active counter-defenses by agents against adversarial choice architectures; ignores visual/multimodal nudge dynamics.
Internal Contradictions: Chain-of-thought (CoT) and memory streams collected from agents failed to clearly reflect the underlying hierarchical decision rules (rating -> price -> nudge) established by causal experimental trials.
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Not in source
Missing Controls/Confounders: Potential CoT unfaithfulness; LLM-as-a-judge bias in evaluating thought/memory streams; non-commensurable economic rationality when presenting BOGO incentives on durable goods.
Untested Scenarios: Sustained multi-turn search with dynamic inventory changes; active adversarial agent tools for detecting web manipulations; choice sets with >3 options under matched conditions.
Proposed Research Questions: How do agent deliberation styles and time horizons interact with susceptibility to choice architecture manipulations in real-time environments?

Paper: INJECAGENT: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
Research Focus: Evaluating the vulnerability of tool-integrated Large Language Model (LLM) agents to Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) attacks across various functional domains.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Benchmarked 30 LLM agents using INJECAGENT (1,054 test cases covering 17 user tools and 62 attacker tools across finance, smart home, email, and social media domains). Evaluated prompted agents (ReAct frame) and fine-tuned agents under base and enhanced ('hacking prompt') settings using Attack Success Rate (ASR-valid).
Key Findings: Prompted LLM agents are highly vulnerable to IPI attacks (e.g., ReAct-prompted GPT-4 achieved 24% ASR in base setting and 47% in enhanced setting; ReAct Llama2-70B exceeded 80% ASR). Fine-tuned agents displayed greater resilience (fine-tuned GPT-4 achieved 7.1% ASR in enhanced setting). User case parameters/content freedom exhibited a stronger statistical correlation with attack success than attacker cases.
Author-Stated Limitations: Fixed/pre-defined hacking prompts used without evaluating diverse prompt injection techniques; limited evaluation of complex multi-turn or multi-step attacker instructions; assumption that external content only contains malicious instructions rather than mixed benign/malicious content; limited scope of fine-tuned models evaluated due to availability.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of dynamic, multi-turn defense and evaluation mechanisms for tool-integrated agents operating in continuous environments; insufficient investigation into non-promoted multi-modal injection vectors.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While StruQ (Chen et al., 2024) asserts near-zero vulnerability (<2% ASR) against manual IPI attacks via structured instruction tuning and front-end delimiters, INJECAGENT shows that safety/security instructions within system prompts (ReAct) fail to protect agents, highlighting that system-level ReAct security prompts do not equate to structural data-control separation.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation did not control for varying system message lengths, token window positioning, or system-level content-filtering safety layers applied outside the LLM agent framework.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-turn user-agent interactions; indirect prompt injections embedded within mixed context (interspersed benign and malicious text); adaptive/optimized adversarial attacks (e.g., GCG or TAP) against tool-integrated agents.
Proposed Research Questions: How do fine-tuned tool-calling LLMs hold up against optimization-based adversarial injections (e.g., GCG) within tool responses? Can multi-turn dialog context dilute or exacerbate the success rate of indirect prompt injections?

Paper: StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries
Research Focus: Defending LLM-integrated applications against prompt injection attacks by enforcing a structural separation of instruction (prompt) and data via structured queries.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Developed StruQ, combining a secure front-end (formatting prompts/data with special reserved tokens and recursive filtering) and a fine-tuned LLM using 'structured instruction tuning'. Evaluated on Llama-7B and Mistral-7B across 15+ manual and optimization-based prompt injection attack types (e.g., GCG, TAP, HackAPrompt) and measured utility using AlpacaEval 1.0.
Key Findings: StruQ reduced manual attack success rates from up to 96% down to <2% with virtually no loss in utility on AlpacaEval. For optimization-based attacks, StruQ reduced TAP attack success rates on Llama from 97% to 9% and GCG from 97% to 58%.
Author-Stated Limitations: StruQ is limited to programmatic applications (APIs) and cannot be directly applied to open-ended, multi-turn conversational chatbots without user interaction friction. It remains partially vulnerable to computationally expensive optimization-based attacks like GCG (58% ASR) and TAP (9% ASR).
Inferred Research Gaps: Inability to completely mitigate white-box gradient-based adversarial suffix attacks (GCG) without introducing severe utility loss or non-differentiable execution layers.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: BIPIA (Yi et al., 2023) reported strong injection defense using standard delimiter tuning, whereas StruQ demonstrated that BIPIA fails to generalize to unseen instruction sets (suffering 54% ASR on standard benchmark datasets) due to overfitting and lack of front-end delimiter filtering.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Did not evaluate performance impact or attack resistance under dynamic system-prompt modifications or real-time variable-length user context windows.
Untested Scenarios: Application to agentic frameworks requiring multi-step tool execution, autonomous loop interactions, or multi-modal prompt inputs.
Proposed Research Questions: Can input/attention masking between prompt and data tokens during pre-training eliminate susceptibility to white-box gradient-based injections (GCG) without requiring test-time front-end filters?

Paper: DoomArena: A Framework for Testing AI Agents Against Evolving Security Threats
Research Focus: Developing a modular, plug-in evaluation framework to conduct dynamic, stateful, and fine-grained multi-threat security evaluations of AI agents across diverse domains (web, tool-use, computer OS).
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Tested frontier LLM agents (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, GPT-4o-mini) across 3 environments: τ-Bench (airline/retail tool calling), BrowserGym/WebArena (Reddit/Shopping web tasks), and OSWorld (39 desktop tasks). Evaluated multiple threat models (malicious user, malicious catalog/banners/pop-ups, combined attacks) and defenses (LlamaGuard, GPT-4o judge). Calculated ASR, TSR (with/without attack), and Stealth Rate over 3 trials.
Key Findings: Frontier agents exhibit model-dependent vulnerabilities with no single Pareto-dominant model across all threat models. 2) Combined attacks interact constructively/destructively, significantly reducing TSR and boosting ASR. 3) Rule/classifier defenses (LlamaGuard) fail against indirect prompt injections (0% detection), while LLM-as-a-judge defenses (GPT-4o) reduce ASR substantially but degrade utility and remain vulnerable to complex attacks.
Author-Stated Limitations: The framework focuses on inference-time attacks and does not natively implement training-time attacks (though environment triggers can be injected); it leaves data minimization/governance to the testing team and relies on user-provided attack gateway wrappers.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of automated dynamic attack discovery (relies on predefined attack libraries/agents); unexamined resource consumption overheads (latency/token usage) caused by multi-turn attack iterations; absence of adaptive human-in-the-loop recovery mechanisms when an agent's task is aborted by guardrails.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: While Task Shield (Jia et al.) argues that LLM-based test-time verification can defend against indirect injections without task failure, DoomArena demonstrates that LLM-as-a-judge defenses cause significant task execution drops (TSR drops) or complete task aborts upon detecting attacks.
Missing Controls/Confounders: Lacks systemic measurement of token budget consumption and latency delays induced by guardrail LLM judges during episode execution.
Untested Scenarios: Evaluation of multimodal web agents (text-only accessibility tree agents were primarily evaluated in BrowserGym); complex multi-agent collaborative workflows; long-horizon agent execution traps leading to resource exhaustion.
Proposed Research Questions: How can agentic systems automatically recover and complete primary tasks after encountering and aborting malicious injections detected by LLM guardrails without entering infinite execution loops?

Paper: PlanGuard: Defending Agents against Indirect Prompt Injection via Planning-based Consistency Verification
Research Focus: Execution-level defense against Actionable Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in LLM agents.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated using DeepSeek-V3.2 backbone under compliance-inducing prompts on the InjecAgent benchmark (1,054 test cases, 17 user tools, 62 attacker tools across Direct Harm and Data Stealing scenarios). Uses a two-stage verifier (Hard Rules + LLM-based Intent Verifier).
Key Findings: Achieved 0.0% Attack Success Rate (ASR) across all test cases. Reduced False Positive Rate (FPR) from 27.0%/38.01% (Stage I only) to 0.97%/3.28% (Full PlanGuard) on DH and DS subsets respectively.
Author-Stated Limitations: Incurs additional computational/token overhead from extra LLM inferences (Isolated Planner and Stage II Verifier). Struggles with Context-Dependent Argument Hijacking due to information asymmetry (Isolated Planner lacks access to external contexts to verify implicit parameter ground truths).
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluation against multi-step, adaptive prompt injection attacks; reliance on general-purpose LLMs rather than specialized lightweight models for intent verification.

Cross-Paper Contradictions: Not in source
Missing Controls/Confounders: Evaluation under natural (non-compliance-inducing) prompts to assess baseline alignment interactions was omitted.
Untested Scenarios: Performance under highly complex multi-turn workflows, non-English prompts, or real-time web browsing environments with dynamic API schema changes.
Proposed Research Questions: How can specialized Small Language Models (SLMs) replace general-purpose LLM verifiers to reduce latency while preserving zero-ASR security guarantees?
Supporting Citations: Zhan et al. (2024) InjecAgent benchmark

Paper: Hidden in Memory: Sleeper Memory Poisoning in LLM Agents
Research Focus: Sleeper memory poisoning attacks against stateful, memory-augmented LLM assistants.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Evaluated a three-stage attack pipeline (injection, retrieval, adversarial usage) across 6 models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek v4 Pro) in tool-based and external-manager regimes using 700 injection samples (500 LLM Behavior, 200 Agent Action) and 400 post-injection samples. Tested 4 prompt-based defenses and 1 scanner defense.
Key Findings: Universal actor-critic payloads achieved up to 99.8% injection on GPT-5.5. Successfully retrieved memories induced attacker-intended actions in 60-89% of goal-adjacent agentic evaluations across models. Prompt-based defenses were brittle against adaptive attacks (AC+), though activation probes achieved high AUROC (>0.95) for detection.
Author-Stated Limitations: Relies on an LLM judge for post-injection evaluation; provider-specific memory pipelines are only partially observable (relying on leaked/reconstructed prompts); evaluates single-document threat models rather than multi-document compound attacks; does not systematically test memory editing/deletion as defenses.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of evaluations on multi-turn compound poisoning or memory deletion/correction mechanics; missing investigation into real-time defense mechanisms within external memory managers like Mem0.
Internal Contradictions: Not in source
Cross-Paper Contradictions: Not in source
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for potential latent memory interference or long-horizon context rot across extensive multi-session interactions.
Untested Scenarios: Multi-document/compound exposures, multi-turn iterative injections, and explicit user-driven memory correction or deletion workflows.
Proposed Research Questions: How can memory management architectures detect and sanitize dormant adversarial injections without compromising legitimate personalization state?

Paper: Honeyval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for LLM-powered HTTP Honeypots
Research Focus: Standardized evaluation of LLM-powered HTTP honeypots using autonomous hacking agents.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Grounded on 16 backend web application APIs from BaxBench. Evaluated 5 cost-efficient LLM honeypot backends (Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen 3.5 9B, GPT 5.4 Nano) against 4 hacking agents (ReActAgent with 2 backends, Claude Code, Gemini CLI) across main and control tasks.
Key Findings: LLM honeypots sustained significantly longer interactions than rule-based mocks (~82.6 vs 30.6 requests) and maintained low detection rates (<40% in most setups) while preserving a running cost advantage over agentic attackers.
Author-Stated Limitations: Relies on a naive full-context honeypot harness; scope is restricted to 16 HTTP REST applications without coverage of shell/OS-level honeypots; high response latency in current LLMs remains a detectable signal.
Inferred Research Gaps: Missing evaluations on stateful, long-horizon multi-protocol honeypot setups and automated anti-fingerprinting response caching.

Cross-Paper Contradictions: Not in source
Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for network-layer latency discrepancies or server fingerprinting outside HTTP payload bodies.
Untested Scenarios: High-throughput concurrent attacker traffic, shell/SSH command simulation, and complex enterprise microservice architectures.
Proposed Research Questions: Can distilled, ultra-low-latency LLMs simulate complex REST APIs without leaking timing side-channels to AI hacking agents?

Paper: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
Research Focus: Creating a realistic, reproducible, and standalone web environment for benchmarking web-based autonomous agents.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Built an environment featuring 4 web applications (E-commerce, Social Forum, GitLab, CMS) alongside maps, tools, and Wikipedia. Evaluated LLM-based agents (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Text-Bison-001) using direct and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting across 812 task instructions with programmatic functional correctness validation.
Key Findings: SOTA agents struggled significantly on complex web tasks: the best GPT-4 agent achieved an end-to-end success rate of only 14.41% (11.70% with unachievable hint), far below the human baseline of 78.24%. Subtle prompt variations (e.g., unachievable instructions) caused high rates of false-positive early stopping.
Author-Stated Limitations: Environment reset requires restarting Docker containers; accessibility trees and viewports truncate lengthy contexts; relies on few-shot prompting without explicit long-term memory architectures.
Inferred Research Gaps: Unexplored integration of active exploration, long-term state tracking, and autonomous error recovery mechanisms for web agents.

Missing Controls/Confounders: Does not control for visual/modal context loss when relying strictly on text-based accessibility trees vs visual screenshots.
Untested Scenarios: Adversarial web navigation traps, prompt injection embedded in web DOMs, and persistent agent workflows across multi-day sessions.
Proposed Research Questions: How can autonomous web agents develop robust long-horizon planning and self-correction to bridge the 63%+ gap with human performance?

Paper: Denial of wallet—Defining a looming threat to serverless computing
Research Focus: Defining, modeling, and quantifying Denial of Wallet (DoW) attacks—forced financial exhaustion targeting pay-as-you-go serverless/FaaS architectures.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Created an isolated serverless testbed using OpenFaaS, Apache, ModSecurity WAF, and Snort IPS across a 4-PC network setup. Built a Python-based Serverless Platform Pricing Emulator to calculate cost damage across AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions, and IBM Cloud Functions using real platform pricing models under LOIC HTTP floods and image parameter exploitation.
Key Findings: Traditional DoS mitigations (e.g., WAF rate-limiting) fail against long-time-span, slow-rate 'leech' attacks or parameter exploitation (e.g., sending high-res images to thumbnail functions). A modest botnet of 1,000 nodes running slow-rate requests can incur ~ $40,000/month or >$ 400,000/year in unchecked cloud execution charges.
Author-Stated Limitations: Absence of real-world historical DoW attack data requires relying on simulated attack models and synthetic workloads.
Inferred Research Gaps: Lacks empirical evaluation of automated detection algorithms (e.g., graph-based Sybil detection or RL-based traffic anomaly monitoring) inside live FaaS auto-scaling loops.

Proposed Research Questions: What runtime telemetry signals best distinguish benign usage surges from stealthy, low-rate DoW leech attacks before budget exhaustion?

Paper: WebGPT: Browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback
Research Focus: Training LLMs to perform long-form question answering (LFQA) by interacting with a text-based web browsing environment and leveraging human feedback.
Methodology/Experimental Scope: Fine-tuned GPT-3 models (760M, 13B, 175B) using Behavior Cloning (BC) on human web-browsing demonstrations, Reward Modeling (RM) on human preference comparisons, Reinforcement Learning (PPO), and Rejection Sampling (Best-of-n). Evaluated performance on ELI5, TruthfulQA, and TriviaQA datasets.
Key Findings: WebGPT 175B Best-of-64 model responses were preferred 56% of the time over human demonstrator answers and 69% over top Reddit ELI5 answers. WebGPT outperformed base GPT-3 on TruthfulQA (75% true, 54% true and informative). Rejection sampling provided greater performance gains than PPO reinforcement learning alone.
Author-Stated Limitations: WebGPT occasionally produces non-imitative falsehoods (paraphrasing/synthesis errors) and quotes from unreliable sources when encountering out-of-distribution questions; susceptibility to reinforcement of human/query stance bias and confirmation bias; potential for overreliance due to authoritative tone and citations ('automation bias').
Inferred Research Gaps: Lack of defensive constraints or sanitization mechanisms against untrusted web page content, exposing browser-assisted agents to potential indirect prompt injection attacks.

Missing Controls/Confounders: Comparison with Reddit baseline answers was unblinded regarding stylistic variations, which could confound human labeler preferences.

Proposed Research Questions: How can browser-assisted agents distinguish factual web references from malicious adversarial injections embedded in retrieved web page snippets?
